meta.title: Gītā Companion
meta.about: The verse text is a fresh study translation of the 700-verse standard text of the Bhagavad Gītā (Mahābhārata, Bhīṣma Parvan 23–40). Key Sanskrit terms appear in brackets, and translator's notes (✦) mark genuine ambiguities in the Sanskrit. The introduction, study footnotes (†), analyses, diagrams, questions and glossary were written for this companion. They draw on the classical commentators (Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, Madhva, Abhinavagupta, Jñāneśvara) and on modern scholarship.

intro.title: Entering the Gītā
intro.lede: What a serious reader needs before the first verse: the text and its setting, the problem it addresses, the inherited ideas it works with, the frameworks through which it has been read, and the questions scholars still argue over.

sections.title: Why read the Gītā, and how
paras: The *Bhagavad Gītā*, "the Song of the Blessed One," is seven hundred verses long, about the length of a short novella. It has probably been commented on, translated and argued over more than any other Indian text. It has been called the essence of the Vedas, a gospel of action, a manual of meditation, a hymn of devotion, a defense of caste, an allegory of the inner war, and a justification of violence. Each of these readings has a foothold in the text. That is one reason the Gītā rewards slow, serious study. The best way to read it is as what it presents itself to be: a dialogue at a moment of crisis. A man who must act cannot. His teacher does not give him a rule but walks him, step by step, through a sequence of arguments. Each argument answers the last objection and opens a deeper question. The Gītā is less a treatise than a course of instruction. Its claims are pitched at different levels, and later teachings qualify earlier ones. A verse read out of its place in that sequence can mean almost the opposite of what it means within it. This companion therefore keeps the order of the text but adds layers you can open as needed. These are footnotes on difficult verses, a **reconstruction** of each section's argument in its own terms, an **analysis** of its structure and tensions, its **sources**, its place in the **wider conversation** of philosophy and religion, and **questions** for discussion. A good first reading is simply the verses with the footnotes. A second reading is the study panels. A third is your own notes.

sections.title: The text: place, date and form
paras: The Gītā is not a free-standing book. It forms Chapters 23–40 of the *Bhīṣma Parvan*, the sixth of the eighteen books of the [[Mahābhārata]]. It is spoken on the first morning of the great war, as the armies face each other at [[Kurukṣetra]]. The blind king [[Dhṛtarāṣṭra]] asks his charioteer [[Sañjaya]], who has been given divine sight, what happened. The whole dialogue between [[Kṛṣṇa]] and [[Arjuna]] is Sañjaya's report. Dating is uncertain. Most scholars place the composition of the Gītā somewhere between the 2nd century BCE and the 1st century CE, with the epic itself growing over a longer period (c. 400 BCE–400 CE). Arguments for dating rely on its relation to the Upaniṣads (which it quotes), to early Buddhism (whose word *nirvāṇa* it adopts), to the classical systems of Sāṅkhya and Yoga (whose vocabulary it uses in pre-systematic form), and to the rise of devotional worship of Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa, attested in inscriptions from the 2nd century BCE (for instance the Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar, c. 110 BCE). Was the Gītā always part of the epic, or inserted later? Nineteenth- and early twentieth-century German scholars (Richard Garbe, Rudolf Otto and others) tried to peel the text into an "original" core and later "interpolations," usually a theistic or Vedāntic layer added to an older heroic or Sāṅkhya poem. More recent scholarship (Angelika Malinar, James Fitzgerald, Alf Hiltebeitel, and the critique of German Indology by Vishwa Adluri and Joydeep Bagchee) has been sceptical of these reconstructions. It reads the Gītā as a deliberately composed whole, written with the epic in view. This companion follows that approach: the text is read as it stands. The Gītā is written in the *anuṣṭubh* (*śloka*) meter, with longer *triṣṭubh* stanzas at moments of heightened intensity, above all in the vision of Chapter 11. Each chapter ends with a colophon calling the Gītā an *upaniṣad*, a "science of brahman" and a "scripture of yoga." The 700-verse text is the one Śaṅkara commented on in the 8th century. A slightly longer Kashmir recension, used by Abhinavagupta, differs in a few verses.

sections.title: The epic setting: the war and its people
paras: The Mahābhārata tells of a dynastic feud. Two brothers, the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu, have sons. Dhṛtarāṣṭra's hundred sons, the [[Kauravas]] led by [[Duryodhana]], refuse to share the kingdom with Pāṇḍu's five sons, the [[Pāṇḍavas]]. The Pāṇḍavas are cheated at dice, their shared wife Draupadī is humiliated in the assembly hall, and they are sent into thirteen years of exile. When they return and ask for their share, even five villages, Duryodhana refuses. War follows, and nearly every warrior in India is drawn in on one side or the other. The war is a war among kin. On the Kaurava side stand [[Bhīṣma]], great-uncle to both parties, and [[Droṇa]], who taught them all to fight. With them is [[Karṇa]], who is secretly the Pāṇḍavas' eldest brother. Kṛṣṇa, cousin and friend to the Pāṇḍavas, has refused to bear arms but agreed to drive Arjuna's chariot. That situation is the Gītā's point of departure. The enemy is one's own family, the cause is just but the cost is monstrous, and the person beside you is God. It matters that the Gītā comes at the *beginning* of the war. Everything that follows in the epic tests what it teaches: the deaths of Bhīṣma, Droṇa and Karṇa (each by a stratagem Kṛṣṇa advises), the near-extermination of both sides, and the joyless victory. The epic does not let the Gītā's answers go unchallenged. Readers who know only the Gītā miss this dialogue between the teaching and its aftermath.

sections.title: Arjuna's dilemma: the problem of action
paras: Arjuna's objections in Chapter 1 are not cowardice, though Kṛṣṇa first treats them so. They are a set of serious moral arguments. Killing kin brings evil {1.36}. It destroys the family's ritual and moral order {1.40}. That leads to social chaos and the ruin of the ancestors {1.41–42}. Winning a kingdom is worthless if those one wanted to share it with are dead {1.32–33}. Better to die unresisting {1.46}. Philosophers have recognized here a genuine *moral dilemma*, a situation in which every option violates a serious obligation. Arjuna's duty as a warrior to fight a just war collides with his duty to family and teachers. Amartya Sen has argued that Arjuna's consequence-sensitive reasoning deserves more respect than the tradition has given it. Bimal Krishna Matilal used the episode to show that classical Indian thought took moral conflict seriously. In Arjuna's own words his mind is "confused about dharma" {2.7}. Beneath the moral dilemma lies a metaphysical one. In the world the Gītā inherits, *all* action binds. Every deed produces fruits that must be reaped, in this life or another, keeping the agent on the wheel of rebirth. The obvious way out, taken by many renunciant movements of the time (Upaniṣadic, Buddhist, Jain), was to withdraw from action as far as possible. Arjuna's "I will not fight" {2.9} sounds like that renunciant's answer. Kṛṣṇa's task is to show that withdrawal is neither possible {3.5} nor the real meaning of renunciation. The real meaning is to act without being bound.

sections.title: The inherited worldview: karma, saṁsāra, mokṣa
paras: Three linked ideas form the background against which the Gītā speaks. **[[karma|Karma]]** first meant ritual action, but by the Upaniṣads it named the moral causality by which actions ripen into consequences. **[[saṁsāra|Saṁsāra]]** is the round of birth and death those consequences sustain. **[[mokṣa|Mokṣa]]** (liberation, also called *nirvāṇa*) is release from that round. In this frame, the deepest question is not "what is the right thing to do?" but "how can any doing be compatible with freedom?" The Gītā's distinctive answer is that the binding force lies not in action itself but in *attachment* (*saṅga*) and *desire* (*kāma*) for its fruit. Action done from equanimity, as sacrifice, or as an offering to God, leaves no residue. "Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits" {2.47} is the formula. Alongside this soteriology runs the social order of **[[dharma]]**: the four classes ([[varṇa]]), the stages of life ([[āśrama]]), and the duties proper to each. The aims of life ([[puruṣārtha]]) are dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation. Much of the Gītā's originality lies in holding together the world-affirming order of dharma and the world-transcending goal of liberation, which other traditions set at odds.

sections.title: Sāṅkhya: nature, person and the three guṇas
paras: **[[Sāṅkhya]]** ("enumeration") supplies the Gītā's psychology and much of its cosmology. Reality has two irreducible principles. **[[puruṣa|Puruṣa]]**, the "person," is pure consciousness: inactive, unchanging, a witness. **[[prakṛti|Prakṛti]]**, "nature," is everything else. It is the dynamic matrix that evolves into understanding (*buddhi*), I-making (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*manas*), the senses, and the elements. Nature is woven from three strands, the **[[guṇa|guṇas]]**. **Sattva** is clarity, lightness and goodness. **Rajas** is passion, activity and craving. **Tamas** is darkness, inertia and delusion. Every thing, act and state is a mixture of the three. Chapters 14, 17 and 18 use this scheme to classify knowledge, action, agents, faith, food, gifts and happiness. The key Sāṅkhya insight for the Gītā is that *all action belongs to nature*. "Actions are performed in every case by the guṇas of nature, but one deluded by I-making thinks, 'I am the doer'" {3.27}. Bondage is the self's mistaken identification with nature's activity. Freedom begins with seeing that the self is not the agent. The Gītā's Sāṅkhya, however, is not yet the atheistic classical system of Īśvarakṛṣṇa's *Sāṅkhya-kārikā*. It is theistic. Nature is God's nature, and both principles are his "lower" and "higher" natures {7.4–5}.

sections.title: Upaniṣadic background: ātman and brahman
paras: The [[Upaniṣad|Upaniṣads]] taught that the innermost **self** ([[ātman]]) is unborn and undying, and that the **absolute** ([[brahman]]) underlies all things. The most radical among them taught that the two are one. The Gītā quotes them, especially the [[Kaṭha Upaniṣad]]: the self "is not born, nor does it die" {2.20}; the hierarchy of senses, mind and understanding {3.42}; the inverted world-tree {15.1}. The [[Īśā Upaniṣad]] had already suggested that one could go on acting and live a hundred years, because "action does not cling" to the one who sees the Lord in all. The Gītā develops this into a full doctrine. It also inherits the Upaniṣadic ideal of seeing "all beings in the self and the self in all beings" {6.29}. How the self relates to brahman, and both to the personal God who speaks in the Gītā, is the great question that divides the later Vedānta schools. The text supports more than one answer. It calls brahman "neither being nor non-being" {13.12}, yet has Kṛṣṇa declare himself "the foundation of brahman" {14.27} and the Supreme Person beyond both perishable and imperishable {15.18}.

sections.title: The three yogas and their harmony
paras: "Yoga" in the Gītā means a disciplined way of joining oneself to the highest. Three such ways are usually distinguished. **[[karma-yoga|Karma-yoga]]**, the yoga of action, is doing one's duty without attachment to results. **[[jñāna-yoga|Jñāna-yoga]]**, the yoga of knowledge, is liberating insight into the self. **[[bhakti-yoga|Bhakti-yoga]]**, the yoga of devotion, is loving self-offering to God. A fourth, **[[dhyāna|dhyāna]]** or meditation (Chapter 6), is sometimes added. A traditional division groups the eighteen chapters into three "hexads": 1–6 on action, 7–12 on devotion, 13–18 on knowledge. It is a useful map (see the diagram above), though each theme appears throughout. Which yoga is highest? Here the commentators part ways. For Śaṅkara, knowledge alone liberates, and action and devotion prepare the mind for it. For Rāmānuja, devotion is the culmination, with knowledge and action as its supports. For Tilak, selfless action for the world is the Gītā's final word. Vivekananda saw the Gītā's originality precisely in *harmonizing* paths that rival schools had set against each other. A careful reader will notice that the text itself tends to say "both" where we expect "either/or": "Children, not the wise, speak of Sāṅkhya and yoga as different" {5.4}.

sections.title: The God of the Gītā
paras: The speaker of the Gītā gradually reveals himself. First he is a friend and charioteer. Then he is the teacher of an ancient yoga {4.1}. Then he is the one who takes birth "age after age" to restore dharma {4.7–8}, the source and dissolution of the whole world {7.6}, and the one in whom all beings rest, though he does not rest in them {9.4–5}. Finally, in Chapter 11, he appears as the terrifying universal form, "time, the destroyer of worlds" {11.32}. This God is both immanent and transcendent. He is "the taste in water, the light in sun and moon" {7.8}, "seated in the heart of all" {15.15}, yet "greater even than Brahmā" {11.37}. He is impartial, "no one is hateful to me, and no one is dear" {9.29}, yet loving: "you are dear to me" {18.65}. And he acts. "There is nothing I need to do, yet I continue in action" {3.22}. God himself is the model of the karma-yogin. The Gītā's theology has been called *panentheism*: all is in God, but God is more than all. Its emphasis on grace ([[prasāda]]) and on devotion ([[bhakti]]) made it the charter text of the great devotional movements of medieval India.

sections.title: Ethical frameworks: duty, consequences, character
paras: Readers trained in Western moral philosophy often try to place the Gītā within its categories. It invites comparison with **deontology**: do your duty because it is your duty, "because it ought to be done" {18.9}. Kant's "duty for duty's sake" is the obvious parallel. It invites comparison with **virtue ethics**: the long portraits of the sage {2.55–72}, the devotee {12.13–20}, and the divine qualities {16.1–3} describe a character rather than a rule. Its insistence that the agent give up concern for outcomes seems to set it against **consequentialism**, though Kṛṣṇa also appeals to consequences: disgrace {2.34}, and the world's cohesion ([[loka-saṅgraha]]) {3.20}. Perhaps the Gītā's most original contribution is to the ethics of **agency and motivation**. It asks not only what to do but from where to act. An act done from fear, greed or the ego's need to win differs from the same act done from equanimity. The text even claims that one free of I-making "does not kill and is not bound, even if he kills" {18.17}. This is among the most contested claims in the text, because it seems to remove the agent from moral responsibility. Any serious reading must also face the Gītā's **social ethics**: its acceptance of the four social orders ([[varṇa]]), its fear of their "mixing" {1.41}, and its statement that one should do one's own duty even if flawed {18.47–48}. B. R. Ambedkar read the Gītā as a defense of caste. Many modern readers reinterpret its categories as temperament and vocation. Both responses should be weighed honestly.

sections.title: Commentators and the history of reading
paras: Because the Gītā is one of the three foundations (*prasthāna-traya*) of Vedānta, with the Upaniṣads and the *Brahma-sūtra*, every major Vedāntic teacher wrote on it. **[[Śaṅkara]]** (8th c.) gives the oldest surviving commentary and the Advaita reading. **[[Rāmānuja]]** (11th–12th c.) gives the qualified non-dualist reading centered on devotion. **[[Madhva]]** (13th c.) gives the dualist reading. Outside Vedānta, **[[Abhinavagupta]]** (10th–11th c.) read it as a Kashmir Śaiva, and the Marathi poet **[[Jñāneśvara]]** (13th c.) turned it into a vernacular masterpiece of devotional non-dualism. Later commentators include Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (16th c.), who tried to reconcile Advaita with fervent devotion, and Viśvanātha Cakravartin and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa of the Bengal Vaiṣṇava tradition. That tradition's modern descendant, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda's *Bhagavad-gītā As It Is* (1968), is one of the most widely distributed books in the world. Reading the commentaries side by side is the best training in interpretation. The same verse is made to say "renounce all action," "act without attachment," or "surrender to God," often by small differences of syntax or emphasis. The translator's notes (✦) in this companion flag such places.

sections.title: The modern Gītā: nation, non-violence and the West
paras: The Gītā's modern career is a story of its own. Charles Wilkins's English translation (1785) introduced it to Europe. Warren Hastings's preface predicted that it would survive when British rule was forgotten. Schlegel and Humboldt admired it, and Humboldt called it perhaps "the deepest and loftiest thing the world has to show." Emerson and Thoreau read it at Walden. In India it became the scripture of the independence movement. **[[Tilak]]** read it as a call to selfless political action. **[[Aurobindo]]** read it, from prison, as a spiritual synthesis. **[[Gandhi]]**, its most famous modern devotee, called it his "spiritual dictionary" and read its war as the inner battle against selfishness, in harmony with non-violence. **[[Vivekananda]]** presented it as a philosophy of strength and of work without selfish motive. Its influence also reached unexpected places. T. S. Eliot paraphrased it in *Four Quartets* ("And do not think of the fruit of action. Fare forward."). J. Robert Oppenheimer, who read it in Sanskrit, recalled {11.12} and {11.32} at the first atomic test. In our own century it shapes discussions of leadership, mindfulness and work, often in popular forms that trim away its theology and its violence.

sections.title: Current scholarship and open questions
paras: Several debates are live today. **Composition and unity**: is the Gītā a layered text or a unified composition, and how does it relate to the rest of the Mahābhārata? (Malinar, *The Bhagavadgītā: Doctrines and Contexts*, 2007; Adluri and Bagchee, *The Nay Science*, 2014.) **Religious context**: how does it respond to Buddhism and to renunciant movements, and to the ritualism of Vedic orthodoxy? **Theology**: is its final teaching non-dual, theistic, or deliberately both? (Chakravarthi Ram-Prasad, *Divine Self, Human Self*, 2013.) **Ethics and violence**: can a text that urges a warrior to fight ground an ethic of non-violence? How should its claims about agency and responsibility be judged? (Sen, *The Idea of Justice*, 2009; Matilal, *Ethics and Epics*, 2002.) **Caste and gender**: are its social categories essential or historical? **Reception**: how did the Gītā become *the* Hindu scripture in the 19th and 20th centuries? (Richard H. Davis, *The Bhagavad Gita: A Biography*, 2015.) Psychologists have also built empirical measures of "non-attachment" (*anāsakti*) and of the guṇas, and studied their relation to wellbeing. This work is promising but early. These debates are flagged in each chapter's "Current research" panel. They are invitations to think, not settled verdicts.

sections.title: Using this companion
paras: Each chapter opens with a summary, an overview and a concept map. The chapter is then divided into sections that follow its argument (based on the traditional synopsis of the Gītā Press edition). Each section gives the verses, then its study panels. Tap any underlined term for a definition. Select text to highlight it in one of five colors, or attach a note. Tap a verse number to highlight the whole verse or add a note to it. In diagrams, use the Highlight button to color boxes. Everything you mark is gathered in **My notes**, organized by chapter and section and searchable. **Search** looks across the verses, footnotes, analysis, glossary and your own notes at once. A suggestion for book clubs: read one chapter aloud together, then take two or three discussion questions from the sections and one from the chapter's seminar questions.

nodes.label: Crisis: Arjuna cannot act (Ch. 1–2.10)
nodes.text: A warrior at the moment of decision collapses into grief and moral confusion. The whole Gītā is the answer to this breakdown.

nodes.label: The undying self (2.11–30)
nodes.text: First answer: the self is not killed when the body is killed. Grief rests on a mistake about what we are.

nodes.label: One's own dharma (2.31–38)
nodes.text: Second answer: as a warrior, your duty is to fight a just battle.

nodes.label: Hexad I (Ch. 1–6): the yoga of action
nodes.text: Chapters 1–6 teach how to act without being bound: equanimity, non-attachment, sacrifice, meditation. Madhusūdana Sarasvatī and others group these six chapters as the hexad of action.

nodes.label: Hexad II (Ch. 7–12): God and devotion
nodes.text: Chapters 7–12 reveal who is speaking: the source of all, glimpsed in the universal form, approached by loving devotion.

nodes.label: Hexad III (Ch. 13–18): knowledge
nodes.text: Chapters 13–18 analyze the field and its knower, the three guṇas and the Supreme Person, and gather everything into the final teaching on renunciation and surrender.

nodes.label: Surrender and resolve (18.66–73)
nodes.text: "Abandon all dharmas and take refuge in me." Arjuna's delusion is gone, and he says, "I will do as you say."

nodes.label: Upaniṣads
nodes.text: Source of the doctrines of ātman and brahman, and of many near-quoted verses.

nodes.label: Sāṅkhya
nodes.text: Source of the categories of nature, person and the three guṇas.

chapters.title: The Yoga of Arjuna's Despair

verses.text: On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus [*dharma-kṣetre kuru-kṣetre*], gathered together and eager to fight, what did my sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu do, Sañjaya?
verses.speaker: Dhṛtarāṣṭra
fnotes: *Dharma-kṣetre kuru-kṣetre*: the opening words pair a moral field with a geographical one. Commentators note that the Gītā's first word is *dharma* and its last (18.78) is *mama*, "my" ("in my opinion"). Some read the whole text as framed between the cosmic order and a personal judgment. Dhṛtarāṣṭra's phrase "my sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu" already divides the world into *mine* and *other*, the attachment the Gītā will diagnose.

verses.text: Seeing the army of the Pāṇḍavas drawn up for battle, King Duryodhana then approached his teacher [*ācārya*, Droṇa] and spoke these words:
verses.speaker: Sañjaya
fnotes: Duryodhana goes to Droṇa, not to Bhīṣma, the commander. His words to his teacher are edged with reproach. Droṇa trained Dhṛṣṭadyumna (1.3), the very man born to kill him.

verses.text: "Teacher, look at this great army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, arrayed by the son of Drupada, your own gifted student.
fnotes: The son of Drupada is Dhṛṣṭadyumna, commander of the Pāṇḍava army. According to the epic he was born from a sacrificial fire to kill Droṇa. Duryodhana's "your own gifted student" is a barb.

verses.text: Here are heroes, great archers, equal in battle to Bhīma and Arjuna: Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, a great chariot-warrior;
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the valiant king of Kāśī; Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaibya, a bull among men;
bold Yudhāmanyu and valiant Uttamaujas, the son of Subhadrā, and the sons of Draupadī, all of them great chariot-warriors.
But know also, best of the twice-born, the most distinguished on our side, the leaders of my army. I name them for your information:
fnotes: "Best of the twice-born" (*dvijottama*): Droṇa is a brāhmaṇa who has taken up arms, itself a departure from his class's dharma, which the epic notices.

verses.text: yourself and Bhīṣma, Karṇa and Kṛpa, victorious in battle; Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, and the son of Somadatta;
and many other heroes, ready to give up their lives for my sake, armed with various weapons, all skilled in war.
Our strength, guarded by Bhīṣma, is unlimited [*aparyāptam*]; their strength, guarded by Bhīma, is limited [*paryāptam*].
tnotes: the two words can also mean "insufficient" and "sufficient." Read that way, Duryodhana is privately admitting that his army is weaker. Both readings are old.
fnotes: See the translator's note. If *aparyāptam* means "insufficient," Duryodhana is betraying his anxiety. The two readings make him either boastful or afraid, and both fit his character.

verses.text: So all of you, stationed in your positions along every line of advance, protect Bhīṣma above all."
To bring him joy, the aged grandsire of the Kurus, full of power, roared a lion's roar and blew his conch.
fnotes: Bhīṣma blows his conch "to bring him joy," that is, to cheer Duryodhana. The aged grandsire knows the Kaurava cause is unjust but fights from loyalty to the throne he has sworn to serve.

verses.text: Then conches and kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and horns suddenly sounded, and the noise was tumultuous.
Then, standing in their great chariot yoked to white horses, Mādhava [Kṛṣṇa] and the son of Pāṇḍu [Arjuna] blew their divine conches.
fnotes: The white horses and the great chariot are gifts of the fire-god Agni to Arjuna (*Mahābhārata* 1.216). Kṛṣṇa (Mādhava) blows first: the divine is the first to answer.

verses.text: Hṛṣīkeśa blew Pāñcajanya; Dhanañjaya blew Devadatta; Vṛkodara [Bhīma, "wolf-belly"], of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
fnotes: Each conch has a name. Kṛṣṇa's *Pāñcajanya* was taken from the demon Pañcajana; Arjuna's *Devadatta* means "god-given." Kṛṣṇa is called *Hṛṣīkeśa*, "lord of the senses," an epithet that will become thematic when the senses must be mastered.

verses.text: King Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, blew Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka.
The king of Kāśī, supreme archer, and Śikhaṇḍin, the great chariot-warrior, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Virāṭa and the unconquered Sātyaki,
Drupada and the sons of Draupadī, O lord of the earth, and the strong-armed son of Subhadrā, all blew their conches, each his own.
That uproar, echoing through sky and earth, tore the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
fnotes: The noise "tore the hearts" of the Kauravas: the sound itself is a weapon, a recurring epic motif.

verses.text: Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra drawn up, as the clash of weapons was about to begin, the son of Pāṇḍu, whose banner bears the monkey [Hanumān], raised his bow
fnotes: The "monkey-bannered" one: Hanumān rides on Arjuna's flag, a sign of protection from the Rāmāyaṇa world.

verses.text: and spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa, O lord of the earth. *Arjuna said:* Acyuta, place my chariot between the two armies,
fnotes: Arjuna calls Kṛṣṇa *Acyuta*, "the unfallen, the unshakable," just as he himself is about to be shaken. He *commands* God to drive his chariot. Kṛṣṇa, as charioteer, obeys. The roles are about to reverse.

verses.text: so that I may look over these men standing here eager for battle, and see with whom I must fight in this undertaking of war.
I want to see those who have gathered here ready to fight, wishing to please the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle.
Addressed thus by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa stationed that finest of chariots between the two armies,
verses.speaker: Sañjaya
fnotes: *Guḍākeśa*, "thick-haired" or (by a later etymology) "master of sleep" (*guḍākā* + *īśa*). The epithet is sometimes read ironically here: the one who has conquered sleep is about to be overwhelmed by delusion.

verses.text: in front of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and all the rulers of the earth, and said: "Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled."
fnotes: Kṛṣṇa's first words in the Gītā are only these: "Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled." The single word *Kurūn*, "Kurus," includes both armies, since both descend from Kuru. Some interpreters see it as a deliberate provocation. Kṛṣṇa makes Arjuna look at the enemy as family.

verses.text: There the son of Pṛthā saw, standing in both armies, fathers and grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends,
fnotes: The list (fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends) is the whole web of relationship that constitutes a person in an epic world.

verses.text: fathers-in-law and companions. Seeing all these kinsmen arrayed, the son of Kuntī,
filled with deep pity [*kṛpā*], said in despair [*viṣīdan*]: *Arjuna said:* Kṛṣṇa, seeing my own people here, eager to fight, drawn near,
fnotes: *Kṛpayā parayāviṣṭaḥ*: "filled with deep pity." The word *kṛpā* is ambiguous. It can be noble compassion or weak sentimentality. Kṛṣṇa will diagnose it in 2.2–3 and 2.7 as faintness and weakness of heart. Vivekananda argued that it is tamas wearing the mask of sattva.

verses.text: my limbs give way, my mouth dries up, my body trembles, and my hair stands on end.
fnotes: The symptoms (trembling, dry mouth, hair standing on end, burning skin) are the standard signs of overwhelming emotion in Sanskrit poetics, here in a register of terror and grief. Ironically, the same horripilation (*romaharṣa*) will mark the ecstatic wonder of 11.14 and 18.74.

verses.text: Gāṇḍīva [my bow] slips from my hand, my skin burns, I cannot stand still, and my mind seems to whirl.
I see adverse omens, Keśava, and I foresee no good [*śreyas*] in killing my own people in battle.
I do not want victory, Kṛṣṇa, nor kingship nor pleasures. What use is kingship to us, Govinda, or enjoyments, or even life?
fnotes: Arjuna's argument about the worthlessness of goods anticipates Kṛṣṇa's critique of desire, but from the opposite side. Arjuna renounces the fruit because it would be bitter. Kṛṣṇa will ask him to renounce the fruit even when it is sweet.

verses.text: Those for whose sake we desire kingship, enjoyments, and pleasures stand here in battle, having given up life and wealth:
teachers, fathers, sons, and grandfathers too, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other kinsmen.
I do not wish to kill them, Madhusūdana, even if they kill me. I would not do it even for sovereignty over the three worlds, much less for the earth.
What joy could be ours, Janārdana, after killing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra? Evil [*pāpa*] alone would cling to us for slaying these aggressors [*ātatāyin*].
fnotes: *Ātatāyin*: a legal term for an aggressor (arsonist, poisoner, armed attacker, thief of land or wife). Dharma texts permit killing such a person. Arjuna concedes the Kauravas are aggressors but argues that killing them would still bring evil. Śaṅkara does not dwell on the point, but later commentators debate whether Arjuna is here rejecting a legal permission for moral reasons.

verses.text: So we ought not to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, our own kin. How could we be happy, Mādhava, having killed our own people?
Their minds are overpowered by greed, and they do not see the wrong in destroying a family or the crime in betraying friends.
But why should we not have the sense to turn back from this evil, Janārdana, we who do see the wrong in destroying a family?
When a family is destroyed, its timeless family dharmas perish. When dharma perishes, adharma overcomes the whole family.
When adharma prevails, Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family are corrupted. When the women are corrupted, Vārṣṇeya, the social orders become mixed [*varṇa-saṅkara*].
fnotes: The concern for women's "corruption" and the mixing of classes reflects the patriarchal and hierarchical logic of the dharma texts: lineage depends on control of marriage. Readers should note this frankly rather than explain it away.

verses.text: This mixing leads both the family and its destroyers to hell, for their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water.
fnotes: The *piṇḍa* (rice-ball) and water offerings sustain the ancestors in the afterlife. Without legitimate descendants to make them, the ancestors "fall." The argument links metaphysics, ritual and family.

verses.text: By these wrongs of the family-destroyers, which cause the mixing of social orders, the timeless dharmas of birth-group [*jāti*] and family [*kula*] are destroyed.
For men whose family dharmas are destroyed, Janārdana, a dwelling in hell is certain. So we have heard.
Alas! We are resolved to commit a great evil, ready to kill our own people out of greed for the pleasures of kingship.
If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, were to kill me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me.
Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.
verses.speaker: Sañjaya
fnotes: Arjuna "sank down on the seat of the chariot": the physical posture of refusal. The chapter ends not with a decision but with a collapse.

chapters.summary: On the field of Kurukṣetra the two armies face each other. Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to drive his chariot between them, sees his teachers, kinsmen and friends ready to die, and collapses. He gives four arguments against fighting, lays down his bow and sinks down in grief.
overview: The first chapter is pure narrative and lament, with no teaching from Kṛṣṇa at all. Yet it is indispensable. It sets out the problem that the remaining seventeen chapters must solve, and it shows that problem not as an abstract puzzle but as a breakdown in a particular person at a particular moment. The chapter moves in a tightening spiral. It opens wide, with a blind king asking a seer what is happening, then the enemy commander listing champions, then the roar of conches. It narrows to Arjuna's chariot between the armies, then to what Arjuna sees, and finally to Arjuna's own trembling body and his collapse. The structure enacts the way a public crisis becomes a private one. Arjuna's arguments deserve to be taken seriously, and much modern scholarship does. He reasons from consequences (no good can come of killing kin), from the moral order of the family and its dharma, from the logic of desire (what is a kingdom without those to share it with?), and from a principle of non-resistance. Kṛṣṇa will not refute these arguments directly. He will change the level at which the question is asked.
research: Scholars disagree on how to judge Arjuna. The commentarial tradition (Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja) treats his arguments as delusion (*moha*) produced by attachment, and the chapter's title, *viṣāda*, "despair," supports this. Modern moral philosophers have been more sympathetic. Amartya Sen (*The Idea of Justice*, 2009) argues that Arjuna's attention to the actual consequences of war, the *nyāya* or realized outcomes as opposed to the *nīti* or rules, is a serious ethical position that Kṛṣṇa's duty-based reply does not simply defeat. B. K. Matilal (*Ethics and Epics*) reads Chapter 1 as one of the classic expressions of genuine moral dilemma. Literary scholars stress that the Gītā's frame matters. The story is told by Sañjaya to a blind father who cannot stop the war. Alf Hiltebeitel and others read the chapter in the light of the epic's larger concern with dharma's "subtlety." Recent work on emotion in Sanskrit literature has also looked at the chapter's bodily rendering of grief (trembling, dry mouth, horripilation), which the aesthetic tradition associates with the pathetic mood (*karuṇa rasa*).
questions: Arjuna's arguments appeal to consequences, social order, the value of goods, and non-resistance. Which is strongest? Which would Kṛṣṇa find easiest to answer?
Why might the Gītā begin with a chapter in which the teacher says nothing? What does the reader learn from watching the collapse before any answer is given?
Duryodhana and Arjuna both survey the opposing army. Compare what each sees and what that reveals about them.
Is Arjuna's despair a moral achievement (he sees what others miss) or a moral failure (he loses his nerve)? Can it be both?

nodes.label: The field of dharma
nodes.text: The war is set "on the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus." The double name makes the battlefield a moral arena from the first line.

nodes.label: Kaurava army
nodes.text: Led by Duryodhana, anxious and boastful, relying on Bhīṣma.

nodes.label: Pāṇḍava army
nodes.text: Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna blow divine conches; the sound tears the hearts of the other side.

nodes.label: Arjuna sees his own people
nodes.text: Between the armies he sees fathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons and friends.

nodes.label: Bodily collapse
nodes.text: Limbs fail, mouth dries, the bow slips. The crisis is physical before it is argued.

nodes.label: No good in killing kin
nodes.text: A consequence argument: victory and pleasures are worthless at this price, and evil would cling to us.

nodes.label: Family dharma will collapse
nodes.text: A social-order argument: destroying families destroys the dharma that holds society and the ancestors together.

nodes.label: Better to die unresisting
nodes.text: Arjuna concludes he would rather be killed unarmed than fight.

nodes.label: Mixing of social orders
nodes.text: Arjuna's chain of feared consequences: lawlessness, corrupted women, mixed orders, fallen ancestors.

nodes.label: They are blinded by greed; we are not
nodes.text: An asymmetry argument: the enemy's wrong does not license ours.

sections.title: The blind king's question and Duryodhana's review of the armies
sections.lead: The frame is set. A blind king asks what his sons are doing, and the Kaurava leader nervously reviews the champions on both sides.
reconstruction: The chapter's first move is to locate us. We do not stand on the battlefield; we listen from the palace, with a king who cannot see. Dhṛtarāṣṭra's question is the question of an anxious father. It is already shaped by partiality, "my sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu," and by fear: what *did* they do, now that they are gathered on a field called "the field of dharma"? Duryodhana's speech then presents the war from the side of worldly calculation. He counts heroes, compares forces, and issues tactical orders, "protect Bhīṣma above all." It is the voice of a man who understands war entirely as power, numbers and positions. Nothing in his speech raises the question of whether the war should be fought. He is not divided against himself. That will be Arjuna's distinction.
insight: The narrative frame is a structural argument in miniature. Each layer of narration (Vyāsa's epic, Sañjaya's report, Duryodhana's review) shows a different way of *seeing* the same event. The blind king cannot see. Sañjaya sees everything by divine gift. Duryodhana sees only power. Arjuna will see too much, and Kṛṣṇa will finally give him a "divine eye" (11.8). The Gītā is from its first verse a meditation on vision. Duryodhana's list is long and dry. That is deliberate. Its catalog of names and titles creates the weight of social reality, a whole warrior aristocracy assembled, against which Arjuna's individual conscience will soon break.
sources: The frame narrative belongs to the *Bhīṣma Parvan* of the Mahābhārata, where Vyāsa grants Sañjaya divine sight so that he can narrate the war (*Mahābhārata* 6.2). The names of warriors in 1.4–9 match the epic's lists of the two armies' champions. The reference to the "son of Somadatta" is Bhūriśravas.
context: Literature that opens on the eve of battle with a catalog of champions is widespread: the "Catalogue of Ships" in *Iliad* 2, the muster of the hosts in Norse and Irish epic. As in the *Iliad*, the catalog is followed by a story about one warrior whose inner state matters more than all the numbers. Homer's Achilles withdraws from battle in wrath. Arjuna withdraws in grief.
matters: The opening teaches the reader to ask *who is seeing* and *from where*. That question will turn out to be the Gītā's deepest one: whether we see the world as "mine and theirs," or as the field in which one self is present in all.
questions: What is the effect of hearing the war through a blind king's question rather than directly?
Duryodhana addresses Droṇa rather than the commander Bhīṣma. What might this reveal about him?
How does the first verse's pairing of "field of dharma" and "field of the Kurus" prepare for what follows?

premises.label: The war is a field of dharma
premises.text: The setting is moral as much as physical.

premises.label: Duryodhana sees only power and numbers
premises.text: He compares forces and gives tactical orders, but never questions the war.

claim.label: The question of how to see the war is opened
claim.text: Different narrators see the same event differently. The Gītā will be about learning to see rightly.

implications.label: Arjuna will see what Duryodhana cannot
implications.text: His sight of kinsmen will turn the war into a moral crisis.

sections.title: The conches sound
sections.lead: Bhīṣma's lion-roar and conch begin the battle signals; Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna answer with divine conches.
reconstruction: After the speech of calculation comes the language of sound. Bhīṣma's lion-roar is meant to steady a frightened leader. The Pāṇḍava conches answer one by one, named and owned, until the uproar fills heaven and earth. The war has effectively begun. There is now a public commitment that would be shameful to retract.
insight: The section works by escalation. One conch, then a din of instruments, then a precise roll-call of the Pāṇḍava conches, then the earth itself resounding. The momentum is collective and almost irresistible. The poet makes us feel how hard it would be for any single warrior to step out of this rhythm. That is exactly what Arjuna is about to do.
sources: The conch names and their origins are recorded in the epic (*Mahābhārata* 6.23 and parallel lists). The conch (*śaṅkha*) is also one of Viṣṇu's four emblems, which Arjuna will see Kṛṣṇa holding in 11.17 and 11.46 together with mace and discus.
context: Ritual sound before battle (trumpets at Jericho, war-cries in the *Iliad*, bagpipes in Highland warfare) binds a group into a single will. The Gītā sets the solitary voice of conscience against this collective sound.
matters: Moral crises often arrive after commitments have already been made publicly. Arjuna's doubt comes after the conches have sounded. The Gītā does not pretend that conscience operates in a vacuum.
questions: Why does the text name each conch? What does naming add?
How does the escalating sound make Arjuna's coming silence more dramatic?

premises.label: Bhīṣma signals battle out of loyalty
premises.text: Even the wisest elder is swept into the collective act.

premises.label: Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna answer with divine conches
premises.text: The Pāṇḍava side commits publicly.

claim.label: The war has momentum beyond any individual
claim.text: The sound fills heaven and earth; retreat would now be shameful.

implications.label: Arjuna's doubt will interrupt a collective will
implications.text: The stage is set for a solitary crisis inside a public act.

sections.title: Arjuna surveys the field
sections.lead: Arjuna asks to be placed between the armies to see whom he must fight, and sees his own family.
reconstruction: Arjuna wants to *see* whom he must fight. It is a warrior's request for reconnaissance. Kṛṣṇa places the chariot in front of Bhīṣma and Droṇa, the two people Arjuna loves most on the other side, and says only "behold the Kurus." Arjuna looks and sees not enemies but relations. The category "enemy" dissolves, and with it the possibility of acting as a warrior.
insight: This is the hinge of the chapter. Kṛṣṇa says almost nothing, but his placement of the chariot is itself the first teaching. Everything Arjuna has suppressed in order to be a warrior is now set before his eyes. The section suggests that the crisis is not caused by new information but by *seeing* what one already knew. That is a profound point about moral perception, which philosophers like Iris Murdoch have emphasized: moral life is first of all a matter of attention.
sources: The kinship relations listed in 1.26–27 correspond to the epic's genealogy. Bhīṣma is great-uncle to both parties. Droṇa and Kṛpa are their teachers. Śalya (on the Kaurava side) is maternal uncle to the twins Nakula and Sahadeva. Many sons and grandsons fight on each side.
context: Moral philosophy has much to say about the "particular other": the face (Levinas), the special obligations of kinship (Bernard Williams on "one thought too many"), and the partiality of love. Arjuna's crisis is that the impersonal role of the warrior and the personal bonds of kinship meet in the same bodies.
matters: We act more easily on categories ("the enemy," "the other side") than on persons. The Gītā makes us watch what happens when the category breaks down. That is a concern for anyone in a role that may require harming others: soldier, judge, surgeon, executive.
questions: Kṛṣṇa's only words in Chapter 1 are "behold these Kurus." Why is this a fitting first teaching?
Is Arjuna's crisis caused by what he sees, or by how he sees it?
What do roles (warrior, judge, parent) allow us to do that we could not do as private persons? What is the cost?

premises.label: Arjuna asks to see whom he must fight
premises.text: A practical, warrior's request.

premises.label: Kṛṣṇa places him before Bhīṣma and Droṇa
premises.text: The chariot is positioned to make Arjuna face those he loves.

claim.label: Arjuna sees kin, not enemies
claim.text: The role of warrior collapses into the web of relationships.

implications.label: Attention transforms the moral situation
implications.text: Nothing new has happened. What has changed is how Arjuna sees.

sections.title: Arjuna's despair and his arguments against fighting
sections.lead: Overcome with pity, Arjuna describes his bodily collapse and gives reason after reason why he should not fight, then sits down and lets his bow fall.
reconstruction: Arjuna's reasoning has four strands, each serious. **Consequences**: no good can come of this. Victory would be bitter, because the people for whom one wants a kingdom would be dead {1.32–35}. **Moral pollution**: even though the Kauravas are aggressors, killing them would make us evil {1.36–37}. **Asymmetry**: they are blinded by greed, but we see the wrong. Their blindness does not license ours {1.38–39}. **Social order**: war destroys families, families carry dharma, and the collapse of dharma ruins women, lineage and ancestors {1.40–44}. From these he concludes that it would be better to be killed unresisting {1.46}. This is the logic of the renunciant: if action necessarily brings evil, refuse to act, and accept the consequences.
insight: The argument is stronger than the tradition sometimes allows. Its consequence-strand is persuasive in its own terms. Its asymmetry-strand is an early statement of the principle that wrongs done to us do not justify wrongs we do. Yet there are visible tensions. Arjuna claims not to want kingdom or pleasure {1.32}, yet his arguments are full of concern for his own happiness: "how could we be happy?" {1.37}. He appeals to dharma {1.40} but abandons his own dharma as a warrior. And his conclusion that he would rather die passive {1.46} would not stop the war. It would only remove him from it. Kṛṣṇa will exploit these tensions. He will argue that Arjuna's grief rests on a confusion about what dies {2.11}, that his abandonment of duty is itself a breach of dharma {2.33}, and above all that Arjuna's real motive is not dharma but attachment (*moha*) to his own people.
sources: Arjuna's social argument draws on the ideology of the *Dharmaśāstras*. The *Mānava Dharmaśāstra* (Laws of Manu) treats the "mixing of classes" (*varṇa-saṅkara*) as a fundamental danger, and its rules on ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*) are the background of 1.42. The legal concept of the *ātatāyin* appears in Vasiṣṭha's and Manu's law codes (e.g., *Manu* 8.350–351), which say an aggressor may be slain without sin.
context: Arjuna's arguments have counterparts across moral traditions. His refusal resembles pacifist arguments that killing defiles the killer whatever the cause (e.g., early Christian refusal of military service, Tolstoy). His asymmetry argument recalls Socrates in the *Crito*: one must never return wrong for wrong. His consequence-reasoning anticipates utilitarian critiques of war. Simone Weil, who read the Gītā in Sanskrit during the Second World War, was deeply troubled by the question of whether Arjuna should fight.
matters: The chapter shows that moral seriousness and moral confusion can coexist. Arjuna sees real goods and real harms, yet his paralysis also serves his own grief. Learning to tell these apart in ourselves is a lifelong task, and the Gītā begins it here.
questions: Reconstruct Arjuna's four arguments as premises and conclusions. Which premise would you challenge?
Arjuna admits the Kauravas are aggressors (*ātatāyin*). Does this weaken or strengthen his refusal?
How should a modern reader handle 1.41's language about women and caste? Is it possible to take Arjuna's argument seriously while rejecting its premises?
Is "better to die unresisting" a principled pacifism or a flight from responsibility?

premises.label: Killing kin can bring no good
premises.text: Victory and pleasure are worthless when those we love are dead, and evil would cling to us.

premises.label: War destroys the family and its dharma
premises.text: Collapse of family dharma leads to lawlessness, mixed orders, and fallen ancestors.

premises.label: Their blindness does not license ours
premises.text: We see the wrong; therefore we must refrain.

claim.label: Better to be killed unresisting than to fight
claim.text: The renunciant's conclusion: refuse action, accept the cost.

implications.label: Arjuna lays down his bow
implications.text: The crisis is complete. Teaching must begin.

implications.label: Kṛṣṇa must change the level of the question
implications.text: Rather than refuting each argument, he will question the understanding of self, duty and action on which they all rest.

chapters.colophon: Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the first chapter, called “The Yoga of Arjuna's Despair.”

chapters.title: The Yoga of Understanding

verses.text: To him, thus overcome with pity, his eyes filled with tears and troubled, sinking in despair, Madhusūdana spoke these words.
verses.speaker: Sañjaya

verses.text: From where has this faintness [*kaśmala*] come upon you at this moment of crisis, Arjuna? It is not the way of the noble [*anārya-juṣṭa*, "followed by the ignoble"]. It does not lead to heaven and it brings disgrace.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: *Kaśmala*: a "stain," "faintness" or "stupor." The word suggests both moral taint and loss of consciousness. *Anārya-juṣṭa*, "practiced by the ignoble": Kṛṣṇa appeals to the warrior aristocracy's code of honor.

verses.text: Do not yield to unmanliness [*klaibya*], Pārtha; it does not suit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and stand up, scorcher of foes!
fnotes: *Klaibya*, "unmanliness," literally the condition of a eunuch. It was the harshest insult in the warrior code. Vivekananda considered this verse the whole message of the Gītā: "Yield not to weakness." Note that Kṛṣṇa begins with an emotional shock, not an argument.

verses.text: How can I fight Bhīṣma and Droṇa in battle with arrows, Madhusūdana? They are worthy of worship, slayer of enemies.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: Better to live in this world on alms than to kill these honored teachers. If I kill my teachers, even though they want gain, I would enjoy here only pleasures smeared with blood.
tnotes: *artha-kāmān* can describe the teachers ("who seek gain") or the pleasures ("pleasures of wealth and desire").
fnotes: Arjuna's alternative, living on alms (*bhaikṣya*), is the life of a renunciant. He is not merely refusing to fight; he is proposing a different path of life.

verses.text: Nor do we know which is better for us: that we conquer them or that they conquer us. The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stand before us, and if we killed them we would not wish to live.
fnotes: The structure of a true dilemma: neither victory nor defeat would be good. This is perhaps Arjuna's strongest single statement.

verses.text: My very being is struck by the flaw of pity [*kārpaṇya-doṣa*], and my mind is confused about dharma. I ask you: tell me decisively what is better [*śreyas*]. I am your student. Instruct me, for I have taken refuge in you.
fnotes: The turning point of the Gītā. Arjuna says his very nature (*svabhāva*) is struck by a flaw, confesses confusion about dharma (*dharma-sammūḍha-cetāḥ*), and formally becomes a disciple: *śiṣyas te 'haṁ*, "I am your student." Teaching in the Indian tradition begins with such a request.

verses.text: I do not see what would drive away this grief that dries up my senses, even if I won unrivaled, prosperous kingship on earth, or even lordship over the gods.
Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, scorcher of foes, said to Govinda, "I will not fight," and fell silent.
verses.speaker: Sañjaya

verses.text: Then, O Bhārata, between the two armies, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words to him as he sank in despair.
fnotes: "As if smiling" (*prahasann iva*): Kṛṣṇa's smile, at the moment of greatest anguish, is much commented on. Is it compassion, irony, or the serenity of one who sees the whole?

verses.text: You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, and yet you speak words of wisdom. The wise [*paṇḍita*] grieve neither for the dead nor for the living.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: "You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, and yet you speak words of wisdom." Kṛṣṇa catches Arjuna's performance of wisdom: he has argued like a sage while acting from grief. This verse begins the teaching proper.

verses.text: Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these rulers of men. Nor will there ever be a time hereafter when we all shall cease to be.
fnotes: A verse on the plurality and eternity of selves. "I, you, these kings" all always existed. Advaitins read the plurality as conventional speech. Rāmānuja cites this verse as proof that individual selves are real and eternal, even in liberation.

verses.text: In this body the embodied one [*dehin*] passes through childhood, youth, and old age. In the same way it passes to another body. The steadfast [*dhīra*] are not bewildered by this.
fnotes: The analogy: as the self persists through childhood, youth and age, it persists through death. The argument rests on personal identity across bodily change.

verses.text: Contacts of the senses with their objects [*mātrā-sparśa*], son of Kuntī, give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and are impermanent. Endure them, Bhārata.
fnotes: *Mātrā-sparśa*, "contacts of the senses with their measures," i.e., sense-objects. The first lesson in equanimity: sensations are impermanent. Endure them (*titikṣasva*).

verses.text: The person whom these do not disturb, bull among men, who is the same in pain and pleasure and steadfast, is fit for immortality [*amṛtatva*].
Of the unreal [*asat*] there is no coming to be; of the real [*sat*] there is no ceasing to be. Those who see the truth [*tattva-darśin*] have seen where the two meet.
fnotes: Perhaps the Gītā's most compressed metaphysical axiom. "Of the unreal (*asat*) there is no coming to be; of the real (*sat*) there is no ceasing to be." Śaṅkara takes it as the foundation of Advaita: what changes is not ultimately real. The Greek parallel with Parmenides ("what is, is; what is not, cannot be") is often noted.

verses.text: Know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded. No one can destroy this imperishable.
The embodied one is eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable, but its bodies are said to come to an end. Therefore fight, Bhārata.
One who thinks this a killer and one who thinks it killed both fail to understand. It does not kill, and it is not killed.
fnotes: Nearly identical to *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 2.19. The killer and the killed are both mistaken about the self, which neither kills nor is killed.

verses.text: It is never born, nor does it ever die. It did not come into being, nor will it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, primeval, it is not killed when the body is killed.
fnotes: *Kaṭha* 2.18. Note the cascade of negations and the triṣṭubh meter, which marks heightened speech.

verses.text: One who knows it to be indestructible, eternal, unborn, and unchanging: how can that person kill anyone, Pārtha, or cause anyone to kill?
As a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied one casts off worn-out bodies and enters new ones.
fnotes: The famous image of clothing. It implies a strong dualism of self and body, which some readers find consoling and others troubling.

verses.text: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, wind does not dry it.
It cannot be cut, burned, wetted, or dried. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, unmoving, everlasting.
It is called unmanifest [*avyakta*], unthinkable, unchangeable. Therefore, knowing it to be such, you should not grieve.
And even if you think it is constantly born and constantly dies, even then, mighty-armed one, you should not grieve.
fnotes: A remarkable concession: "even if you think it is constantly born and constantly dies." Kṛṣṇa argues that even on a materialist or Buddhist view, grief over the inevitable is pointless.

verses.text: For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died. Therefore you should not grieve over what cannot be avoided.
Beings are unmanifest in their beginning, manifest in their middle, Bhārata, and unmanifest again in their end. What is there to lament?
Someone sees it as a marvel; another speaks of it as a marvel; another hears of it as a marvel. Yet even having heard of it, no one knows it.
fnotes: Echoes *Kaṭha* 2.7: the self is a marvel; "even having heard of it, no one knows it." The truth cannot be transmitted as information.

verses.text: This embodied one in the body of everyone can never be harmed, Bhārata. Therefore you should not grieve for any being.
Look also to your own dharma [*svadharma*] and do not waver. For a warrior [*kṣatriya*] nothing is better than a battle fought in accord with dharma.
fnotes: *Svadharma*, "one's own dharma," appears for the first time. For a kṣatriya, a dharmic war (*dharmya yuddha*) is the highest good. The argument shifts from metaphysics to social ethics.

verses.text: Happy are the warriors, Pārtha, who meet such a battle by chance, an open door to heaven.
fnotes: "An open door to heaven": the warrior's heaven (*svarga*) was a standard reward in epic ideology for dying in battle. The Gītā will later criticize heaven-seeking (2.42–44), so this appeal is clearly provisional.

verses.text: But if you will not fight this battle of dharma, you will abandon your own dharma and your honor and incur evil.
People will speak of your undying disgrace, and for one who has been honored, disgrace is worse than death.
fnotes: Disgrace "worse than death" (*maraṇād atiricyate*): the shame-culture of the warrior aristocracy.

verses.text: The great chariot-warriors will think you withdrew from battle out of fear. They held you in high esteem, and now they will think little of you.
Your enemies will say many unspeakable things, mocking your ability. What could be more painful than that?
Either you will be killed and attain heaven, or you will conquer and enjoy the earth. So stand up, son of Kuntī, resolved to fight.
fnotes: A dilemma in Arjuna's favor: if killed, heaven; if victorious, the earth. Either way, act.

verses.text: Treat alike pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat, and gird yourself for battle. In this way you will not incur evil.
fnotes: Crucial bridge verse. "Treat alike pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat… thus you will not incur evil." It already undercuts the appeals to heaven and honor just made: fight, but not for these reasons.

verses.text: This understanding [*buddhi*] has been declared to you according to Sāṅkhya. Now hear it according to yoga. Joined to this understanding, Pārtha, you will throw off the bondage of action [*karma-bandha*].
fnotes: "Sāṅkhya" and "yoga" here mean two standpoints: theoretical discrimination (just given, 2.11–30) and practical discipline (now to come). This is not yet the classical Sāṅkhya system.

verses.text: In this no effort is lost and no setback occurs. Even a little of this dharma protects from great fear.
fnotes: "In this no effort is lost": unlike ritual, which fails if done imperfectly, this yoga has no "reverse effect." Even a little protects.

verses.text: Here, joy of the Kurus, the understanding whose essence is resolve [*vyavasāyātmikā buddhi*] is single. The understandings of the irresolute are many-branched and endless.
fnotes: *Vyavasāyātmikā buddhi*: the understanding whose very nature is resolve. It is unified, set against the "many-branched" minds of the irresolute. The theme of inner unification runs through the whole Gītā.

verses.text: The undiscerning delight in the letter of the Veda [*veda-vāda*], Pārtha, and say "there is nothing else." They utter flowery speech,
fnotes: *Veda-vāda-ratāḥ*: "delighting in the letter of the Veda." The criticism targets ritualists who use Vedic rites to get heaven and power, an attitude associated with the Mīmāṁsā school.

verses.text: full of desire and intent on heaven. That speech offers rebirth as the fruit of action and abounds in special rites aimed at enjoyment and power.
Those attached to enjoyment and power have their minds carried off by that speech. In them the understanding whose essence is resolve is not established in concentration [*samādhi*].

The Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain. Be free of the three guṇas, Arjuna: free from the pairs of opposites [*dvandva*], always established in clarity [*nitya-sattva-stha*], free of acquiring and keeping, possessed of the self.
fnotes: *Nistraiguṇya*, "free of the three guṇas." It is the first mention of the guṇas, introduced to say the Vedas' domain is nature, and that one should go beyond it.

verses.text: When there is a flood of water on every side, a well is of little use. All the Vedas are of as little use to a brāhmaṇa who truly understands.
fnotes: A deliberately shocking image: the Vedas are to the knower like a well in a flood. Commentators soften it: the Veda's ends are contained in the knower's realization, as the well's water is in the flood.

verses.text: Your right [*adhikāra*] is to action alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, and do not be attached to inaction.
fnotes: The most famous verse of the Gītā. *Karmaṇy evādhikāras te, mā phaleṣu kadācana*. Four clauses: (1) your right is to action alone; (2) never to its fruits; (3) do not let fruit be your motive (*hetu*); (4) do not be attached to inaction. Note that (4) blocks the misreading "if fruits don't matter, why act?"

verses.text: Steadfast in yoga, perform actions, Dhanañjaya. Abandon attachment and be the same in success and failure. Equanimity [*samatva*] is called yoga.
fnotes: "Equanimity is called yoga" (*samatvaṁ yoga ucyate*). One of the Gītā's three short definitions of yoga (with 2.50 and 6.23).

verses.text: Action by itself is far inferior to the yoga of understanding [*buddhi-yoga*], Dhanañjaya. Seek refuge in understanding. Pitiable are those whose motive is the fruit.
fnotes: "Pitiable are those whose motive is the fruit" (*kṛpaṇāḥ phala-hetavaḥ*). The word *kṛpaṇa* echoes Arjuna's *kārpaṇya* (2.7). Craving makes one poor.

verses.text: One joined to understanding leaves behind, here and now, both good and bad deeds. Therefore yoke yourself to yoga. Yoga is skill in actions [*yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam*].
fnotes: "Yoga is skill in actions" (*yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam*). Śaṅkara takes it to mean that the skill is in acting without being bound. A more modern reading is "excellence in work." Both are possible.

verses.text: The wise, joined to understanding, give up the fruit born of action. Freed from the bondage of birth, they go to the place beyond sorrow.
When your understanding crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, you will become indifferent to what you will hear and what you have heard.
Your understanding is now bewildered by what you have heard [*śruti*, the Veda]. When it stands unmoving, stable in concentration, you will attain yoga.
fnotes: *Śruti-vipratipannā*: "bewildered by what you have heard," that is, by conflicting scriptural teachings. Arjuna's confusion is partly the confusion of too many authorities.

verses.text: What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady [*sthita-prajña*], who is established in concentration, Keśava? How does one of steady thought speak? How does he sit? How does he move?
verses.speaker: Arjuna
fnotes: Arjuna's questions are practical: how does such a person speak, sit, move? He wants to recognize the sage, and to become one.

verses.text: One who abandons all desires that have entered the mind, Pārtha, and is content in the self by the self alone, is called steady in wisdom.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: The first mark: one gives up all desires and is "content in the self by the self alone." Satisfaction no longer depends on external objects.

verses.text: One whose mind is not shaken in sorrows and who has no craving in pleasures, from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed: that sage [*muni*] is called steady in thought.
One who is unattached everywhere, who neither rejoices nor hates on meeting this or that, good or bad: that one's wisdom is established.
When one withdraws the senses from their objects on every side, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, that one's wisdom is established.
fnotes: The tortoise: a classic image. The withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra* in later yoga) is voluntary and reversible, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs.

verses.text: Sense objects fall away from the embodied one who does not feed on them, but the taste for them [*rasa*] remains. Even the taste falls away once the supreme has been seen.
fnotes: A subtle point. Abstaining removes objects but not the *taste* (*rasa*) for them. Only seeing the supreme removes the taste itself. Asceticism alone is insufficient.

verses.text: Even for the wise person who strives, son of Kuntī, the turbulent senses forcibly carry off the mind.
Restraining them all, one should sit yoked, intent on me. For one whose senses are under control, wisdom is established.
fnotes: *Mat-paraḥ*, "intent on me": the first hint of devotion in the Gītā. The sage controls the senses by turning toward God.

verses.text: When a person dwells on the objects of the senses, attachment to them arises. From attachment arises desire [*kāma*]; from desire arises anger;
fnotes: The causal chain begins: dwelling on objects leads to attachment, attachment leads to desire, and desire leads to anger.

verses.text: from anger comes delusion; from delusion, confusion of memory; from confusion of memory, loss of understanding; and from loss of understanding, one perishes.
fnotes: And continues: anger leads to delusion, delusion to confusion of memory (*smṛti-vibhrama*), that to loss of understanding (*buddhi-nāśa*), and that to ruin. Note "memory." In 18.73 Arjuna's cure will be the recovery of *smṛti*.

verses.text: But one who moves among the objects of the senses with senses free from attraction and aversion and governed by the self, self-mastered, attains serenity [*prasāda*].
In serenity all one's sorrows come to an end, for when the mind is serene, the understanding quickly becomes steady.
The unyoked have no understanding and no power of meditation [*bhāvanā*]. Without meditation there is no peace, and without peace, where is happiness?
When the mind follows the roaming senses, it carries away one's wisdom, as the wind carries a ship on the water.
Therefore, mighty-armed one, one whose senses are entirely withdrawn from their objects has established wisdom.
What is night for all beings, the self-controlled one is awake to. What beings are awake to is night for the sage who sees.
fnotes: "What is night for all beings, the self-controlled one is awake to." The sage's values invert the world's. What others ignore, he attends to; what excites them, he sleeps through.

verses.text: The waters flow into the ocean, which is ever being filled yet stays unmoved in its depth. The one into whom all desires enter in that way attains peace, not the one who desires desires.
fnotes: The ocean image: rivers flow in and it stays full and unmoved. Desires still come, but they do not disturb.

verses.text: The person who gives up all desires and moves about free of longing, without "mine" and without I-making [*ahaṅkāra*], attains peace.
This is the state of brahman [*brāhmī sthiti*], Pārtha. Having attained it, one is not deluded. Remaining in it even at the hour of death, one reaches the nirvāṇa of brahman [*brahma-nirvāṇa*].
fnotes: *Brāhmī sthiti* and *brahma-nirvāṇa*: the first appearance of "nirvāṇa," a word of Buddhist resonance, here made "of brahman."

chapters.summary: Arjuna becomes Kṛṣṇa's student. Kṛṣṇa answers his grief first with the doctrine of the undying self, then with the warrior's duty, then with the yoga of understanding: act, but without attachment to the fruit. The chapter closes with the portrait of the person whose wisdom is steady.
overview: Chapter 2 is the Gītā in miniature. Nearly every major theme of the later chapters is introduced here: the self, dharma, action without attachment, critique of ritualism, equanimity, sense-control, and the peace of brahman. Traditional teachers often say that one who understands the second chapter understands the whole. The chapter has a clear argumentative structure. After Arjuna surrenders as a student {2.7}, Kṛṣṇa gives two arguments for fighting that work at different levels. The first is metaphysical: the self cannot be killed, so grief is misplaced {2.11–30}. The second is ethical and social: a warrior's own dharma is to fight a just war, and refusing will bring disgrace {2.31–38}. Then Kṛṣṇa announces a new teaching, *buddhi-yoga*, the yoga of understanding {2.39}. This shifts the question from *whether* to act to *how* to act, culminating in the famous verse on action and its fruits {2.47} and in the definition "equanimity is called yoga" {2.48}. The chapter ends with Arjuna's question about the sage {2.54} and Kṛṣṇa's portrait of the *sthita-prajña*, the person of steady wisdom. Its psychological analysis of how desire leads to ruin {2.62–63} is among the most quoted passages in Indian literature.
research: Scholars have long debated how the two opening arguments relate. The metaphysical argument of 2.11–30 seems to prove too much: if no one is ever killed, why should anything matter, including duty? The social argument of 2.31–38 seems to prove too little, since it appeals to honor and heaven, motives the Gītā later rejects. One influential reading (developed in different ways by Malinar and by Ram-Prasad) is that both are *preparatory*. They loosen Arjuna's grip on his grief and on his warrior identity. The real teaching only begins with *buddhi-yoga* at 2.39. The phrase *sāṅkhya* at 2.39 has also been studied closely. In the Gītā it does not yet name Īśvarakṛṣṇa's classical system but an earlier, broader way of "discriminating" knowledge. Its relation to early Sāṅkhya fragments in the Mahābhārata's *Mokṣadharma* section is an active research topic (Johannes Bronkhorst, Gerald Larson). Psychologists have drawn on 2.47–48 and 2.62–63 to build measures of non-attachment (*anāsakti*), and studies (e.g., by Pande and Naidu, 1992) report associations with lower stress. This literature is suggestive but methodologically young.
questions: Do the arguments of 2.11–30 and 2.31–38 support each other, or pull in different directions?
What changes when the question moves from "should I act?" to "from what state should I act?"
Is the person of steady wisdom (2.55–72) a model for everyone, or only for a renunciant elite?
Can the analysis of desire in 2.62–63 be tested against modern psychology? What would count as evidence?

nodes.label: Arjuna's grief and surrender
nodes.text: Arjuna admits his confusion and becomes a student. Teaching becomes possible.

nodes.label: The self is undying
nodes.text: First argument: what is real never ceases to be. The self is not killed when the body is killed.

nodes.label: Your own dharma: fight
nodes.text: Second argument: for a warrior a just battle is a duty; refusing brings disgrace.

nodes.label: The yoga of understanding
nodes.text: A new standpoint: not whether to act but from what understanding to act.

nodes.label: Critique of ritual for rewards
nodes.text: Those who use the Veda for heaven and power have scattered, many-branched minds.

nodes.label: Right to action, not to fruits
nodes.text: The famous formula: act, but do not make the result your motive.

nodes.label: Equanimity is yoga
nodes.text: Sameness in success and failure; yoga is skill in action.

nodes.label: How desire ruins
nodes.text: Dwelling on objects leads to attachment, then desire, anger, delusion, loss of memory and understanding, and ruin.

nodes.label: The person of steady wisdom
nodes.text: Content in the self, unshaken, senses withdrawn like a tortoise's limbs, full like the ocean.

nodes.label: The state of brahman
nodes.text: Without "mine" or I-making, one attains peace, the nirvāṇa of brahman.

sections.title: Rebuke, confession, and surrender
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa's first response is a stinging rebuke; Arjuna answers with the strongest form of his dilemma, then admits his confusion and asks to be taught.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa first tries the language of honor. Arjuna's despair is unworthy of a noble warrior and will bring disgrace, so he should stand up. Arjuna answers that the issue is not courage. How can one shoot arrows at those one should worship? Better to beg than to enjoy blood-smeared pleasures. Neither outcome of the war is good. Then something changes. Arjuna stops arguing and admits that his own nature is damaged and his mind confused about dharma. He no longer claims to know what is right. He asks to be taught. Having said "I will not fight," he falls silent. Kṛṣṇa, smiling, begins to speak.
insight: The section dramatizes a precondition of learning: the collapse of one's own certainty. While Arjuna argued in Chapter 1, he was still confident in his reasoning. Only when he confesses that his reasoning itself is clouded does teaching become possible. Philosophically, this is the recognition that the faculty that judges, the *buddhi*, can itself be distorted, which is exactly what Kṛṣṇa will address with the "yoga of understanding." Kṛṣṇa's failed first move matters too. Shame does not work on someone with a real moral objection. The Gītā shows its teacher adjusting his method to the student, a pattern it will repeat many times.
sources: The ideal of the disciple who approaches a teacher in humility echoes the Upaniṣads (e.g., *Muṇḍaka* 1.2.12: approach a teacher "fuel in hand"). The structure of crisis followed by request for instruction also opens the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad*, where Naciketas, granted three boons by Death, asks about what lies beyond death.
context: Many philosophical traditions begin with an admission of ignorance: Socratic *aporia*, Augustine's restlessness in the *Confessions*, Descartes's resolve to doubt. The Gītā's version is distinctive in being personal and urgent. Arjuna must act within hours.
matters: Admitting that one's own judgment may be compromised is the hardest and most important step in any serious inquiry, moral, therapeutic or intellectual.
questions: Why does Kṛṣṇa's appeal to honor fail? What does that teach about moral persuasion?
What exactly does Arjuna confess in 2.7? Is the confession itself a moral achievement?
How do you read Kṛṣṇa's smile in 2.10?

premises.label: Arjuna's grief is unworthy of a warrior
premises.text: Kṛṣṇa's first, failed appeal to honor.

premises.label: Neither victory nor defeat would be good
premises.text: Arjuna restates the dilemma at its strongest.

claim.label: Arjuna surrenders his certainty and asks to be taught
claim.text: The pivot of the Gītā: confession of confusion and request for instruction.

implications.label: Teaching can now begin
implications.text: Kṛṣṇa, smiling, starts the real instruction.

sections.title: The undying self
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa's first argument: the self is eternal and cannot be killed; grief rests on mistaking what we are.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa's first argument is that Arjuna's grief rests on a mistake about what a person is. What is real does not cease to be, and what is unreal does not come to be {2.16}. The body is unreal in this sense: it comes and goes. The embodied self is real. It passed through childhood, youth and age without perishing {2.13} and passes through death the same way {2.22}. Weapons, fire and water cannot touch it {2.23}. So no one is really killed in battle {2.19}. Grief over the dead or the living is misplaced {2.11}. The argument closes with a fallback {2.26–27}. Even if the self were born and died constantly, death would be certain for whatever is born. Grieving over the inevitable is therefore pointless on any view.
insight: The argument is powerful but strange. Its strength is that it attacks the root of Arjuna's distress: the identification of persons with their bodies. Its strangeness is that, taken alone, it seems to prove too much. If no one is ever killed, then killing is morally neutral, and so is saving life. Critics from early Western Indologists to contemporary ethicists have pointed out that such an argument could justify any violence. The tradition's best reply is that the argument is not a justification of killing but a cure for one particular delusion: the grief-paralysis that makes a person unable to act at all. It must be read together with what follows. The self's eternity removes *fear and grief*. It does not settle *what ought to be done*. That is the work of dharma (2.31–38) and of the yoga of understanding (2.39ff.). The fallback argument of 2.26–27 also shows Kṛṣṇa's pedagogy. He does not stake everything on one metaphysics.
sources: Close parallels with the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* (2.7, 2.18–19) are certain. The self as unborn, eternal and indestructible is the core of Upaniṣadic teaching (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka* 4.4.22–25: "this self is not this, not this… it does not tremble, it is not harmed"). The axiom of 2.16 also resembles the *Chāndogya*'s argument (6.2.1–2) that being cannot come from non-being.
context: The section invites comparison with Plato's *Phaedo*, where Socrates, facing death, argues for the soul's immortality and chides his friends for weeping. Both use metaphysics to transform grief. It also invites comparison with Buddhism's denial of a permanent self (*anātman*). The Gītā's 2.26 seems to address that view directly. Modern philosophy of personal identity (Locke, Parfit) asks what persists through change, the very question of 2.13.
matters: How we understand ourselves shapes how we grieve, fear and act. Whatever one thinks of the metaphysics, the section asks a question every person faces: what am I, if I am not my body's fate?
questions: Does the argument from the self's immortality prove too much? How would Kṛṣṇa answer that objection?
