Compare the clothing image (2.22) with Socrates in the *Phaedo*. Is either consoling? To whom?
What work does the fallback argument of 2.26–27 do? Why include it?
Read 2.16 slowly. What does it mean for something to be "real" in this sense?

premises.label: The real never ceases to be
premises.text: Being and non-being cannot turn into each other.

premises.label: The self passes through changes without perishing
premises.text: Childhood, youth, age, and death are changes of body, not of self.

premises.label: The self cannot be harmed
premises.text: It neither kills nor is killed; weapons and fire do not touch it.

claim.label: Grief for the dead and living is misplaced
claim.text: Arjuna's sorrow rests on a mistake about what persons are.

implications.label: Even on other views, grief over the inevitable is pointless
implications.text: A fallback argument that works without the metaphysics.

implications.label: The self's eternity cures fear, but does not yet say what to do
implications.text: That question is answered by dharma and by the yoga of understanding.

sections.title: The warrior's own dharma
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa's second argument appeals to Arjuna's own duty as a warrior, to honor and to heaven, and ends with the first statement of equanimity.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa now argues on the level Arjuna himself had appealed to: dharma. Arjuna's dharma is that of a warrior, and for a warrior nothing is better than a just war {2.31}. To abandon it would be to abandon both duty and honor and to incur evil {2.33}. People would say he fled from fear {2.35}. Either outcome, death or victory, is good for him {2.37}. Then comes the decisive qualification. He should fight treating victory and defeat alike {2.38}, and only so will he avoid evil.
insight: The section is a rhetorical bridge. It meets Arjuna where he is, in a world of dharma, honor and heaven, and then, in its final verse, quietly prepares to leave that world behind. The appeal to disgrace is a "lower" motive, and Kṛṣṇa knows it. The equanimity of 2.38 is not about honor at all. Many commentators read this structure as Kṛṣṇa's skillful means: lower motives are invoked only to be transcended. There is a real tension here. Arjuna had argued from *family* dharma (1.40). Kṛṣṇa argues from *class* dharma. Neither is the final word. The Gītā will finally speak of a dharma that is God's to protect (4.7) and then of abandoning all dharmas (18.66). Readers should notice how many layers of "duty" the text contains.
sources: The warrior's duty to fight and the promise of heaven for those slain facing the enemy are standard in the Dharmaśāstras (e.g., *Manu* 7.87–89). The epic's warrior ethos (*kṣatra-dharma*) is debated within the Mahābhārata itself, notably by Yudhiṣṭhira, who repeatedly questions it.
context: The appeal to role-duty and honor recalls Homer's Sarpedon (*Iliad* 12): the nobles must fight in front because they are honored. Contemporary role-ethics (and debates about professional duty: the lawyer, the soldier) asks how far a role can justify acts that private morality would forbid.
matters: Most people meet the question "should I?" through roles: parent, employee, citizen, soldier. The section asks how far a role's duties bind us, and hints that they bind best when performed without craving for reward or fear of shame.
questions: Is Kṛṣṇa's appeal to honor and heaven sincere, or merely tactical? What is the evidence in the text?
How does 2.38 change the meaning of the preceding verses?
Arjuna appealed to family dharma, Kṛṣṇa to warrior dharma. How should conflicts between dharmas be resolved?

premises.label: A just war is a warrior's highest duty
premises.text: For a kṣatriya, nothing is better than a dharmic battle.

premises.label: Refusing would bring disgrace and evil
premises.text: Abandoning duty and honor is itself a wrong.

claim.label: Fight, as your dharma requires
claim.text: Either outcome is good; so stand up and fight.

implications.label: But fight with equanimity
implications.text: Treat victory and defeat alike. Only then is the act free of evil. This opens the next teaching.

sections.title: The yoga of understanding: action without attachment
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa announces a new teaching: act with a resolute, single understanding, renounce the fruits, and let equanimity be your yoga.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa now shifts the ground. What matters is not only *that* one acts but the *understanding* (*buddhi*) from which one acts. An understanding that is resolute is single. One scattered among desires is many-branched {2.41}. The ritualists who use the Veda to get heaven and power have scattered minds {2.42–44}. One should go beyond the guṇas, beyond the pairs of opposites, beyond acquiring and keeping {2.45}. The practical rule follows. One has a right to the action, never to its fruit. Do not act for the fruit, and do not fall into inaction {2.47}. Act steadily, giving up attachment, the same in success and failure {2.48}. Such action does not bind. It leaves behind both good and bad deeds {2.50}. When the understanding passes beyond delusion and stands firm in concentration, one reaches yoga {2.52–53}.
insight: This is the conceptual heart of karma-yoga and arguably of the Gītā. Its decisive move is to separate two things ordinarily fused: *doing* something and *staking oneself on its outcome*. The agent is responsible for the act, its rightness and skill, but not owner of the results. This dissolves the renunciant's dilemma. Action binds through attachment, and one can act without attachment. Critics have raised two objections. First, can one act intentionally without caring about results? Intentional action seems to *aim* at outcomes. The best reply is that 2.47 forbids making the fruit one's *motive* (*hetu*), not foreseeing it. The agent aims at doing the right act well, and the outcome follows or does not. Second, does indifference to consequences license recklessness? Here 18.25 helps: action "without regard to consequences" is called tamasic. The Gītā wants attention to consequences without anxiety about them. That distinction is fine but real.
sources: The critique of desire-driven ritual draws on Upaniṣadic criticism of sacrifice (*Muṇḍaka* 1.2.7–10 calls ritualists "fools" who return again to this world). The single-pointed understanding resembles the *Kaṭha*'s image of the disciplined intellect as charioteer (*Kaṭha* 3.3–9). The *Īśā Upaniṣad* 2 ("action does not cling to a person") is the nearest anticipation of 2.47.
context: Comparisons abound. Kant's good will, whose worth lies not in what it accomplishes but in its principle, is a near cousin. So is Stoic ethics (Epictetus, *Enchiridion* 1): some things are up to us (our acts and judgments), others not (outcomes), and freedom lies in caring only for the former. Both T. S. Eliot ("And do not think of the fruit of action. / Fare forward," *Four Quartets*) and Gandhi took 2.47 as a life-rule. Modern psychology's distinction between "process" and "outcome" goals, and research on performance anxiety, give the verse an empirical dimension.
matters: Most suffering in work and relationships comes not from effort but from anxious attachment to results we cannot control. These verses offer a way to act wholeheartedly while staying free, a teaching that has helped soldiers, athletes, activists and ordinary workers.
questions: Can a person act intentionally without making the outcome their motive? Construct an example.
What is the difference between not caring about consequences and not being attached to them?
Compare 2.47 with Epictetus's distinction between what is and is not "up to us." Where do they differ?
Why does Kṛṣṇa add "do not be attached to inaction"? What misreading does it prevent?

premises.label: Action binds through attachment to its fruit
premises.text: Not action itself but the ego's stake in outcomes creates bondage.

premises.label: A resolute understanding is single, not scattered
premises.text: Desire-driven minds are many-branched.

claim.label: Act without attachment, the same in success and failure
claim.text: Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits. Equanimity is yoga.

implications.label: Such action does not bind
implications.text: One leaves behind good and bad deeds and reaches the place beyond sorrow.

implications.label: Ritual for rewards is superseded
implications.text: The Veda's purposes are fulfilled in the knower's understanding.

sections.title: The person of steady wisdom
sections.lead: Arjuna asks what the sage is like; Kṛṣṇa answers with a portrait of equanimity, sense-mastery and peace.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa's answer is a description, not a rule. The sage is content in the self, so desires lose their grip {2.55}. The sage is unshaken in sorrow and without craving in pleasure {2.56}, withdraws the senses at will {2.58}, and controls them by turning toward the highest {2.61}. The reason control matters is given in a precise psychology: brooding on objects breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, frustrated desire becomes anger, anger clouds memory and understanding, and the person is destroyed {2.62–63}. By contrast, one who moves among objects without attraction or aversion gains serenity, and in serenity sorrow ends {2.64–65}. Such a person is like the ocean, full and still while rivers pour in {2.70}. Without "mine" and without I-making, he reaches the peace of brahman {2.71–72}.
insight: The passage is a phenomenology of freedom. Its insight is that the problem is not the senses or the world but *dwelling* (*dhyāyataḥ*) on objects, the mind's repeated return to what it wants. The chain of 2.62–63 is a remarkably modern model, in which attention drives appetite, appetite drives frustration, and frustration distorts cognition. The portrait also resolves an apparent paradox: how can one act fully without desire? The sage is not without inclinations (the "rivers" keep coming) but is not *moved* by them. The ideal is not a stone but an ocean, full and therefore undisturbed. One tension remains. The sage here "withdraws" and is "free of longing," while Arjuna is asked to fight. The portrait describes the inner state from which action should come, not a withdrawal from action. That reconciliation is the work of Chapter 3.
sources: The tortoise image and the restraint of the senses appear in the epic's *Mokṣadharma* and in *Manu* 7.105. The chariot model of *Kaṭha* 3.3–9 lies behind the passage on the senses carrying off the mind (2.60, 2.67). The ocean image recalls *Muṇḍaka* 3.2.8 (rivers merging in the sea).
context: Stoic *apatheia* and the Epicurean *ataraxia* (tranquility) are close parallels, as is the Buddhist account of craving (*taṇhā*) arising from contact and feeling in the twelvefold chain of dependent origination. Contemporary cognitive science of craving, and mindfulness-based interventions for addiction, explicitly describe the "elaboration" of desire through rumination, the *dhyāyataḥ* of 2.62. Gandhi had 2.54–72 recited every evening at his prayer meetings.
matters: The passage offers a picture of a free and peaceful person who is not cut off from the world, and a precise account of how we lose that freedom. It is one of the most practically useful pages in world literature.
questions: Trace the chain of 2.62–63 in an experience of your own. Where could it be broken?
What is the difference between suppressing a desire and losing the taste for it (2.59)?
Is the ocean (2.70) a better image of the ideal than the tortoise (2.58)? What does each emphasize?
Why might Gandhi, an activist, have chosen these verses for daily recitation?

premises.label: Dwelling on objects breeds desire, anger and ruin
premises.text: A causal chain from attention to destruction.

premises.label: Moving among objects without attraction or aversion brings serenity
premises.text: Control of the senses yields clarity and the end of sorrow.

claim.label: The sage is content in the self and unshaken
claim.text: Full like the ocean, the sage is not moved by desires that still arise.

implications.label: Without "mine" and I-making, one reaches peace
implications.text: Freedom from possessiveness is the key to peace.

implications.label: The state of brahman, even at death
implications.text: The goal of the teaching is named.

chapters.colophon: Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the second chapter, called “The Yoga of Understanding.”

chapters.title: The Yoga of Action

verses.text: If you hold that understanding is superior to action, Janārdana, then why do you urge me to this terrible action, Keśava?
verses.speaker: Arjuna
fnotes: *Ghora karma*, "terrible action": Arjuna means the killing in battle. His objection is fair. 2.49 had said action alone is "far inferior" to understanding.

verses.text: Your words seem to conflict, and they confuse my understanding. Tell me decisively the one thing by which I may reach the better [*śreyas*].
fnotes: *Vyāmiśra*, "mixed, seemingly conflicting" words: Arjuna asks for a single clear answer, the same word (*niścitam*, "decisively") as in 2.7.

verses.text: In this world, sinless one, I taught long ago a twofold foundation: the yoga of knowledge [*jñāna-yoga*] for followers of Sāṅkhya, and the yoga of action [*karma-yoga*] for yogins.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: The "twofold foundation" (*dvividhā niṣṭhā*): knowledge for Sāṅkhyas, action for yogins. Śaṅkara takes these as two different paths for two kinds of people. Others take them as two stages of one path.

verses.text: A person does not reach freedom from action [*naiṣkarmya*] by not undertaking actions, nor reach perfection by renunciation [*saṁnyāsa*] alone.
fnotes: *Naiṣkarmya*, "freedom from action," the renunciant's goal, is reached *not* by abstaining. A paradox the chapter will unpack.

verses.text: No one can remain even for a moment without acting. The guṇas born of nature [*prakṛti*] make everyone act, whether they will it or not.
fnotes: A key premise: "no one can remain even for a moment without acting." Breathing, digesting and thinking are action. Nature acts through us.

verses.text: One who restrains the organs of action but sits remembering sense objects with the mind is a deluded self, called a hypocrite.
fnotes: *Mithyācāra*, "hypocrite," literally "one of false conduct": the ascetic who restrains the body while the mind feasts on objects.

verses.text: But one who controls the senses with the mind, Arjuna, and without attachment undertakes the yoga of action with the organs of action, excels.
Perform your prescribed [*niyata*] action, for action is better than inaction. Without action you could not even maintain your body.
fnotes: *Niyata karma*, "prescribed" or "regulated" action: one's appointed duty. Even sustaining the body requires action.

verses.text: This world is bound by action, except for action done for the sake of sacrifice [*yajña*]. Perform action for that purpose, son of Kuntī, free from attachment.
fnotes: *Yajñārtha*, "for the sake of sacrifice." Some commentators (following *Taittirīya Saṁhitā* 1.7.4, "sacrifice is Viṣṇu") read it as "for the sake of Viṣṇu," i.e., of God.

verses.text: Long ago, having created creatures together with sacrifice, the Lord of creatures [*Prajāpati*] said: "By this you shall multiply. Let this be your wish-fulfilling cow.
fnotes: Prajāpati, the creator in the Vedic Brāhmaṇas, creates beings *together with* sacrifice. The *kāmadhuk* is the wish-fulfilling cow of myth.

verses.text: Nourish the gods with this, and let the gods nourish you. Nourishing one another, you will reach the highest good.
fnotes: *Parasparaṁ bhāvayantaḥ*, "nourishing one another": an ecology of reciprocity between gods and humans.

verses.text: Nourished by sacrifice, the gods will give you the enjoyments you desire." One who enjoys their gifts without giving to them in return is simply a thief.
fnotes: "Simply a thief" (*stena eva saḥ*): one who takes without giving back breaks the wheel.

verses.text: The good, who eat what remains from the sacrifice, are released from all faults. The wicked, who cook only for themselves, eat evil.
fnotes: Eating "what remains from the sacrifice" (*yajña-śiṣṭa*): in Hindu practice, food is offered before being eaten (*prasāda*). Cooking only for oneself is "eating evil."

verses.text: Beings arise from food; food arises from rain; rain arises from sacrifice; sacrifice arises from action.
fnotes: The cycle of 3.14–15: beings, food, rain, sacrifice, action, brahman (the Veda), the imperishable. It is a cosmic food chain.

verses.text: Know that action arises from brahman [here, the Veda], and brahman arises from the imperishable. Therefore the all-pervading brahman is always established in sacrifice.
fnotes: *Brahma* here most likely means the Veda (sacred word), which prescribes action. Some take it as the supreme brahman.

verses.text: One who does not keep turning the wheel set in motion here lives an evil life, delighting in the senses. That one lives in vain, Pārtha.
fnotes: "Does not keep turning the wheel" (*pravartitaṁ cakram*): the image of a wheel set in motion, also Buddhism's "wheel of dharma."

verses.text: But the person who delights in the self alone, content in the self and satisfied in the self alone, has nothing that must be done.
fnotes: The self-content person "has nothing that must be done" (*kāryaṁ na vidyate*). This verse is Śaṅkara's key text for the knower's freedom from duty.

verses.text: That person gains nothing by acting here and nothing by not acting, and depends on no being for any purpose.
fnotes: Such a person "depends on no being for any purpose." Complete independence, yet in the next verse Kṛṣṇa says "therefore act."

verses.text: Therefore, without attachment, always perform the action that must be done. By performing action without attachment, a person reaches the highest.
fnotes: *Tasmāt*, "therefore": the link between 3.17–18 and the command to act is disputed. Does it follow from the knower's freedom, or address Arjuna, who is not yet such a knower?

verses.text: Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone. You too should act, looking to the holding-together of the world [*loka-saṅgraha*].
fnotes: Janaka, the philosopher-king of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, is the model of the royal sage. *Loka-saṅgraha*, "holding-together of the world," is introduced.

verses.text: Whatever the best person does, others do too. Whatever standard that one sets, the world follows.
fnotes: The principle of exemplarity: "whatever the best person does, others do too." A leader's conduct sets the standard.

verses.text: For me, Pārtha, there is nothing whatever to be done in the three worlds, and nothing unattained to attain. Yet I continue in action.
fnotes: God's own example: "there is nothing whatever to be done… yet I continue in action." Divine action is wholly free of need.

verses.text: For if I ever ceased to act tirelessly, Pārtha, people would follow my path in every way.
If I did not perform action, these worlds would perish. I would cause confusion and destroy these creatures.
fnotes: *Saṅkara*, "confusion, mixing," the same word Arjuna used for the social disaster of war (1.41). Kṛṣṇa turns it around: *not* acting would cause confusion.

verses.text: The unwise act attached to action, Bhārata. The wise should act in the same way but without attachment, wishing to hold the world together.
fnotes: The wise and unwise do the same deeds. The difference is entirely in attachment. Outward behavior does not reveal inner freedom.

verses.text: The wise should not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant who are attached to action. Acting with yoga themselves, they should lead them to delight in all actions.
fnotes: *Buddhi-bheda*, "splitting the understanding": the wise should not confuse the ignorant by preaching inaction. This is a principle of pedagogical tact.

verses.text: Actions are performed in every case by the guṇas of nature, but one deluded by I-making thinks, "I am the doer."
fnotes: Programmatic Sāṅkhya: "actions are performed in every case by the guṇas of nature." The deluded self thinks "I am the doer" (*kartāham*). Ahaṅkāra is the false claim of agency.

verses.text: But one who knows the truth about how the guṇas and their actions are divided, mighty-armed one, thinks "guṇas are moving among guṇas" and is not attached.
fnotes: *Guṇā guṇeṣu vartante*, "guṇas move among guṇas": the senses (products of the guṇas) engage with objects (also products of the guṇas). The self only witnesses.

verses.text: Those deluded by the guṇas of nature are attached to the actions of the guṇas. One who knows the whole should not unsettle the slow-witted who know only in part.
Surrender all actions to me with your mind on the inner self [*adhyātma*]. Free from longing and from "mine," fight, with your fever gone.
fnotes: *Mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi saṁnyasya*: "surrendering all actions to me." It is the first explicit instruction of devotional action: "fight, with your fever gone."

verses.text: Those who always follow this teaching of mine, full of faith and without grumbling, are also freed from actions.
But those who grumble at it and do not follow my teaching are bewildered in all knowledge. Know them to be lost and mindless.
Even the wise person acts according to his own nature. Beings follow nature. What will restraint accomplish?
fnotes: "What will restraint accomplish?" A striking concession to nature. Commentators balance it with 3.34: one should not *come under* the power of attraction and aversion.

verses.text: Attraction and aversion lie in wait in the objects of each sense. One should not come under their power, for they are one's enemies on the road.
Better one's own dharma, though imperfect, than another's dharma well performed. Better death in one's own dharma; another's dharma is dangerous.
fnotes: *Śreyān sva-dharmo viguṇaḥ*: "better one's own dharma, though without merit (imperfect)." Repeated almost exactly at 18.47.

verses.text: Then what drives a person to commit evil, Vārṣṇeya, even unwillingly, as if forced?
verses.speaker: Arjuna
fnotes: A classic question of moral psychology: weakness of will (Greek *akrasia*). Why do people do wrong "even unwillingly, as if forced"?

verses.text: It is desire, it is anger, born of the guṇa of rajas: all-devouring and greatly evil. Know it as the enemy here.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: *Kāma eṣa krodha eṣa*: "it is desire, it is anger." They are one force in two forms, born of rajas. *Mahāśana*, "all-devouring," literally "great-eater."

verses.text: As fire is covered by smoke, a mirror by dust, and an embryo by the womb, so this [knowledge] is covered by that [desire].
fnotes: Three images in descending degrees of obscuration: fire covered by smoke (easily cleared), a mirror covered by dust (needs effort), an embryo covered by the womb (needs time).

verses.text: Knowledge is covered, son of Kuntī, by this constant enemy of the wise, which takes the form of desire, an insatiable fire.
The senses, the mind, and the understanding are said to be its seat. Through these it covers knowledge and deludes the embodied one.
fnotes: Desire's "seat" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the senses, mind and understanding, so the enemy occupies all the faculties.

verses.text: Therefore, bull of the Bhāratas, first control the senses. Then kill this evil thing, which destroys knowledge and discernment [*jñāna-vijñāna*].
The senses are high, they say. Higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the understanding; but what is higher than the understanding is *he* [the self].
fnotes: The hierarchy echoes *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 3.10: objects, then senses, mind, understanding, the great self, the unmanifest, and finally the person. The Gītā's "he" (*saḥ*) beyond understanding is the self.

verses.text: Knowing what is higher than the understanding, steady the self by the self, mighty-armed one, and kill the enemy that takes the form of desire, so hard to overcome.
fnotes: *Ātmānam ātmanā*: "steadying the self by the self." The doubled reflexive anticipates 6.5.

chapters.summary: Arjuna asks why, if understanding is higher than action, he must do something terrible. Kṛṣṇa answers that no one can stop acting; what binds is not action but acting from desire. Action done as sacrifice, for the holding-together of the world, as God himself acts, does not bind. The chapter ends by naming the real enemy: desire.
overview: Chapter 3 answers a confusion Chapter 2 created. Kṛṣṇa had praised the "yoga of understanding" over mere action {2.49}, and Arjuna reasonably asks: then why urge me to act at all {3.1}? The chapter's answer is the classic statement of *karma-yoga*. The argument proceeds in five steps. First, action is unavoidable: nature makes everyone act, and fake renunciation is hypocrisy {3.4–8}. Second, action can be done as *sacrifice* (*yajña*), which sustains the cosmic order rather than binding the agent {3.9–16}. Third, even the liberated person, and God himself, act for the "holding-together of the world" {3.17–24}. Fourth, the wise act like the ignorant but without attachment, knowing that "guṇas move among guṇas" {3.25–35}. Fifth, Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong, and Kṛṣṇa names desire and anger, which can be conquered by the self that stands above the understanding {3.36–43}. The chapter thus moves from cosmology (the wheel of sacrifice) through ethics (example and social cohesion) to psychology (desire as the enemy within). It also contains one of the Gītā's most quoted and most contested lines: "Better one's own dharma, though imperfect, than another's dharma well performed" {3.35}.
research: Interpreters have long divided over Chapter 3. Śaṅkara argues that karma-yoga is for those not yet ready for knowledge. It purifies the mind, but the knower, who "has nothing to do" {3.17}, renounces action. Tilak's *Gītā Rahasya* argues the reverse: 3.20–25 show that even the knower must act for *loka-saṅgraha*, and this is the Gītā's real teaching. This debate is still the key fault line in readings of the Gītā's ethics. Historians of religion study 3.9–16 as evidence of the Gītā's relationship to Vedic ritualism. The text keeps the cosmic logic of sacrifice but universalizes it, a move parallel to the "interiorization of sacrifice" in the Upaniṣads (studied by J. C. Heesterman and others). Recent work on 3.35 (*svadharma*) examines how the verse was used both to defend caste and, by modern reformers, to defend individual vocation. Readers interested in the psychology of 3.36–43 will find parallels in contemporary research on "ego depletion" and self-control, though the theoretical frameworks differ sharply.
questions: Is the knower who "has nothing to do" (3.17) obliged to act (3.20–25)? Reconstruct both Śaṅkara's and Tilak's answers.
What does it mean to treat ordinary work as "sacrifice"? Does the idea survive outside its ritual context?
Is "better one's own dharma" (3.35) a conservative principle, a liberating one, or both?
Kṛṣṇa locates the enemy inside the agent (3.37). How does this reframe Arjuna's original problem of fighting enemies outside?

nodes.label: Why act, if understanding is higher?
nodes.text: Arjuna's question exposes an apparent contradiction in Chapter 2.

nodes.label: No one can stop acting
nodes.text: Nature's guṇas make every being act. Outward abstention with inner craving is hypocrisy.

nodes.label: Act as sacrifice
nodes.text: Action done for sacrifice does not bind; it keeps the wheel of the world turning.

nodes.label: The wheel: food, rain, sacrifice, action
nodes.text: Beings come from food, food from rain, rain from sacrifice, sacrifice from action, action from brahman.

nodes.label: Act for the world's cohesion
nodes.text: Even the one with nothing to gain should act, to hold the world together and set an example.

nodes.label: God acts without need
nodes.text: If I stopped acting, the worlds would perish. God is the first karma-yogin.

nodes.label: Guṇas move among guṇas
nodes.text: The self is not the doer; seeing this frees one from attachment.

nodes.label: Better one's own dharma
nodes.text: One's own imperfect path is safer than another's well-performed one.

nodes.label: The enemy is desire
nodes.text: Born of rajas, all-devouring: desire and anger cover knowledge like smoke over fire.

nodes.label: The self above understanding
nodes.text: Senses, mind, understanding, then the self beyond. From there, desire can be conquered.

sections.title: Why act at all? Action is unavoidable
sections.lead: Arjuna objects that Kṛṣṇa's teaching seems contradictory; Kṛṣṇa answers that no embodied being can stop acting.
reconstruction: Arjuna's objection is logical. If understanding is superior, why perform this terrible act? Kṛṣṇa first grants that there are two traditional paths, knowledge and action {3.3}. Then he argues that the choice is not between acting and not acting. Freedom from action cannot be won by abstaining {3.4}. Every being acts constantly, driven by nature {3.5}. One who stops the body while the mind keeps desiring is a hypocrite {3.6}. So the only real question is *how* to act. One who controls the senses with the mind and acts without attachment excels {3.7}. Therefore, perform your prescribed action {3.8}.
insight: The argument rests on an empirical premise, that action is unavoidable, and turns it against the renunciant ideal. If even sitting still is action, then "not acting" is not an available option, and the question must be about the *spirit* of action. This is a decisive move in the history of Indian ethics, because it denies the monastic withdrawal its claim to be the only route to freedom. The hypocrite of 3.6 is a sharp image. Outward abstention can mask inward craving, and that is worse than honest engagement. The Gītā thus relocates the moral question from behavior to motivation.
sources: The dilemma of action and liberation is central to the *Mokṣadharma* section of the Mahābhārata's twelfth book and to the debates between renunciants and householders (e.g., Janaka's dialogue with the nun Sulabhā, *Mahābhārata* 12.308). The *Īśā Upaniṣad* 2 (keep doing works; action does not cling) is the closest Upaniṣadic precedent.
context: The debate between contemplative and active lives runs through Western thought: Aristotle's two lives (theoretical and political) in *Nicomachean Ethics* X, Martha and Mary in Luke 10, and medieval debates on the *vita activa* and *vita contemplativa*. Hannah Arendt's *The Human Condition* revived it. The Gītā's distinctive claim is that the two need not be chosen between.
matters: Many people imagine that peace requires escape: from work, from responsibility, from the world. The Gītā argues that escape is impossible and that peace must be found within action. That is a demanding but realistic teaching.
questions: Is Kṛṣṇa's premise in 3.5 true? Are there forms of "non-action" that are genuinely possible?
Who is the "hypocrite" of 3.6 in modern life?
If both knowledge and action lead to the goal (3.3), why does Kṛṣṇa insist that Arjuna act?

premises.label: No one can stop acting even for a moment
premises.text: Nature drives all beings to act.

premises.label: Outward abstention with inner craving is hypocrisy
premises.text: Renunciation of behavior is not renunciation of desire.

claim.label: Perform your prescribed action, without attachment
claim.text: The question is not whether to act but how.

implications.label: Freedom from action comes within action
implications.text: The renunciant's goal is reached by the karma-yogin.

sections.title: Action as sacrifice: the wheel of the world
sections.lead: Action done as sacrifice does not bind; it participates in the reciprocal wheel that sustains gods, humans and nature.
reconstruction: The world is bound by action, except action done for sacrifice {3.9}. At creation, the Lord of creatures made beings together with sacrifice and told them that through it they would prosper {3.10}. Gods and humans nourish one another {3.11}. To take nature's gifts without giving back is theft {3.12}. Those who eat after offering are freed from fault, and those who cook only for themselves eat evil {3.13}. A great wheel links beings, food, rain, sacrifice, action and the Veda, which is rooted in the imperishable {3.14–15}. Whoever refuses to turn this wheel, living only for the senses, lives in vain {3.16}.
insight: The passage turns an ancient ritual cosmology into an ethic of reciprocity. Its core claim is that the self-enclosed agent, who takes and does not give, both violates the order of the world and binds itself. Action done *as* offering, as participation in a larger cycle, has a different structure. It is not appropriation but circulation. Philosophically the passage relocates the "fruit" of action. In sacrifice the fruit is not kept but passed on. The agent eats only "what remains." This gives karma-yoga a concrete form. It is not an abstract renunciation of results but a practice of offering them back to the whole.
sources: The creation-with-sacrifice motif is Vedic: *Ṛg Veda* 10.90 (the Puruṣa hymn) describes the world created from a primordial sacrifice. Prajāpati's creative sacrifice dominates the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*. The chain of rain and food recalls *Manu* 3.76 ("the oblation duly cast into fire reaches the sun; from the sun comes rain; from rain, food; from food, creatures").
context: Reciprocal gift as the basis of social and cosmic order was famously theorized by Marcel Mauss (*The Gift*, 1925) and reexamined by Lewis Hyde. Contemporary environmental ethics, for instance Robin Wall Kimmerer's *Braiding Sweetgrass*, also proposes that taking without giving back is a kind of theft from the earth. The Gītā's wheel offers an ancient articulation of an ethics of reciprocity with nature.
matters: The passage asks us to see our work and consumption as part of a cycle that sustains others, and to ask whether we are givers or thieves in it.
questions: Is the idea of "sacrifice" still meaningful in a secular context? What would count as sacrifice in your work?
What is the ethical difference between "eating what remains from the sacrifice" and "cooking only for oneself"?
Compare 3.12's "thief" with ecological ideas of reciprocity. Is this anthropocentric, cosmocentric, or neither?

premises.label: The world is bound by action, except action for sacrifice
premises.text: Sacrificial action has a different structure: it offers rather than appropriates.

premises.label: Gods, humans and nature sustain one another
premises.text: A wheel of reciprocity: food, rain, sacrifice, action.

claim.label: Take part in the wheel; do not take without giving
claim.text: One who enjoys gifts without offering is a thief and lives in vain.

implications.label: Eating "what remains" frees from fault
implications.text: The practice of offering before enjoying makes action non-binding.

sections.title: The wise and God act for the holding-together of the world
sections.lead: Even one who has nothing left to gain should act, for the world's sake, as Janaka did and as God himself does.
reconstruction: One who delights in the self alone has nothing that must be done and depends on no one {3.17–18}. Yet Kṛṣṇa says, "therefore act without attachment" {3.19}. Janaka and other royal sages reached perfection through action, and they acted for the holding-together of the world {3.20}. People imitate the best, so their conduct sets the standard {3.21}. God himself has nothing to gain, yet he acts {3.22}. If he did not, people would follow his example. The worlds would perish and he would cause confusion {3.23–24}.
insight: This is the passage on which activist readings of the Gītā rest. Its argument has two parts. One is *exemplary*: the wise must act because others follow them. The other is *cosmic*: God's ceaseless action sustains the world, and the sage participates in that action. Both make action independent of personal need. The knower does not act *for* anything, yet acts. There is a genuine tension with 3.17–18, which Śaṅkara exploits. If the knower has nothing to do, then the command to act seems to apply only to the unenlightened. Tilak replies that 3.20–25 explicitly extend the duty to the wise "for the world's sake." Both readings fit parts of the text. The question is whether the Gītā's highest ideal is a renouncer who acts *despite* freedom, or one who acts *from* it.
sources: Janaka appears as a king-sage in *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.1–4.4 and in many Mahābhārata dialogues. The theme of the king as exemplar is central to Indian political thought (e.g., *Arthaśāstra* 1.19: "if the king is energetic, his subjects will be energetic").
context: Plato's *Republic* (VII) poses the same problem. Why should the philosopher who has seen the Good return to the cave to govern? Plato's answer (duty to the city that formed him) and the Gītā's (loka-saṅgraha, divine imitation) can be fruitfully compared. In Mahāyāna Buddhism, the bodhisattva who delays nirvāṇa to save others offers another parallel.
matters: The passage addresses anyone who has "made it," materially or spiritually, and asks what they owe to others. Its answer: everything, without needing anything in return.
questions: Does the knower of 3.17 have duties? Argue both sides.
How strong is the argument from example (3.21)? Can a private person be a "best person" whom others follow?
Compare the return to the cave in Plato with 3.20–25. What motivates each return?

premises.label: The self-content have nothing they must do
premises.text: Complete freedom from need.

premises.label: Others follow the example of the best
premises.text: Leaders' conduct sets the standard.

premises.label: God acts without any need, to sustain the world
premises.text: Divine action is free and ceaseless.

claim.label: The wise should act, for the holding-together of the world
claim.text: Action without need, for others.

implications.label: Withdrawal would cause confusion
implications.text: Arjuna's fear of "confusion" is reversed: inaction, not action, brings chaos.

sections.title: The wise and the unwise; the guṇas act; one's own dharma
sections.lead: The wise act outwardly like the ignorant but inwardly free, knowing that nature acts and the self is not the doer; one should follow one's own dharma.
reconstruction: The wise act like the ignorant, but without attachment, for the world's sake {3.25}. They should not unsettle those attached to action; they should model good action {3.26}. All action is done by nature's guṇas, and only the deluded self thinks "I am the doer" {3.27}. One who sees that guṇas act on guṇas is not attached {3.28}. So surrender all actions to me and fight, free of fever {3.30}. Those who follow this teaching are freed {3.31}. Nature is powerful, and even the wise act according to it {3.33}. But one should not fall under the power of attraction and aversion {3.34}. Better to follow one's own dharma imperfectly than another's well {3.35}.
insight: Here the Gītā's metaphysics of agency becomes ethics. If nature acts and the self only witnesses, then the feeling "I did this, so the result is mine" is an illusion, and attachment collapses with it. The move is subtle. Kṛṣṇa does not say actions do not happen or do not matter. He says the *ownership* of action is misattributed. Two tensions deserve attention. First, if nature acts and "restraint accomplishes nothing" {3.33}, how can one be responsible for anything? The text's implicit answer is that one can choose whether to *identify* with nature's movements. Freedom lies in that identification, not in the movements themselves. Second, 3.35's *svadharma* principle can be read as fatalistic conservatism ("stay in your place") or as a principle of authenticity ("be true to your nature"). Both readings have been dominant in different eras.
sources: The Sāṅkhya theory of the guṇas as sole agents appears in the *Mokṣadharma* and later in *Sāṅkhya-kārikā* 19–20 (the puruṣa is a witness, "non-agent"). *Svadharma* is a Dharmaśāstra principle (*Manu* 10.97 is nearly identical to 3.35).
context: The thesis that "nature acts, the self witnesses" invites comparison with Spinoza (the mind as idea of the body, freedom as understanding necessity) and with contemporary debates on free will and the "illusion of conscious will" (Daniel Wegner). The authenticity reading of 3.35 resembles Kierkegaard's or Nietzsche's "become who you are."
matters: Seeing that much of what we do arises from conditions we did not choose can loosen guilt, pride and anxiety, without dissolving responsibility for how we respond.
questions: If the guṇas act, who is responsible? Reconstruct the Gītā's implicit answer.
Why should the wise not "unsettle the understanding" of the ignorant (3.26)? Is this paternalism or tact?
Read 3.35 as a conservative principle and then as an existentialist one. Which reading does the text support?

premises.label: Nature's guṇas perform all actions
premises.text: The self is a witness, not the doer.

premises.label: The sense "I am the doer" is delusion
premises.text: I-making appropriates nature's acts.

claim.label: Seeing that guṇas move among guṇas, the wise act unattached
claim.text: Surrender all actions to God and fight without fever.

implications.label: Follow your own dharma, though imperfect
implications.text: Act from your own nature rather than imitating another's path.

implications.label: The wise model action for others
implications.text: They should not unsettle the understanding of those who act.

sections.title: Desire, the enemy within
sections.lead: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Kṛṣṇa names desire and anger and teaches how to conquer them.
reconstruction: Arjuna asks why people do wrong as if compelled {3.36}. Kṛṣṇa answers that desire, which becomes anger when frustrated, is the enemy {3.37}. It covers knowledge as smoke covers fire, dust a mirror, or the womb an embryo {3.38}. It is insatiable {3.39}. It operates through the senses, mind and understanding {3.40}. So control the senses first and kill this destroyer of knowledge {3.41}. There is a hierarchy: senses, mind, understanding, and beyond them the self {3.42}. Knowing the self, steady yourself and conquer desire {3.43}.
insight: The section completes the chapter's arc. Arjuna began by asking whether to fight others; he ends by learning that the real enemy is within. The Gītā does not deny the outer battle, but it subordinates it to the inner one. This explains why Gandhi could read the whole text as allegory. The account of weakness of will differs instructively from Socrates' (no one does wrong willingly; wrongdoing is ignorance). For the Gītā, knowledge is real but can be *covered*. One can know the good and be carried away. The remedy is not more information but a reordering of the faculties under the self. That is closer to Aristotle's view of *akrasia* than to Socrates'.
sources: The ordered hierarchy of faculties is from *Kaṭha* 3.10–11 and the chariot allegory (*Kaṭha* 3.3–9). Desire as an insatiable fire appears in *Manu* 2.94 ("desire is never quenched by enjoying objects; it only grows, like fire fed with ghee"), a line that is also in the Mahābhārata.
context: Comparisons include Plato's tripartite soul (reason ruling spirit and appetite, *Republic* IV), Aristotle on *akrasia* (*Nicomachean Ethics* VII), Paul's "the good that I would I do not" (Romans 7:19), and the Buddhist second noble truth that craving (*taṇhā*) is the origin of suffering. Contemporary psychology of self-regulation and addiction gives the question new urgency.
matters: Almost everyone knows the experience of acting against their own better judgment. The Gītā offers both a diagnosis (desire covering knowledge) and a discipline (rule the senses, steady the self).
questions: Compare 3.36–43 with Socrates' and Aristotle's accounts of weakness of will. Which is closest?
What do the three images of 3.38 suggest about degrees of moral blindness?
How does locating the enemy within change the meaning of Arjuna's war?

premises.label: Desire and anger, born of rajas, cover knowledge
premises.text: The enemy hides knowledge like smoke hides fire.

premises.label: The self is higher than the understanding
premises.text: There is a standpoint above desire's seat.

implications.text: The struggle against desire is the condition of right action.

chapters.colophon: Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the third chapter, called “The Yoga of Action.”

chapters.title: The Yoga of Knowledge and the Renunciation of Action

verses.text: I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat [the sun]. Vivasvat told it to Manu, and Manu told it to Ikṣvāku.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: The lineage: Vivasvat (the sun), Manu (first human, law-giver), Ikṣvāku (founder of the solar dynasty, Rāma's lineage). The teaching is thus older than the Vedic ritual order Kṛṣṇa has been criticizing.

verses.text: Handed down in this succession, the royal seers knew it. But with the long passage of time, scorcher of foes, this yoga was lost here.
fnotes: *Rājarṣi*, "royal seers": the yoga was originally a teaching for kings. The epic often presents wisdom as the province of the warrior class (cf. the Upaniṣadic kings Janaka and Pravāhaṇa Jaivali).

verses.text: Today I have declared this same ancient yoga to you, for you are my devotee and my friend. This is the supreme secret.
Your birth was later and Vivasvat's was earlier. How am I to understand that you taught it in the beginning?
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: Many births of mine have passed, Arjuna, and many of yours. I know them all, but you do not know them, scorcher of foes.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: "Many births of mine have passed": the first claim of repeated divine birth. Arjuna, too, has had many births. The difference is knowledge.

verses.text: Though I am unborn and my self is imperishable, though I am lord of beings, I come into being by my own power [*ātma-māyā*], governing my own nature.
fnotes: *Ātma-māyā*, "my own māyā," i.e., power. The divine birth is not compelled by karma but freely chosen, "governing my own nature."

verses.text: Whenever dharma declines, Bhārata, and adharma rises, then I send myself forth.
fnotes: *Yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati*: one of the most recited verses in the Gītā. *Glāni* means "fading, exhaustion."

verses.text: To protect the good, to destroy evildoers, and to establish dharma, I come into being age after age [*yuge yuge*].
fnotes: *Paritrāṇāya sādhūnām*: three purposes of the descent. Note "age after age" (*yuge yuge*).

verses.text: One who truly knows my divine birth and action is not born again on leaving the body. That one comes to me, Arjuna.
Free from passion, fear, and anger, absorbed in me and taking refuge in me, purified by the austerity of knowledge, many have come to my state of being.
In whatever way people approach me, in that way I share myself with them [*bhajāmi*]. Everywhere, Pārtha, people follow my path.
fnotes: *Ye yathā māṁ prapadyante tāṁs tathaiva bhajāmy aham*: God responds to each according to their approach. Vivekananda and others read the second half ("people everywhere follow my path") as a charter of religious pluralism.

verses.text: Wanting success from their actions, people here sacrifice to the gods, for in the human world success born of action comes quickly.
I created the four social orders [*cātur-varṇya*] according to the division of guṇa and action. Though I am their maker, know me as the non-doer, imperishable.
tnotes: The verse grounds the four social orders in *guṇa* and *karma* (quality and action), not explicitly in birth. Readers have long debated whether birth is implied.
fnotes: See the translator's note. *Cātur-varṇya*, the "fourfold order," is grounded in guṇa and karma. Its implications for caste are hotly debated.

verses.text: Actions do not taint me, and I have no longing for their fruit. One who knows me in this way is not bound by actions.
fnotes: God as model of non-attached action: "actions do not taint me."

verses.text: Knowing this, the ancient seekers of liberation also performed action. So perform action, as the ancients did long ago.
What is action? What is inaction? Even the wise are confused here. I will explain action to you, and knowing it you will be freed from evil.
fnotes: *Kiṁ karma kim akarmeti kavayo 'py atra mohitāḥ*: "even poets/seers are confused."

verses.text: One must understand action, understand wrong action [*vikarma*], and understand inaction. The way of action is deep.
fnotes: Three categories: *karma* (action), *vikarma* (wrong or forbidden action, or by some readings "special" action), *akarma* (inaction). *Gahanā karmaṇo gatiḥ*: "deep is the way of action."

verses.text: One who sees inaction in action and action in inaction is wise among humans. That one is yoked, even while performing all action.
fnotes: The central paradox. Śaṅkara reads it as: the knower sees that the self does not act even when the body acts (inaction in action), and that the ignorant renunciant who claims to do nothing is actually acting (action in inaction). Rāmānuja reads "inaction" as knowledge of the self present within action.

verses.text: When all of a person's undertakings are free of desire and intention [*saṅkalpa*], and that person's actions are burned up in the fire of knowledge, the wise call that person learned.
fnotes: *Jñānāgni-dagdha-karmāṇam*: actions "burned by the fire of knowledge," like seeds roasted so that they cannot sprout.

verses.text: Abandoning attachment to the fruit of action, always content and dependent on nothing, such a person does nothing at all, even while engaged in action.
fnotes: *Naiva kiñcit karoti saḥ*: such a one "does nothing at all," even while acting.

verses.text: Without longing, with mind and self restrained, giving up all possessions, doing action with the body alone, one incurs no fault.
Content with whatever comes by chance, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, the same in success and failure, such a person is not bound even when acting.
fnotes: *Yadṛcchā-lābha-santuṣṭaḥ*: "content with whatever comes by chance."

verses.text: When a person's attachment is gone and he is free, with mind established in knowledge and acting for the sake of sacrifice, his action dissolves entirely.
fnotes: *Pravilīyate*: action "dissolves," leaving no karmic residue.

verses.text: The offering is brahman; the oblation is brahman, poured by brahman into the fire that is brahman. One who sees brahman in action, as in concentration, will reach brahman.
fnotes: *Brahmārpaṇaṁ brahma haviḥ*: the most famous verse of this section, recited by many Hindus as a grace before meals. Every element of the sacrifice (offering, oblation, fire, offerer, goal) is brahman. It is an Advaitic verse par excellence.

verses.text: Some yogins offer sacrifice to the gods alone; others offer sacrifice, by sacrifice itself, into the fire of brahman.
fnotes: Two kinds of yogins: some sacrifice to the gods (ritual), others offer "sacrifice by sacrifice," which may mean offering the self into brahman.

verses.text: Some offer hearing and the other senses into the fires of restraint; others offer sound and the other objects into the fires of the senses.
fnotes: Two forms of sense-discipline: offering the senses into restraint (withdrawal), and offering objects into the senses (non-attached enjoyment).

verses.text: Others offer all the actions of the senses and of the vital breath into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge.
Others sacrifice with material goods, with austerity, or with yoga, and ascetics of strict vows sacrifice through study and knowledge.
fnotes: *Dravya-yajña*, sacrifice with goods; *tapo-yajña*, of austerity; *yoga-yajña*, of yoga; *svādhyāya-jñāna-yajña*, of study and knowledge.

verses.text: Others, intent on breath-control, offer the in-breath into the out-breath and the out-breath into the in-breath, restraining the course of both.
fnotes: Breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*): in-breath (*prāṇa*) and out-breath (*apāna*) offered into each other. Early evidence for breath practices later systematized in haṭha yoga.

verses.text: Others, restricting their food, offer breaths into breaths. All of these know sacrifice, and their faults are destroyed by sacrifice.
Eating the nectar that remains from sacrifice, they go to eternal brahman. This world is not for one who does not sacrifice, best of Kurus, much less the next.
fnotes: "This world is not for one who does not sacrifice," *nāyaṁ loko 'sty ayajñasya*.

verses.text: Many kinds of sacrifice are spread out like this in the mouth of brahman. Know that they are all born of action. Knowing this, you will be freed.
fnotes: *Brahmaṇo mukhe*: "in the mouth of brahman," either the Veda or the fire as divine mouth.

verses.text: Sacrifice made of knowledge is better than sacrifice of material things, scorcher of foes. All action without exception, Pārtha, culminates in knowledge.
fnotes: *Jñāna-yajña*, "the sacrifice of knowledge," is better than material sacrifice. All action culminates (*parisamāpyate*) in knowledge.

verses.text: Learn this by bowing down, by inquiry, and by service. The wise who see the truth will teach you knowledge.
fnotes: *Praṇipātena paripraśnena sevayā*: three means of learning: prostration, inquiry and service. *Tattva-darśinaḥ*, "those who see the truth."

verses.text: Knowing it, Pāṇḍava, you will not fall into delusion like this again. By it you will see all beings without exception in the self, and then in me.
fnotes: "You will see all beings in the self, and then in me" (*ātmany atho mayi*): a sequence from self-knowledge to knowledge of God.

verses.text: Even if you were the worst of all evildoers, the boat of knowledge alone would carry you across all wickedness.
fnotes: A radical promise: "even the worst of all evildoers" crosses over by the "boat of knowledge."

verses.text: As a kindled fire reduces its fuel to ashes, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.
Nothing here purifies like knowledge. One perfected in yoga finds it, in time, within oneself.
fnotes: *Na hi jñānena sadṛśaṁ pavitram iha vidyate*: "nothing here purifies like knowledge."

verses.text: One who has faith [*śraddhā*], is intent on knowledge, and restrains the senses gains it. Having gained knowledge, one soon reaches supreme peace.
fnotes: *Śraddhāvāl labhate jñānam*: "one who has faith gains knowledge." Faith is a precondition, not an opponent, of knowledge.

verses.text: The ignorant self, without faith and full of doubt, perishes. For the doubter there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness.
fnotes: *Saṁśayātmā vinaśyati*: "the doubting self perishes." A strong condemnation of chronic doubt.

verses.text: Actions do not bind one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubt has been cut away by knowledge, and who possesses the self, Dhanañjaya.
So take the sword of knowledge and cut this doubt in your heart, born of ignorance. Resort to yoga. Stand up, Bhārata!
fnotes: The chapter ends as Chapter 2 began: "Stand up!" (*uttiṣṭha*).

chapters.summary: Kṛṣṇa reveals that he taught this yoga at the beginning of time and takes birth "age after age" to restore dharma. He explains the subtle relation of action and inaction, describes many forms of sacrifice, and praises knowledge as the fire that burns all action to ashes. Arjuna is told to cut his doubt with the sword of knowledge and stand up.
overview: Chapter 4 changes the status of the speaker. Until now Kṛṣṇa has spoken as a wise friend. Now he claims to have taught this yoga to the sun at the dawn of the world {4.1}, and he reveals the doctrine of divine descent: "whenever dharma declines… I send myself forth" {4.7}. The teaching is no longer simply wise; it is revealed. The chapter then deepens the theory of action. The famous paradox "one who sees inaction in action and action in inaction is wise" {4.18} becomes the key to a life of action without bondage. Next comes a remarkable catalogue of "sacrifices" {4.24–32}: offering the senses, the breath, study, austerity. It extends the ritual idea of 3.9–16 to every discipline of life. Finally knowledge is praised as the supreme sacrifice and the supreme purifier {4.33–39}, preparing the integration of action and knowledge that Chapter 5 will complete. The chapter title joins three terms: knowledge, action and renunciation. Its project is to show that they are not rivals.
research: Chapter 4 is a key text for the history of *avatāra* theology. The word itself is absent, but 4.7–8 became its classic charter. Scholars debate how early Kṛṣṇa's identification with Viṣṇu was, and whether the Gītā presupposes a developed doctrine of multiple descents (Freda Matchett, Noel Sheth). Recent work by Angelika Malinar reads Chapter 4 as a political theology: the king-god who protects dharma models the ideal ruler. Another focus is 4.13's account of the four social orders "according to guṇa and action." Historians of caste (e.g., Brian K. Smith) read the verse within brahmanical ideology. Others, including some modern commentators, use it to argue that the Gītā defines class by character and conduct. The interpretive stakes for contemporary Hindu ethics are high. The catalogue of sacrifices in 4.25–32 is valuable evidence for the variety of ascetic and yogic practices of the period. Historians of yoga (e.g., David Gordon White, James Mallinson and Mark Singleton) use it alongside early Buddhist and Jain sources.
questions: How does the revelation of 4.1–8 change the authority of Kṛṣṇa's teaching? Should it change how we evaluate his earlier arguments?
Explain 4.18 in your own words. Construct an example of "inaction in action" and of "action in inaction."
Why does the Gītā redescribe so many practices as "sacrifice"? What is gained and what is lost?
Is faith (4.39–40) a condition of knowledge, or a substitute for it?

sections.title: The ancient yoga and God's descent
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa reveals that he taught this yoga at the beginning and that he takes birth again and again to restore dharma.
reconstruction: This yoga is not new. Kṛṣṇa taught it at the beginning to the sun, and it passed down through royal sages until it was lost {4.1–2}. Arjuna objects that Kṛṣṇa was born recently {4.4}. Kṛṣṇa answers that he has had many births. Though unborn, he comes into being by his own power whenever dharma declines, to protect the good, destroy the wicked and restore order {4.5–8}. Whoever understands this divine birth and action is freed from rebirth {4.9–10}. God meets everyone in the way they approach him {4.11}. He created the four orders according to quality and action, yet is not their doer, since actions do not touch him {4.13–14}. Knowing this, the ancients acted, and so should Arjuna {4.15}.
insight: The section transforms the dialogue. Earlier arguments could be judged on their merits. Now the speaker claims divine authority. Some readers see this as a weakening: argument gives way to revelation. Others see a deepening. The model of non-attached action is no longer a hypothetical sage but God himself, who acts constantly, takes birth freely, and is never bound. The doctrine of descent also gives the Gītā a philosophy of history. Dharma is not static. It decays and must be renewed, and the divine enters history to renew it. This links the teaching to the war. Arjuna's battle is part of God's work of restoring dharma.
sources: The solar lineage (Vivasvat, Manu, Ikṣvāku) belongs to Purāṇic and epic genealogy. The idea of God's repeated intervention is developed later in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* and *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* lists of avatāras. The religious context is the Bhāgavata or Pāñcarātra worship of Vāsudeva, attested from the 2nd century BCE.
context: Comparisons include the Christian doctrine of incarnation, which differs in being singular and in involving real suffering and death. Religious pluralism read from 4.11 resonates with Ramakrishna's "as many faiths, so many paths" and with John Hick's pluralist hypothesis in philosophy of religion.
matters: The section raises a lasting question: when moral order collapses, does help come from beyond human effort? It also offers one of the oldest scriptural bases for religious pluralism.
questions: Does the revelation of Kṛṣṇa's divinity strengthen or weaken the force of his arguments?
Compare the Gītā's descent (avatāra) with Christian incarnation. What are the key differences?
Can 4.11 support religious pluralism? What in the text resists that reading?

premises.label: This yoga is ancient and was lost
premises.text: Its authority predates the Vedic ritual order.

premises.label: God takes birth freely, by his own power
premises.text: Unborn, he is not compelled by karma.

claim.label: God descends age after age to restore dharma
claim.text: Divine action enters history to protect the good.
