implications.text: He is the model of non-attached action.

implications.label: Knowing this frees from rebirth
implications.text: Understanding divine action is itself liberating.

sections.title: Action, inaction and wrong action
sections.lead: Even the wise are confused about action; the true sage sees inaction in action and action in inaction.
reconstruction: What action is, and what inaction is, puzzles even sages {4.16}. One must understand action, wrong action and inaction, for the way of action is deep {4.17}. The wise person sees inaction in action and action in inaction {4.18}. When undertakings are free of desire and intention, action is burned in knowledge's fire {4.19}. Without attachment to fruit, content and independent, one acts yet "does nothing at all" {4.20}. With a controlled mind and no possessiveness, bodily action incurs no fault {4.21}. Content with what comes, beyond opposites, the same in success and failure, one is not bound {4.22}. For one free and acting for sacrifice, action dissolves {4.23}.
insight: The paradox of 4.18 is the conceptual knot of karma-yoga. It distinguishes the *outer form* of an act from its *inner reality*. An outwardly busy life can be inwardly still; an outwardly idle one can be inwardly frantic. "Action," in the binding sense, is the inner movement of desire and appropriation, not bodily movement. Once this is seen, Arjuna's dilemma (act and be bound, or refrain and be free) dissolves. He can act and be free. The danger is that the paradox can excuse anything: "I am not really acting." The Gītā blocks this by tying the state to strict conditions. Desire, intention, attachment and possessiveness must be gone {4.19–22}. The paradox is a description of a rare achievement, not a license.
sources: The image of actions as seeds burned by knowledge appears in the *Yoga-sūtra* commentarial tradition and in Buddhist texts (the arhat's actions as "roasted seeds"). The phrase "deep is the way of action" echoes the epic's frequent "subtle is dharma."
context: Daoism's *wu wei* ("non-action," acting without forcing) in the *Daodejing* (e.g., ch. 48: "doing nothing, yet nothing is left undone") is the closest parallel in world thought. Meister Eckhart's "releasement" (*Gelassenheit*) and contemporary psychology of "flow" (Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi), in which skilled action is effortless and self-forgetful, are also illuminating.
matters: Most of us experience either busy agitation or guilty idleness. The Gītā describes a third possibility, full action with inner stillness, and defines its conditions precisely.
questions: Give a concrete example of "inaction in action" and of "action in inaction" (4.18).
How does the paradox avoid becoming an excuse for doing anything at all?
Compare 4.18 with Daoist *wu wei*. Is "non-action" the same idea in both?

premises.label: Action binds through desire and intention
premises.text: The binding element is inner, not outward movement.

premises.label: The self is not the true agent
premises.text: Without attachment, one "does nothing at all" even while acting.

claim.label: The wise see inaction in action and action in inaction
claim.text: The inner reality of action differs from its outer form.

implications.label: Action done as sacrifice dissolves
implications.text: It leaves no binding residue.

implications.label: Contentment and evenness are the conditions
implications.text: The paradox is not a license but a description of achievement.

sections.title: The many forms of sacrifice
sections.lead: Every discipline, from ritual to breath-control to study, can be a sacrifice offered into brahman.
reconstruction: In the highest view, every element of sacrifice is brahman {4.24}. From there, Kṛṣṇa lists the many sacrifices people make. Some offer to the gods, some offer the self into brahman {4.25}. Some offer the senses into restraint, some offer objects into the senses {4.26}. Some offer the activity of senses and breath into the fire of self-control {4.27}. Some offer goods, austerity, yoga, study {4.28}. Some practice breath-control or fasting {4.29–30}. All of them, eating the "nectar" of sacrifice, reach brahman. Without sacrifice, neither this world nor the next is possible {4.31}. All are born of action; knowing this, one is freed {4.32}.
insight: This section universalizes sacrifice. The Vedic fire-ritual becomes a template for every kind of disciplined self-offering. The effect is twofold. First, it validates many paths: ritualist, ascetic, yogin and scholar all perform genuine sacrifices. Second, it shifts the essence of sacrifice from the external act to the inner attitude of offering. This is the bridge between the ritual world and the world of yoga and devotion. The opening verse (4.24) is also philosophically striking. It suggests a vision in which the distinction between agent, act, instrument and goal collapses into one reality. Advaitins treat it as a description of liberated action, which is entirely non-dual.
sources: The interiorization of sacrifice is anticipated in the Upaniṣads, e.g., the *prāṇāgnihotra* (offering into the breath as a fire, *Chāndogya* 5.19–24) and the idea of "the sacrifice of the self" in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*. Breath-control as sacrifice is described in the *Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad* 2.5 ("the inner fire-offering").
context: The spiritualization of sacrifice is a cross-cultural phenomenon. Compare the Hebrew prophets ("I desire mercy, not sacrifice," Hosea 6:6), Paul's "living sacrifice" (Romans 12:1), and Guy Stroumsa's *The End of Sacrifice* on late antiquity. The Gītā shows a parallel transformation in India.
matters: The passage suggests that any committed discipline (study, generosity, self-restraint, attention to breath) can be lived as an offering rather than as a means to personal gain. That reframing changes how such practices feel and what they do to us.
questions: Why might 4.24 have become a grace before meals? What does reciting it do?
Is anything lost when ritual sacrifice is "interiorized"?
Which of the sacrifices of 4.25–30 have equivalents in your life?

premises.label: All elements of sacrifice are brahman
premises.text: Offerer, offering, fire and goal are one reality.

premises.label: Many disciplines are forms of sacrifice
premises.text: Sense-restraint, breath-control, austerity, study and more.

claim.label: Every discipline can be an offering into brahman
claim.text: Sacrifice is defined by inner offering, not outward form.

implications.label: Without sacrifice there is no world
implications.text: Self-offering sustains this world and the next.

sections.title: The fire of knowledge
sections.lead: Knowledge is the highest sacrifice and the supreme purifier; with faith and the guidance of teachers, it cuts doubt and frees from all bondage.
reconstruction: Knowledge is the best sacrifice, for all action culminates in it {4.33}. Learn it from those who see the truth, by humility, inquiry and service {4.34}. With it you will see all beings in yourself and in God {4.35}. Even the worst sinner crosses over by its boat {4.36}. Like fire turning wood to ash, it burns all action {4.37}. Nothing purifies like it {4.38}. The one with faith and self-control gains it and finds peace {4.39}. The faithless doubter perishes {4.40}. Actions do not bind one whose doubts are cut by knowledge {4.41}. So cut your doubt with knowledge's sword, take up yoga, and stand {4.42}.
insight: Here knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*karma*) are brought together. Action culminates in knowledge, and knowledge frees action from bondage. Śaṅkara reads this as subordinating action to knowledge. Others read it as fusing them: knowledgeable action. The sword image of 4.42 is telling. Knowledge is not passive contemplation but a weapon that enables action. The treatment of faith and doubt is interesting philosophically. The Gītā does not oppose faith to knowledge. Faith is the disposition of trust that makes learning possible. The "doubting self" is not the critical inquirer (Arjuna's questions are welcomed) but the chronically divided mind that commits to nothing, the "many-branched" understanding of 2.41.
sources: The teacher-student model of 4.34 echoes *Muṇḍaka* 1.2.12–13 and *Chāndogya* 6. The purifying power of knowledge is Upaniṣadic (*Muṇḍaka* 2.2.8: "when he is seen… all his actions perish"). The image of the boat appears in *Muṇḍaka* 1.2.7, ironically there applied to ritual as an "unsteady boat."
context: The relation of faith and reason is a theme in many traditions: Anselm's *fides quaerens intellectum* ("faith seeking understanding"), William James's "The Will to Believe," and the Buddhist *saddhā* that initiates practice. The Gītā's "doubting self" resembles Kierkegaard's critique of the endlessly reflective spectator who never commits.
matters: The passage asks whether understanding grows best through suspicion or through trust. It also suggests that wisdom is best learned in relationship, from those who embody it.
questions: What is the difference between a questioning mind and a "doubting self" (4.40)?
Why must knowledge be learned from teachers (4.34) rather than reasoned out alone?
Does "nothing purifies like knowledge" (4.38) fit with a moral teaching? What kind of knowledge is meant?

premises.label: All action culminates in knowledge
premises.text: Knowledge is the highest sacrifice.

premises.label: Knowledge burns all actions to ashes
premises.text: It removes karmic bondage.

premises.label: Faith and self-control are its conditions
premises.text: Trust makes learning possible.

claim.label: Cut doubt with the sword of knowledge and stand up
claim.text: Knowledge does not replace action; it frees it.

implications.label: The chronically doubting self perishes
implications.text: Endless division of mind prevents both knowledge and action.

chapters.colophon: Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the fourth chapter, called “The Yoga of Knowledge and the Renunciation of Action.”

chapters.title: The Yoga of Renunciation

verses.text: You praise renunciation of actions, Kṛṣṇa, and then again yoga. Tell me decisively which of the two is better.
verses.speaker: Arjuna
fnotes: Arjuna's question repeats 3.1–2: he still hears the teaching as two competing options.

verses.text: Renunciation and the yoga of action both lead to the highest good. But of the two, the yoga of action is better than renunciation of action.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: *Niḥśreyasa-karāv ubhau*: "both lead to the highest good." But *karma-yogo viśiṣyate*, "the yoga of action is better."

verses.text: Know as a constant renunciant the one who neither hates nor desires. Free of the pairs of opposites, mighty-armed one, one is easily freed from bondage.
fnotes: *Nitya-saṁnyāsī*, "constant renunciant": defined not by status but by the absence of hatred and desire.

verses.text: Children, not the wise, speak of Sāṅkhya and yoga as different. One truly established in either finds the fruit of both.
fnotes: *Bālāḥ*, "children": a sharp word for those who oppose Sāṅkhya and yoga.

verses.text: The yogins reach the same state that the followers of Sāṅkhya reach. One who sees Sāṅkhya and yoga as one truly sees.
fnotes: *Yaḥ paśyati sa paśyati*: "one who sees [this] truly sees." The formula recurs at 13.27 and 13.29.

verses.text: But renunciation, mighty-armed one, is hard to attain without yoga. The sage who is yoked in yoga soon reaches brahman.
fnotes: Renunciation "is hard to attain without yoga." Śaṅkara reads it as: formal renunciation (*saṁnyāsa*) is reached through the purifying discipline of karma-yoga.

verses.text: One yoked in yoga is pure in self, self-conquered, and master of the senses. When one's self has become the self of all beings, one is not tainted even when acting.
fnotes: *Sarva-bhūtātma-bhūtātmā*: "whose self has become the self of all beings." An extraordinary compound describing the expanded identity of the realized person.

verses.text: The yoked knower of truth thinks, "I do nothing at all." While seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing,
fnotes: The long list of activities (seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing) emphasizes that the knower remains fully embodied.

verses.text: speaking, releasing, grasping, opening and closing the eyes, such a one holds that only the senses are moving among the objects of the senses.
fnotes: *Indriyāṇīndriyārtheṣu vartante*: "the senses move among the objects of the senses," a variant of 3.28's "guṇas among guṇas."

verses.text: One who acts while placing all actions in brahman and abandoning attachment is not stained by evil, just as a lotus leaf is not stained by water.
fnotes: *Padma-patram ivāmbhasā*: the lotus leaf, which sheds water, is one of the most enduring images of Indian spirituality.

verses.text: To purify themselves, yogins abandon attachment and perform action with the body, the mind, the understanding, or even the senses alone.
fnotes: *Ātma-śuddhaye*, "for self-purification": the purpose of the yogin's action is not results but inner purification.

verses.text: The yoked one, abandoning the fruit of action, attains abiding peace. The unyoked one, attached to the fruit and driven by desire, is bound.
fnotes: The contrast of yukta and ayukta: the yoked find peace, the unyoked are bound "driven by desire."

verses.text: Renouncing all actions with the mind, the embodied one sits happily in control, in the city of nine gates [the body], neither acting nor causing action.
fnotes: *Nava-dvāre pure*, "in the city of nine gates": the body, with its nine openings. The image comes from the *Kaṭha* (5.1) and *Śvetāśvatara* (3.18) Upaniṣads.

verses.text: The Lord [*prabhu*] does not create agency or actions for the world, nor the link between action and fruit. It is inherent nature [*svabhāva*] that is at work.
fnotes: *Svabhāvas tu pravartate*: "it is inherent nature that proceeds." God does not create agency or its fruits; nature does.

verses.text: The all-pervading one does not take on anyone's evil or good deed. Knowledge is covered by ignorance, and that is why beings are deluded.
fnotes: God "does not take on anyone's evil or good deed." This raises the problem of theodicy: is God indifferent to human action?

verses.text: But for those in whom ignorance is destroyed by knowledge of the self, that knowledge lights up the supreme, like the sun.
fnotes: Knowledge "like the sun illuminates the supreme." It is a recurring image (cf. 13.33).

verses.text: Their understanding is on that, their self in that, they are established in that and intent on that. Their faults cleansed by knowledge, they go where there is no return.
The wise see the same in a learned and humble brāhmaṇa, in a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste [*śva-pāka*, "one who cooks dogs"].
fnotes: *Śuni caiva śvapāke ca*: "in a dog and in a dog-cooker (outcaste)." See the chapter's research note on caste.

verses.text: Even here, those whose minds rest in sameness have overcome the cycle of creation. Brahman is flawless and the same in all, so they are established in brahman.
fnotes: *Nirdoṣaṁ hi samaṁ brahma*: "brahman is flawless and the same." The sameness of vision mirrors the sameness of reality.

verses.text: One should not rejoice on getting what is pleasant nor be shaken on getting what is unpleasant. Steady in understanding and undeluded, the knower of brahman is established in brahman.
With the self unattached to outer contacts, one finds happiness in the self. With the self yoked in the yoga of brahman, one reaches imperishable happiness.
fnotes: *Akṣaya sukha*, "imperishable happiness": a positive goal, not merely the absence of suffering.

verses.text: The enjoyments born of contact are wombs of sorrow. They have a beginning and an end, son of Kuntī, and the wise do not delight in them.
fnotes: *Saṁsparśa-jā bhogāḥ*, "enjoyments born of contact," are *duḥkha-yonayaḥ*, "wombs of sorrow." They are temporary by nature.

verses.text: One who can withstand, here before leaving the body, the agitation born of desire and anger, is yoked. That one is a happy person.
fnotes: The test of a yogin: withstanding the agitation of desire and anger "here, before release from the body."

verses.text: The yogin whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within becomes brahman and reaches the nirvāṇa of brahman.
fnotes: *Antaḥ-sukha, antar-ārāma, antar-jyotis*: happiness, delight and light all "within." *Brahma-bhūta*, "having become brahman."

verses.text: Seers whose faults are destroyed and whose doubts are cut away, who are self-controlled and delight in the welfare of all beings, reach the nirvāṇa of brahman.
fnotes: *Sarva-bhūta-hite ratāḥ*: "delighting in the welfare of all beings." A key phrase for those who see the Gītā's liberation as compassionate rather than isolating. It recurs in 12.4.

verses.text: For ascetics who are free of desire and anger, whose thought is controlled and who know the self, the nirvāṇa of brahman is near on every side.
Shutting out outer contacts, fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, and evening out the in-breath and out-breath that move within the nostrils,
fnotes: A compressed meditation instruction: shut out externals, fix the gaze between the eyebrows, balance the breath. It anticipates Chapter 6.

verses.text: the sage whose senses, mind, and understanding are controlled, who is intent on release, and from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed, is forever free.
Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great lord of all the worlds, the friend of all beings, one reaches peace.
fnotes: *Suhṛdaṁ sarva-bhūtānām*, "friend of all beings": the chapter ends on God's universal benevolence.

chapters.summary: Arjuna asks which is better, renouncing action or the yoga of action. Kṛṣṇa answers that both lead to the goal but the yoga of action is better, and that the two are really one. He describes the inner renunciant who acts while knowing that the senses alone move, the equal vision that sees the same in a brāhmaṇa and an outcaste, and the nirvāṇa of brahman.
overview: Chapter 5 resolves the tension between renunciation (*saṁnyāsa*) and action (*karma-yoga*) that has run through Chapters 2–4. Arjuna, still confused, asks for a single verdict {5.1}. Kṛṣṇa gives one: the yoga of action is better {5.2}. Then he immediately dissolves the dichotomy: "Children, not the wise, speak of Sāṅkhya and yoga as different" {5.4}. The key idea is *inner renunciation*. The true renunciant is not one who gives up deeds but one "who neither hates nor desires" {5.3}. Such a person sees, hears, eats, walks and breathes, all the while knowing "I do nothing at all" {5.8–9}. Like a lotus leaf in water, they act and are not stained {5.10}. The chapter's second half turns to vision and peace. The knower sees "the same" in a learned brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste {5.18}. Their happiness is within {5.24}. They reach *brahma-nirvāṇa*, the "blowing-out in brahman" {5.24–26}. A short passage on meditation {5.27–28} anticipates Chapter 6. The final verse introduces God as "friend of all beings" {5.29}.
research: Chapter 5 is central to scholarly discussion of the Gītā's relation to Buddhism. The repeated *brahma-nirvāṇa* {5.24–26} and the emphasis on the extinction of desire and anger have led scholars (e.g., Kashi Nath Upadhyaya, *Early Buddhism and the Bhagavadgītā*, 1971) to see deliberate engagement with Buddhist ideals: the Gītā accepts the Buddhist goal of extinguished craving but grounds it in brahman. The precise relationship is debated, and chronology is uncertain. Verse 5.18's "equal vision" is a focal point for discussions of caste. Some argue it proves the Gītā transcends caste at the level of realization. Others note that "seeing the same" in a dog and an outcaste keeps the hierarchy as the thing to be seen past. Ethicists have connected 5.25's "delighting in the welfare of all beings" (*sarva-bhūta-hite ratāḥ*) to Buddhist and Jain ideals of universal compassion, and to the modern Gandhian notion of *sarvodaya*, the welfare of all.
questions: Does 5.4–5 resolve the tension between renunciation and action, or merely restate it?
Can one sincerely say "I do nothing at all" (5.8) while eating and walking? What would make it true?
How should we read 5.18 in relation to caste? Is equal vision enough for social equality?
What is the relation between "nirvāṇa of brahman" and Buddhist nirvāṇa?

sections.title: Renunciation and the yoga of action are one
sections.lead: Asked to choose, Kṛṣṇa declares the yoga of action better, then shows that the two paths are one.
reconstruction: Arjuna asks which is better, renunciation or yoga {5.1}. Both lead to the highest good, but the yoga of action is better {5.2}. The real renunciant is the one who neither hates nor desires, and such a person is easily freed {5.3}. Only the immature think the paths differ: being established in one yields the fruit of both {5.4}. The goal of Sāṅkhya and of yoga is the same {5.5}. In fact renunciation is hard to attain without yoga, while one who practices yoga soon reaches brahman {5.6}.
insight: The section's logic is reconciliation through redefinition. Renunciation is redefined as an inner state (freedom from hatred and desire), and yoga as action from that state. Once so defined, they converge. The verdict "action is better" {5.2} is not a rejection of renunciation but a claim about the better *means* to the same end. Śaṅkara, who championed formal monastic renunciation, could not accept that action is simply better. He reads 5.2 as relative: for the unenlightened, action is better than premature renunciation. This interpretive tension is a sign of how much the Gītā's stance threatened monastic exclusivism.
sources: The rivalry of Sāṅkhya (knowledge) and yoga (practice) as paths appears throughout the *Mokṣadharma* (e.g., *Mahābhārata* 12.304, "there is no knowledge like Sāṅkhya, no power like yoga"). The Gītā's synthesis adopts the epic's own language.
context: The idea that monastic and lay paths converge has analogues in Mahāyāna Buddhism, where the layman Vimalakīrti outshines monks in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, and in Protestant critiques of monasticism (Luther's sanctification of ordinary vocation). Max Weber's "inner-worldly asceticism" names a similar ideal.
matters: Many people feel that spiritual seriousness requires leaving ordinary life. The Gītā argues the opposite: the decisive renunciation is inward and available anywhere.
questions: Is the verdict of 5.2 consistent with 5.4–5?
Who is a "constant renunciant" (5.3) in ordinary life?
Why would Śaṅkara resist the plain sense of 5.2?

premises.label: Both paths lead to the highest good
premises.text: Renunciation and action are both valid.

premises.label: The true renunciant neither hates nor desires
premises.text: Renunciation is an inner state.

claim.label: Sāṅkhya and yoga are one
claim.text: Only the immature think them different.

implications.label: Yoga is the easier road to the same goal
implications.text: Renunciation is hard to reach without yoga.

sections.title: The inner renunciant: acting without doing
sections.lead: The yoked knower acts with body and senses while knowing that the self does nothing, and like a lotus leaf is not stained.
reconstruction: One yoked in yoga is pure and self-mastered. His self has become the self of all beings, and so he is not tainted by action {5.7}. While seeing, hearing, eating and breathing, he knows that "I do nothing at all," since only the senses are moving among their objects {5.8–9}. Placing actions in brahman without attachment, he is not stained, like a lotus leaf in water {5.10}. Yogins act with body, mind, understanding and senses for self-purification {5.11}. The yoked, abandoning fruit, find peace; the unyoked are bound by desire {5.12}.
insight: The section describes a double awareness. The yogin acts fully in the world, yet his identification is elsewhere: either with the non-acting self (the Sāṅkhya reading) or with the self of all beings (5.7). The second idea is ethically significant. Freedom from the narrow ego is not withdrawal into isolation but expansion into identification with all. The lotus leaf captures the paradox. The leaf is entirely in the water, yet water does not cling to it. The image has been used in debates over whether such detachment is admirable serenity or emotional distance. The Gītā's answer would point to 5.7 and 5.25. The non-attached person delights in the welfare of all beings, so detachment is from ego, not from care.
sources: The lotus image appears in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 4.14.3 ("as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, so evil action does not cling to one who knows this") and in Buddhist texts (*Sutta Nipāta* 812; *Dhammapada* 401).
context: The ideal of being "in the world but not of it" (John 17:14–16) is a familiar Christian parallel. Neo-Stoic and mindfulness-based ideas of "de-centering" (observing one's thoughts and sensations without identifying with them) offer modern psychological analogues.
matters: The section offers a way to remain fully engaged in ordinary activity while being less captured by it, a practical ideal for anyone in demanding work.
questions: What does it mean for one's self to "become the self of all beings" (5.7)? How would such a person act?
Is the lotus leaf an image of serenity or of detachment from others? Defend your view from the text.
How does "the senses move among the objects of the senses" (5.9) relate to 3.28?

premises.label: The senses act among their objects
premises.text: The self is the witness, not the agent.

premises.label: The knower's self has become the self of all
premises.text: Identification widens beyond the ego.

claim.label: The knower acts but "does nothing at all"
claim.text: Like a lotus leaf, he is in the water but not wet.

implications.label: The yoked find peace; the unyoked are bound
implications.text: Attachment to fruit, not action, is the bond.

sections.title: The city of nine gates and the equal vision
sections.lead: The embodied self dwells in the body without acting; knowledge dispels ignorance, and the wise see the same in all beings.
reconstruction: The self sits at ease in the body, the city of nine gates, neither acting nor making others act {5.13}. God does not create agency or its fruits; nature does that {5.14}. He takes on no one's good or evil, and beings are deluded because ignorance covers knowledge {5.15}. When knowledge destroys ignorance, it reveals the supreme like the sun {5.16}. Those fixed on that go beyond rebirth {5.17}. The wise see the same in a learned brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste {5.18}. Those established in sameness have overcome creation, since brahman is the same in all {5.19}. Unmoved by the pleasant and unpleasant {5.20}, and unattached to external contacts, they find imperishable happiness within {5.21}.
insight: Two ideas meet here. The first is metaphysical. God and the self are not the authors of nature's actions or their fruits {5.14–15}. This raises the question of divine responsibility. If God takes on no one's deeds, is God indifferent? Later chapters qualify this. God is "friend of all beings" {5.29}, and devotion brings grace (Chapters 9, 12, 18). The second is ethical. Knowledge produces "equal vision" (*sama-darśana*). Because brahman is the same in all, the knower sees past distinctions of class, species and status {5.18–19}. The equal vision is a powerful ethical resource, perhaps the Gītā's strongest basis for universal moral regard. Yet its strength is metaphysical rather than social. It changes how the knower sees but does not, by itself, change institutions. Modern reformers have tried to draw social conclusions from it. Critics note that the text itself does not.
sources: "The city of nine gates" occurs in *Kaṭha* 5.1 (eleven gates) and *Śvetāśvatara* 3.18 (nine). The equal vision recalls *Īśā* 6–7: "who sees all beings in the self and the self in all beings… what delusion, what sorrow for one who sees oneness?"
context: Universal moral regard grounded in a shared essence appears in Stoic cosmopolitanism (all humans share the logos), in the Christian *imago Dei*, and in Kantian dignity. The Gītā's version includes animals, which brings it close to Jain and Buddhist ethics of all living beings and to contemporary animal ethics.
matters: The equal vision challenges every hierarchy we take for granted. It invites us to ask what changes if we really see "the same" in those we rank below us.
questions: If God "takes on no one's good or evil" (5.15), in what sense is God good?
Does 5.18 support social equality, or only a spiritual equality compatible with hierarchy?
How does the inclusion of animals in 5.18 shape the ethics of equal vision?

premises.label: Nature, not God or self, produces action and fruit
premises.text: Agency belongs to nature.

premises.label: Brahman is flawless and the same in all
premises.text: Reality itself is undivided.

claim.label: The wise see the same in all beings
claim.text: Brāhmaṇa, cow, elephant, dog and outcaste.

implications.label: The equal-minded overcome rebirth here and now
implications.text: Sameness of vision is liberation.

implications.label: Their happiness is inner and imperishable
implications.text: Freed from dependence on external contacts.

sections.title: Inner joy, meditation, and the nirvāṇa of brahman
sections.lead: Pleasures born of contact end in sorrow; the yogin whose joy and light are within reaches the nirvāṇa of brahman and knows God as friend of all.
reconstruction: Pleasures born of contact begin and end, and so breed sorrow. The wise do not delight in them {5.22}. One who can endure the surge of desire and anger in this life is a yogin and happy {5.23}. One whose joy, delight and light are within becomes brahman and reaches its nirvāṇa {5.24}. So do seers whose faults are gone, whose doubts are cut, who are self-controlled and delight in the good of all beings {5.25}. For ascetics free of desire and anger, that nirvāṇa is near {5.26}. Withdrawing from externals, gazing between the brows and balancing the breath, the sage intent on release is free {5.27–28}. Knowing God as enjoyer of sacrifices, lord of worlds and friend of all beings, one reaches peace {5.29}.
insight: The section joins three things often separated: inner bliss, ethical concern for others, and devotion to God. The liberated person is not only inwardly content {5.24} but also "delights in the welfare of all beings" {5.25}, and the culmination is knowledge of God as "friend of all" {5.29}. This triad anticipates the Gītā's whole development. Liberation is joyful, compassionate and theistic. The argument against sensual pleasure {5.22} is not moralistic. It is an observation about structure. Pleasures that depend on contact must end, so attachment to them guarantees loss. The alternative is a happiness with an inner source, which therefore cannot be lost.
sources: *Brahma-nirvāṇa* appears in 2.72 and here repeatedly. "Delight in the welfare of all beings" has close parallels in Buddhist texts (e.g., the *Metta Sutta*: "may all beings be happy"). The meditation instruction anticipates the *Yoga-sūtra*'s *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal) and *prāṇāyāma* (breath control).
context: Epicurus also distinguished "kinetic" pleasures (from stimulation) from "katastematic" pleasure (stable tranquility), preferring the latter. Contemporary well-being research distinguishes hedonic pleasure from eudaimonic fulfillment, and finds the latter more durable.
matters: The section offers a test anyone can apply: does my happiness depend on contact with things that must end? And it ties inner peace to active goodwill toward all.
questions: Is the argument of 5.22 (pleasures of contact are wombs of sorrow) persuasive? Are there exceptions?
How does "delighting in the welfare of all beings" (5.25) answer the charge that liberation is selfish?
Why does the chapter end with God as "friend of all beings"?

chapters.colophon: Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the fifth chapter, called “The Yoga of Renunciation.”

chapters.title: The Yoga of Meditation

verses.text: One who performs the action that should be done, without depending on its fruit, is a renunciant and a yogin. One who merely gives up the sacred fires and the rites is not.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: *Na niragnir na cākriyaḥ*: not one who has abandoned the sacred fires or rites. The formal marks of the saṁnyāsin (who gives up the ritual fires) are explicitly declared insufficient.

verses.text: What they call renunciation, Pāṇḍava, know to be yoga. No one becomes a yogin without renouncing intention [*saṅkalpa*].
fnotes: *Saṅkalpa*, "intention" or "mental projection": the mind's willful scheming about outcomes. Renouncing it is the essence of both renunciation and yoga.

verses.text: For the sage who wishes to climb to yoga, action is said to be the means. Once that same sage has climbed to yoga, calm [*śama*] is said to be the means.
fnotes: *Ārurukṣu* and *yogārūḍha*: "one wishing to climb" and "one who has climbed" to yoga. Action is the means for the first, calm (*śama*) for the second. Śaṅkara uses this verse to argue for monastic renunciation at the advanced stage.

verses.text: When one is not attached to sense objects or to actions and has renounced all intentions, one is said to have climbed to yoga.
One should lift up the self by the self and not let the self sink down. For the self alone is the self's friend, and the self alone is the self's enemy.
fnotes: *Uddhared ātmanātmānaṁ*: "lift up the self by the self." The word *ātman* here works on two levels: the lower, empirical self and the higher self. The verse is a cornerstone of Hindu ethics of self-effort.

verses.text: For one who has conquered the self by the self, the self is a friend. But for one who has not conquered the self, the self acts with hostility, like an enemy.
fnotes: The self conquered by the self is a friend; unconquered, it is an enemy. Compare Plato's "victory over oneself" (*Laws* 626e).

verses.text: For one who is self-conquered and at peace, the supreme self stays concentrated in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor.
A yogin is called yoked when the self is satisfied with knowledge and discernment, unshakable, and master of the senses, and when a clod, a stone, and gold are all the same to that person.
fnotes: *Sama-loṣṭāśma-kāñcanaḥ*: "to whom a clod, a stone, and gold are the same," a formula repeated at 14.24.

verses.text: One who regards with an equal mind well-wishers, friends, enemies, the indifferent, the neutral, the hateful, and relatives, and the good and the wicked alike, excels.
fnotes: A list of seven kinds of people, including the hateful, all regarded with an equal mind.

verses.text: The yogin should constantly concentrate the self, staying in solitude and alone, with thought and self controlled, free of longing and without possessions.
In a clean place, he should set up for himself a firm seat, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass.
fnotes: *Śuci deśa*, a clean place; *sthira āsana*, a firm seat; kuśa grass, deerskin and cloth in layers: the traditional meditation seat.

verses.text: Sitting there, making the mind one-pointed and controlling the activity of thought and senses, he should practice yoga to purify the self.
He should hold body, head, and neck straight and still, steady, gazing at the tip of his nose and not looking around.
fnotes: *Nāsikāgram*, "the tip of the nose": a half-closed, downward gaze. Commentators note that this is not literally staring at the nose but resting the gaze.

verses.text: With the self at peace, free of fear, firm in the vow of celibacy [*brahmacarya*], controlling the mind, he should sit yoked, with his thought on me and intent on me.
fnotes: *Brahmacārī-vrata*: the vow of celibacy, here for the period of practice. *Mac-citta, mat-para*: "thought on me, intent on me." The meditation is devotional.

verses.text: Always concentrating the self in this way, the yogin with controlled mind reaches the peace that culminates in nirvāṇa and abides in me.
But yoga is not for one who eats too much or for one who does not eat at all, Arjuna, nor for one who sleeps too much or stays awake too long.
fnotes: Moderation in food, sleep and wakefulness. The Gītā rejects extreme fasting and sleep deprivation.

verses.text: For one who is moderate in eating and recreation, moderate in effort in action, and moderate in sleep and waking, yoga destroys sorrow.
fnotes: *Yuktāhāra-vihārasya*: one whose eating and recreation are "yoked," i.e., measured.

verses.text: When thought is well controlled and rests in the self alone, free from longing for any desire, one is said to be yoked.
"Like a lamp in a windless place, which does not flicker": this is the image given for the yogin whose thought is controlled, practicing the yoga of the self.
fnotes: *Yathā dīpo nivāta-stho neṅgate*: "a lamp in a windless place does not flicker." One of the Gītā's best-known images.

verses.text: Thought comes to rest, restrained by the practice of yoga, and seeing the self by the self, one is content in the self.
fnotes: *Paśyann ātmanātmānam ātmani tuṣyati*: "seeing the self by the self, one is content in the self." The triple *ātman* marks self-reflexive realization.

verses.text: One knows that infinite happiness which the understanding grasps and which lies beyond the senses. Established there, one does not move from the truth.
fnotes: *Buddhi-grāhyam atīndriyam*: happiness "grasped by the understanding and beyond the senses." Spiritual joy is cognitive, not sensory.

verses.text: Having gained it, one thinks no other gain greater. Established in it, one is not shaken even by heavy sorrow.
Let that be known as yoga: the unyoking from union with sorrow [*duḥkha-saṁyoga-viyoga*]. That yoga should be practiced with resolve and with a mind that does not lose heart.
fnotes: *Duḥkha-saṁyoga-viyogaṁ yoga-saṁjñitam*: the Gītā's wordplay. *Yoga* is defined as *viyoga*, "unyoking" from union (*saṁyoga*) with sorrow.

verses.text: Abandon entirely all desires born of intention, and with the mind alone hold back the whole group of senses on every side.
fnotes: *Saṅkalpa-prabhavān kāmān*: "desires born of intention." Desire arises from the mind's projections.

verses.text: Little by little one should come to rest, with the understanding held firm. Having made the mind abide in the self, one should think of nothing at all.
fnotes: *Śanaiḥ śanaiḥ*, "little by little": the gradualness of practice. *Na kiñcid api cintayet*: "one should think of nothing at all."

verses.text: Whenever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, one should rein it back from there and bring it under the control of the self.
fnotes: Practical advice for wandering attention: whenever the mind strays, bring it back. Every meditator will recognize this.

verses.text: Supreme happiness comes to the yogin whose mind is tranquil, whose passion is stilled, who has become brahman and is free of fault.
fnotes: *Brahma-bhūta*, "having become brahman," as in 5.24.

verses.text: Constantly concentrating the self in this way, the yogin, free of fault, easily attains the infinite happiness of contact with brahman.
One whose self is yoked in yoga and who sees the same everywhere sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self.
fnotes: *Sarva-bhūta-stham ātmānaṁ sarva-bhūtāni cātmani*: the vision of *Īśā* 6, here as the fruit of meditation.

verses.text: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am not lost to that one, and that one is not lost to me.
fnotes: *Tasyāhaṁ na praṇaśyāmi sa ca me na praṇaśyati*: "I am not lost to that one, and that one is not lost to me." A tender, personal verse in the middle of a technical chapter.

verses.text: The yogin who is established in oneness and worships me as dwelling in all beings abides in me, however he lives.
fnotes: *Sarvathā vartamāno 'pi*: "however he lives." The vision matters more than outward lifestyle.

verses.text: One who sees the same in everything by comparison with oneself [*ātmaupamya*], Arjuna, whether pleasure or pain, is considered the supreme yogin.
tnotes: *ātmaupamya*, "taking oneself as the measure," is the Gītā's version of the golden rule. Others' pleasure and pain are felt as one's own.
fnotes: *Ātmaupamya*: see the translator's note. The highest yogin feels the pleasures and pains of others as his own.

verses.text: You have taught this yoga as sameness, Madhusūdana, but because of restlessness I do not see how it can stand firm.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: For the mind is restless, Kṛṣṇa, turbulent, strong, and stubborn. I think it is as hard to restrain as the wind.
fnotes: *Cañcalaṁ hi manaḥ kṛṣṇa pramāthi balavad dṛḍham*: "restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn." It is Arjuna's most personal and relatable objection.

verses.text: No doubt, mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and hard to restrain. But it is held by practice [*abhyāsa*] and dispassion [*vairāgya*], son of Kuntī.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: *Abhyāsena tu kaunteya vairāgyeṇa ca gṛhyate*: "held by practice and dispassion." Identical in substance to *Yoga-sūtra* 1.12.

verses.text: I agree that yoga is hard to attain for one whose self is uncontrolled. But one whose self is controlled and who strives can attain it by the right means.
Consider one who has faith but is not controlled, whose mind strays from yoga before reaching perfection in yoga. What path does that one take, Kṛṣṇa?
verses.speaker: Arjuna
fnotes: *Ayati*, "one who strives but is uncontrolled." It is a person of faith whose practice is incomplete.

verses.text: Fallen from both, without support, bewildered on the path to brahman, does he not perish like a scattered cloud, mighty-armed one?
fnotes: *Chinnābhram iva*: "like a scattered cloud," which belongs neither to the old cloud nor reaches the new. The fear of falling between worldly and spiritual life.

verses.text: Cut away this doubt of mine completely, Kṛṣṇa, for no one but you can cut it away.
Pārtha, there is no destruction for him, either here or hereafter. No one who does good, my friend, comes to a bad end.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: *Na hi kalyāṇa-kṛt kaścid durgatiṁ tāta gacchati*: "no one who does good, my friend, comes to a bad end." *Tāta*, "dear one, my son": an affectionate address.

verses.text: The one fallen from yoga reaches the worlds of the meritorious and dwells there for countless years. Then he is born in the house of the pure and prosperous.
fnotes: *Yoga-bhraṣṭa*, "one fallen from yoga," is reborn in a pure and prosperous family.

verses.text: Or he is born into a family of wise yogins, though such a birth is harder to obtain in this world.
There he regains the understanding he reached in his former body, joy of the Kurus, and from there strives again for perfection.
His former practice carries him along even without his willing it. Even one who only wishes to know yoga goes beyond the word-brahman [the Veda].
fnotes: *Śabda-brahmātivartate*: "goes beyond the word-brahman," i.e., beyond the Veda. Even the desire to know yoga surpasses ritual religion.

verses.text: But the yogin who strives with effort is purified of faults and perfected through many births. Then he reaches the supreme goal.
The yogin is superior to ascetics, superior even to the learned, and superior to those who perform ritual action. Therefore be a yogin, Arjuna.
fnotes: The yogin surpasses ascetics (*tapasvin*), the learned (*jñānin*) and ritualists (*karmin*).

verses.text: And of all yogins, I consider most fully yoked the one who is full of faith and worships me with the inner self absorbed in me.
fnotes: The chapter's last word: among yogins, the devotee who worships "with inner self absorbed in me" is most fully yoked. It is a bridge to Chapters 7–12.

chapters.summary: Kṛṣṇa teaches meditation: the self as its own friend or enemy, the seat, posture and moderation of the meditator, the mind stilled like a lamp in a windless place, and the vision of the self in all beings. Arjuna objects that the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Kṛṣṇa answers with practice and dispassion, and promises that no effort on this path is ever lost.
overview: Chapter 6, *dhyāna-yoga*, completes the first hexad of the Gītā. Having established that one must act, and act without attachment, Kṛṣṇa now teaches the inner discipline that makes such action possible: meditation. The chapter is the Gītā's most technical yoga manual, but it is framed by two non-technical ideas. At the beginning, the true renunciant is one who does what should be done {6.1}. At the end, the highest yogin is the devotee {6.47}. The chapter's movement runs as follows. First comes self-mastery: "lift up the self by the self," for the self is its own friend and its own enemy {6.5–6}. Then comes the practice itself: a clean place, a firm seat, an erect body, moderate food and sleep, and a mind made one-pointed {6.10–17}. Then the fruit: the mind steady as a lamp in a windless place {6.19}, yoga as "unyoking from union with sorrow" {6.23}, and the vision of the self in all beings and all beings in the self {6.29–32}. Arjuna then raises the most honest objection in the Gītā: the mind is restless, "as hard to restrain as the wind" {6.34}. Kṛṣṇa does not deny it. He offers practice and dispassion {6.35} and, to the worried question of what becomes of one who tries and fails {6.37–39}, a reassurance: "no one who does good, my friend, comes to a bad end" {6.40}.
research: Historians of yoga treat Chapter 6 as one of the earliest systematic descriptions of seated meditation in Sanskrit, comparable to *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 2.8–15 and earlier than (or contemporary with) the *Yoga-sūtra*. The relationship between the Gītā's yoga and early Buddhist *jhāna* practice is debated (Johannes Bronkhorst, *The Two Traditions of Meditation in Ancient India*, 1986). The Gītā's emphasis on moderation {6.16–17} resembles the Buddha's "middle way" between indulgence and austerity. Contemporary contemplative science has taken interest in passages like 6.19 (one-pointedness) and 6.23 (yoga as freedom from suffering), sometimes uncritically. Scholars caution against reading modern mindfulness back into the Gītā, whose meditation is explicitly theistic ("with thought on me," 6.14) and soteriological. The teaching on the "one fallen from yoga" {6.37–45} is also discussed as an early Indian theory of moral and spiritual progress across lifetimes, with parallels in Buddhist accounts of the bodhisattva's long path.
questions: What does it mean to be one's own friend or enemy (6.5–6)? Give a concrete example.
Is the moderation of 6.16–17 a moral teaching or a practical one?
Arjuna says the mind is as hard to hold as the wind. Is Kṛṣṇa's answer (practice and dispassion) adequate?
How does the promise of 6.40 ("no one who does good comes to a bad end") function in the life of a practitioner?

sections.title: The true renunciant and the self as friend
sections.lead: The renunciant is one who does what should be done; one must lift oneself up by oneself, for the self is its own friend and enemy.
reconstruction: The true renunciant and yogin is the person who does the work that should be done without depending on its fruit, not the one who merely abandons rituals {6.1}. Renunciation and yoga are the same, since both mean giving up the mind's self-willed intentions {6.2}. Action is the way up, and calm is the way once one has arrived {6.3}. One has arrived when attached neither to objects nor to deeds {6.4}. One must raise oneself by one's own effort, for the self is its own friend and its own enemy {6.5–6}. The self-conquered remain composed in every condition {6.7}. They see a clod, a stone and gold as the same {6.8}, and regard friend and foe, saint and sinner, with an equal mind {6.9}.
insight: The section's center of gravity is 6.5–6: self-responsibility. Neither fate nor others are finally in charge of one's inner life. The self can rescue or ruin itself. This is a striking emphasis on agency in a text that elsewhere says the guṇas do everything {3.27}. The two are reconciled by distinguishing levels. Nature acts, but the self chooses its identification and orientation. The redefinition of renunciation {6.1–2} continues Chapter 5's project. Renunciation is not giving up rituals or work but giving up *saṅkalpa*, the ego's insistent projecting of what must happen. That is subtler and harder than giving up possessions.
sources: The two-level self appears in *Kaṭha* 3.1 (two "drinkers of truth," the lower and higher self) and in *Muṇḍaka* 3.1.1 (two birds on one tree, one eating, one watching). Self-effort (*puruṣakāra*) is a major theme in the epic's debates with fate (*daiva*).
context: The idea that one can be one's own friend or enemy appears in Aristotle (*Nicomachean Ethics* IX.4: the good person is a friend to himself), in Seneca ("What progress have I made? I have begun to be a friend to myself," *Letters* 6), and in modern self-compassion research (Kristin Neff).
matters: The section places the possibility of transformation in our own hands, without self-hatred: the self is to be befriended and raised, not punished.
questions: How can the self be both the one who lifts and the one who is lifted (6.5)?
Is "a clod, a stone and gold are the same" (6.8) wise or inhuman?
What is *saṅkalpa* (6.2), and why is renouncing it the essence of both renunciation and yoga?

sections.title: The practice of meditation
sections.lead: The yogin's seat, posture and moderation lead to the stilled mind, steady as a lamp in a windless place, and to the yoga that is unyoking from sorrow.
reconstruction: The yogin should practice in solitude, with mind and body controlled {6.10}. He sits on a firm seat in a clean place {6.11–12}, holds body, head and neck erect, lets the gaze rest, and turns his thought to God {6.13–14}. Practiced constantly, this brings peace in God {6.15}. Yoga is not for those who eat or sleep too much or too little {6.16}. It is for the moderate in food, recreation, effort and sleep {6.17}. When the controlled mind rests in the self, free of craving, one is yoked {6.18}. It is like a lamp in a windless place {6.19}. Then the mind rests, and one sees and enjoys the self {6.20}. One knows a happiness beyond the senses and does not waver from truth {6.21}. No gain seems greater, and no sorrow shakes it {6.22}. This is yoga: unyoking from sorrow. It is to be practiced resolutely and without discouragement {6.23}.
insight: The passage is notable for its realism and moderation. It does not demand heroic austerities. It warns against them {6.16}. The yogin is not a fakir but a disciplined person with regular habits. The aim is not trance as such but a stable mind and a joy that does not depend on the senses. The definition of yoga in 6.23 is a philosophical pun with a serious point. Ordinary life is a "yoking" to sorrow through attachment. Yoga is the undoing of that yoke. The positive "union" sense of yoga (with God, with the self) and the negative "release" sense (from sorrow) are revealed as two aspects of one movement.
sources: The closest parallel is *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 2.8–15, which describes the meditator's posture, place and breath. The lamp image recurs in later yoga and Buddhist literature (e.g., commentaries on the *Yoga-sūtra*). The *Kaṭha* (6.11) defines yoga as "the steady holding of the senses."
context: Comparisons include the Buddhist *jhānas* (meditative absorptions), the Desert Fathers' instructions on stillness (*hesychia*), Ignatius of Loyola's *Spiritual Exercises* with their attention to posture and place, and modern contemplative research on attention regulation.
matters: The passage offers a simple, sane discipline: a quiet place, an upright body, a moderate life, a steady attention. It makes the extraordinary (a mind like a windless flame) depend on the ordinary.
questions: Why does the Gītā insist on moderation (6.16–17) rather than austerity?
What makes the lamp in a windless place (6.19) such a powerful image? What does the "wind" represent?
Explain the wordplay of 6.23. What does it reveal about the meaning of yoga?

sections.title: The self in all beings
sections.lead: Gradually stilling the mind, the yogin comes to see the self in all beings and all beings in the self, and God everywhere; the highest yogin feels others' pleasure and pain as their own.
reconstruction: Abandoning desires born of intention and restraining the senses with the mind {6.24}, the yogin slowly comes to rest. With understanding held firm, he settles the mind in the self and thinks of nothing else {6.25}. When the mind wanders, he brings it back {6.26}. Supreme happiness comes to the calm, passionless yogin who has become brahman {6.27–28}. Then he sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self {6.29}. Whoever sees God everywhere and everything in God is never lost to God {6.30}. One who worships God in all beings abides in God, however he lives {6.31}. The highest yogin, taking himself as the measure, sees the same in all, pleasure or pain {6.32}.
insight: This section answers a common objection to meditation: that it turns the meditator inward and away from others. Here the inward movement culminates in an outward vision. The self found in meditation is found in all beings. From that vision follows an ethic: others' joys and sorrows become one's own {6.32}. The passage also moves from impersonal to personal language. The self in all {6.29} becomes "me" in all {6.30}, and the vision becomes a relationship of mutual presence ("I am not lost to that one"). This anticipates the theistic turn of Chapters 7–12.
sources: 6.29 closely follows *Īśā Upaniṣad* 6. The ideal of feeling others' suffering as one's own is shared with Buddhist *karuṇā* (compassion) and the Jain principle that all beings value life (*Ācārāṅga Sūtra* 1.2.3).
context: The "golden rule" in its many forms (Confucius' *shu*, the Torah's "love your neighbor as yourself," Kant's universalizability) can be compared with *ātmaupamya*. The Gītā grounds it not in reciprocity or reason but in metaphysical identity. Arthur Schopenhauer, deeply influenced by Indian thought, made a similar move: compassion rests on seeing through the illusion of separate selves.
matters: If the meditator's deepest discovery is that others' pain is one's own, then contemplation and compassion are not opposites but one movement.
questions: How does the vision of 6.29 change the ethics of 6.32?
What does 6.30 add to 6.29? Why the shift from "self" to "me"?
Is the Gītā's golden rule (6.32) stronger or weaker than the reciprocity version?

sections.title: The restless mind and the one who falls from yoga
sections.lead: Arjuna objects that the mind is as unruly as the wind; Kṛṣṇa answers with practice and dispassion and reassures him that no sincere effort is lost.
reconstruction: Arjuna objects: the mind is restless and strong, as hard to hold as the wind, so this yoga of sameness seems unstable {6.33–34}. Kṛṣṇa agrees that the mind is hard to restrain but says it can be held by practice and dispassion {6.35}. Yoga is hard for the uncontrolled but attainable with effort and right means {6.36}. Arjuna then asks about the person of faith who falls short. Does he perish like a scattered cloud, having lost both worlds {6.37–39}? Kṛṣṇa assures him that no one who does good comes to a bad end {6.40}. Such a person enjoys heavenly worlds and is reborn among the pure or among wise yogins {6.41–42}. There he regains his former understanding and is carried forward by past practice {6.43–44}. Through many births he reaches perfection {6.45}. The yogin is above ascetic, scholar and ritualist {6.46}. The greatest yogin is the devotee absorbed in God {6.47}.
insight: The section is the Gītā's most humane moment. Arjuna's objection is the beginner's real experience, and Kṛṣṇa honors it: "without doubt, the mind is hard to restrain." The answer is not a technique but a combination of habit (practice) and loosening of desire (dispassion), each supporting the other. The teaching on the one who falls from yoga introduces a theory of moral momentum. Effort is never wasted. Practice leaves traces that carry forward. Whatever one thinks of rebirth, the claim has psychological truth: the habits and aspirations we cultivate shape what we become. The chapter's turn to devotion at the very end {6.47} suggests that what finally steadies the restless mind is not technique but love.
sources: 6.35 is nearly identical to *Yoga-sūtra* 1.12 (*abhyāsa-vairāgyābhyāṁ tan-nirodhaḥ*). The doctrine of a yogin's rebirth in a favorable family parallels Buddhist accounts of rebirth according to one's practice (e.g., the *Saṅkhāruppatti Sutta*, Majjhima Nikāya 120).
context: The image of the wind and the mind's restlessness recalls Augustine ("our heart is restless until it rests in you") and the "monkey mind" of later Buddhist and modern idiom. The reassurance that no effort is lost can be compared with Aristotle on habituation (we become just by doing just acts) and with modern research on skill acquisition.
matters: Anyone who has tried to meditate, change a habit or keep a resolution knows Arjuna's objection. Kṛṣṇa's answer is realistic and encouraging: it is hard, but practice and loosening desire work, and no sincere effort is wasted.
questions: Is Kṛṣṇa's answer to Arjuna's objection (6.35) sufficient? What would you add?
What fear lies behind the image of the scattered cloud (6.38)? Do you recognize it?
Why does the chapter end by placing the devotee above all other yogins (6.47)?

premises.label: Practice and dispassion hold the mind
premises.text: The two together steady it.

claim.label: No sincere effort on this path is lost
claim.text: The one who falls continues in a later life.

implications.text: Love steadies what technique cannot. This leads into Chapters 7–12.

chapters.colophon: Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the sixth chapter, called “The Yoga of Meditation.”

chapters.title: The Yoga of Knowledge and Discernment

verses.text: Hear, Pārtha, how you will know me completely and without doubt, with your mind attached to me, practicing yoga and relying on me.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: *Mayy āsakta-manāḥ*, "with mind attached to me": after six chapters on non-attachment, the Gītā now commends attachment, to God.

verses.text: I will teach you this knowledge together with discernment [*jñāna-vijñāna*] in full. Once you know it, nothing further remains to be known here.
fnotes: *Jñānaṁ vijñāna-sahitam*: knowledge (of God's transcendent nature) with discernment (of his manifest, specific forms), according to many commentators.

verses.text: Among thousands of people, scarcely one strives for perfection. Of those who strive and are perfected, scarcely one knows me in truth.
fnotes: *Manuṣyāṇāṁ sahasreṣu kaścid yatati siddhaye*: "among thousands, scarcely one strives." A famous verse on the rarity of spiritual seeking.

verses.text: Earth, water, fire, wind, space, mind, understanding, and I-making: this is my nature [*prakṛti*], divided eightfold.
fnotes: The eight items correspond to Sāṅkhya's evolutes: five gross elements plus mind, understanding and I-making. Compare 13.5.

verses.text: This is my lower nature. But know my other, higher nature, mighty-armed one: the principle of life [*jīva-bhūta*], by which this world is sustained.
fnotes: *Parā prakṛti*, the higher nature, is *jīva-bhūta*, "consisting of living beings" or "the life-principle." This places individual souls within God's nature.

verses.text: Understand that all beings have these two as their source. I am the origin and the dissolution of the whole world.
There is nothing whatever higher than me, Dhanañjaya. All this is strung on me like pearls on a thread.
fnotes: *Sūtre maṇi-gaṇā iva*: "like clusters of pearls on a thread." God is the unseen thread that holds the many together.

verses.text: I am the taste in water, son of Kuntī, and the light in moon and sun. I am the syllable Om in all the Vedas, the sound in space, the manhood in men.
fnotes: *Raso 'ham apsu*: "I am the taste in water." Each element is identified by its essential quality: taste for water, light for sun and moon, sound for space.
*Praṇavaḥ sarva-vedeṣu*: "the syllable Om in all the Vedas." *Praṇava* is a name of Om.

verses.text: I am the pure fragrance in the earth and the brilliance in fire. I am the life in all beings and the austerity in ascetics.
Know me, Pārtha, as the eternal seed of all beings. I am the understanding of those who understand and the splendor of the splendid.
fnotes: *Bījaṁ māṁ sarva-bhūtānāṁ viddhi*: "know me as the seed of all beings." The seed image anticipates 10.39 and 14.4.

verses.text: I am the strength of the strong, free from desire and passion. In beings, bull of the Bhāratas, I am the desire that does not oppose dharma.
fnotes: *Dharmāviruddho bhūteṣu kāmo 'smi*: "I am desire not opposed to dharma." A crucial qualification of the Gītā's critique of desire. Desire aligned with right order is divine.

verses.text: Whatever states of being there are, whether of sattva, rajas, or tamas, know that they come from me alone. But I am not in them; they are in me.
fnotes: *Na tv ahaṁ teṣu te mayi*: "but I am not in them; they are in me." Compare 9.4–5.

verses.text: Deluded by these states made of the three guṇas, this whole world does not recognize me, who am beyond them and imperishable.
fnotes: *Tribhir guṇamayair bhāvaiḥ*: "by states composed of the three guṇas." It is the guṇas themselves that veil God.

verses.text: This divine māyā of mine, made of the guṇas, is hard to cross. Those who take refuge in me alone cross over this māyā.
fnotes: *Daivī hy eṣā guṇamayī mama māyā duratyayā*: "this divine māyā of mine, made of guṇas, is hard to cross." Note that māyā is *God's own* power. *Mām eva ye prapadyante*: "those who take refuge in me alone cross it." Grace overcomes what effort cannot.

verses.text: Evildoers do not take refuge in me: the deluded, the lowest of humans, whose knowledge is carried off by māyā and who have taken on a demonic nature.
fnotes: The four marks of those who do not seek refuge: evildoers, the deluded, the lowest of humans, and those whose knowledge is stolen by māyā.

verses.text: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the one who knows, bull of the Bhāratas.
fnotes: *Ārta, jijñāsu, arthārthin, jñānin*: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, the knower. All four are called *sukṛtinaḥ*, "virtuous."

verses.text: Of these the one who knows excels: always yoked and devoted to the One alone. I am exceedingly dear to the one who knows, and that one is dear to me.
fnotes: *Priyo hi jñānino 'tyartham ahaṁ sa ca mama priyaḥ*: "I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to me." Love is mutual.

verses.text: All of these are noble, but I regard the one who knows as my very self. With self yoked, that one abides in me alone as the highest goal.
fnotes: *Jñānī tv ātmaiva me matam*: "I regard the knower as my very self." Advaitins read it as identity, theists as intimate union.

verses.text: At the end of many births, the one who knows takes refuge in me, thinking "Vāsudeva is all." Such a great self is very rare.
fnotes: *Vāsudevaḥ sarvam iti*: "Vāsudeva is all." A succinct statement of the knower's realization. It may be the earliest occurrence of this formula.

verses.text: Those whose knowledge is carried off by various desires take refuge in other gods. They follow this or that rule, constrained by their own nature.
fnotes: *Anya-devatāḥ*, "other gods": worship of deities other than the supreme, motivated by desires.

verses.text: Whatever form any devotee wishes to worship with faith, I make that very faith unshakable.
fnotes: *Tasya tasyācalāṁ śraddhāṁ tām eva vidadhāmy aham*: God himself makes their faith firm. A remarkable form of tolerance.

verses.text: Yoked with that faith, they seek to please that form. From it they obtain their desires, though in truth it is I alone who grant them.
fnotes: *Mayaiva vihitān*: the wishes they obtain "are granted by me alone." The other gods are channels of the one God.

verses.text: But the fruit for those of small understanding is finite. Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; my devotees come to me.
The unintelligent think that I, the unmanifest, have become manifest. They do not know my higher being, imperishable and supreme.
fnotes: The unintelligent think the unmanifest "has become manifest." Rāmānuja reads it as: they think God is an ordinary embodied being. Śaṅkara reads it as: they do not know his transcendent nature.

verses.text: I am not manifest to all, veiled as I am by my yoga-māyā. This deluded world does not recognize me, the unborn and imperishable.
fnotes: *Yoga-māyā-samāvṛtaḥ*: "veiled by yoga-māyā," God's creative power that also conceals him.

verses.text: I know the beings that have passed, those that are present, and those yet to come, Arjuna. But no one knows me.
fnotes: *Māṁ tu veda na kaścana*: "but no one knows me." God's knowledge is total; ours of him is not.

verses.text: All beings, scorcher of foes, fall into bewilderment at birth, through the delusion of the pairs of opposites, which arises from desire and aversion.
But people of good deeds whose evil has come to an end are freed from the delusion of the pairs, and they worship me with firm vows.
Those who take refuge in me and strive for release from old age and death know that brahman fully. They know the inner self [*adhyātma*] and action in its entirety.
fnotes: The technical terms *adhyātma, adhibhūta, adhidaiva, adhiyajña* introduce Chapter 8, which will define them.

verses.text: Those who know me together with what pertains to beings [*adhibhūta*], to the gods [*adhidaiva*], and to sacrifice [*adhiyajña*], with minds yoked, know me even at the time of death.

chapters.summary: Kṛṣṇa begins to teach knowledge of himself. He has a lower nature (the eight elements of the world) and a higher nature (the life that sustains it); all things are strung on him like pearls on a thread. Bewildered by the guṇas and by māyā, most people do not know him. Four kinds of people worship him, and dearest is the one who knows.
overview: Chapter 7 opens the second hexad of the Gītā (Chapters 7–12), whose subject is God. The first hexad asked how to act. This one asks who is acting, and who is the goal of action. Kṛṣṇa promises "knowledge together with discernment" {7.2}, a full account of himself. The chapter's structure is clear. Kṛṣṇa first lays out a two-level ontology. His "lower nature" is the eightfold material world of Sāṅkhya (elements, mind, understanding, I-making), and his "higher nature" is the living principle that sustains it {7.4–5}. Then he declares his presence in the essence of every thing: the taste in water, the light in sun and moon, Om in the Vedas {7.8–11}. The guṇas and their states come from him, yet "I am not in them; they are in me" {7.12}. This is an early statement of the Gītā's panentheism. The rest of the chapter explains why most people do not know him. Bewildered by the guṇas {7.13}, deceived by divine māyā {7.14}, or seeking finite goods from lesser gods {7.20–23}, they miss the source. Among those who do worship him, Kṛṣṇa distinguishes four kinds: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the knower. The knower is "my very self" {7.16–18}. "Vāsudeva is all" is the knower's realization after many births {7.19}.
research: Chapter 7 is fundamental for the theology of the Gītā and for the debate between Advaita and theistic Vedānta. Śaṅkara reads the "lower" and "higher" natures as two aspects of God's māyā, with the absolute itself beyond both. Rāmānuja reads them as God's real "body," matter and souls, with God as their indwelling self. Modern scholars, such as Ram-Prasad in *Divine Self, Human Self*, argue that the Gītā deliberately keeps both the immanent and the transcendent in tension. The four types of worshipers {7.16} and the treatment of other gods {7.20–23} are central to research on Hindu inclusivism (Paul Hacker's term). The Gītā honors other worship as real but finally subordinate, received by Kṛṣṇa himself {9.23}. Some scholars see this as religious generosity, others as subtle hierarchy. Comparative theologians (Francis X. Clooney and others) have used these verses in Hindu–Christian dialogue.
questions: What is the difference between God's "lower" and "higher" nature? Why does the distinction matter?
How can all beings be "in" God while God is "not in them" (7.12)?
Is the treatment of other gods (7.20–23) generous, hierarchical, or both?
Why is the knower "dear" to God (7.17)? What kind of love is meant?

sections.title: The two natures of God
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa promises complete knowledge of himself and describes his lower, eightfold nature and his higher nature, the principle of life.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa promises to teach Arjuna to know him completely, with mind attached to him and yoga practiced {7.1}. This knowledge with discernment leaves nothing more to know {7.2}. Few seek perfection, and fewer still know God in truth {7.3}. God's nature has two levels. The lower is eightfold: the five elements, mind, understanding and I-making {7.4}. The higher is the life-principle that sustains the world {7.5}. All beings come from these two, and God is the origin and dissolution of all {7.6}. There is nothing beyond him. All is strung on him like pearls on a thread {7.7}.
insight: The section transforms Sāṅkhya. In classical Sāṅkhya, matter (*prakṛti*) and the many conscious selves (*puruṣas*) are independent, ultimate principles. Here both are God's "natures." The dualism is kept but subordinated to a single source. This is the decisive move from Sāṅkhya to the Gītā's theistic Vedānta. The pearl-and-thread image is subtle. The thread is invisible, yet without it there is no necklace, only scattered pearls. God is the unity of the many, not another item among them.
sources: The eightfold *prakṛti* follows proto-Sāṅkhya lists in the *Mokṣadharma*. The thread (*sūtra*) image recalls *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.7, where Uddālaka asks about "the thread by which this world and the other world and all beings are strung together," answered by Yājñavalkya with the "inner controller" (*antaryāmin*).
context: The relation of one and many is a perennial philosophical theme: Plotinus's One and its emanations, Spinoza's single substance with infinite attributes, and the medieval debate on universals. Rāmānuja's reading of the world as God's body has been compared to process theology.
matters: The section offers a way of seeing the world in which the many things we deal with are held together by a single source, not as an abstract unity but as their living core.
questions: Why does the Gītā now commend attachment (7.1) after teaching non-attachment?
How does the Gītā transform Sāṅkhya's dualism?
What does the pearl-and-thread image (7.7) capture that other images of unity might miss?

sections.title: God as the essence of things
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa is the taste in water, the light of sun and moon, the life in all beings; the guṇas come from him, but he is not in them.
reconstruction: God is present in each thing as its essence: the taste in water, the light in sun and moon, Om in the Vedas, sound in space, manhood in men {7.8}. He is fragrance in earth, heat in fire, life in beings, austerity in ascetics {7.9}. He is the eternal seed of all beings, the intelligence of the intelligent, the splendor of the splendid {7.10}. He is the strength of the strong free of passion, and desire that does not oppose dharma {7.11}. All states of sattva, rajas and tamas come from him, yet he is not in them; they are in him {7.12}.
insight: The section develops a theology of essence. God is present not in things' accidents but in what makes each thing what it is at its best. This has two effects. First, it sacralizes the ordinary: drinking water becomes tasting God. Second, it introduces an implicit criterion. God is present in things as their *excellence* (the strength free of passion, desire in accord with dharma). The divine presence is therefore also a norm. 7.12 states the asymmetry that defines panentheism. The world is in God, but God is not exhausted by or bound within the world. The guṇas come from God, yet God transcends them.
sources: The identification of God with essential qualities anticipates the *vibhūti* lists of Chapter 10. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* 3.7's "inner controller," who dwells in earth, water and fire but whom they do not know, is a direct antecedent.
context: Compare Thomas Aquinas's doctrine that God is present in all things "by essence, presence and power," and the Islamic mystical idea (associated with Ibn ʿArabī) that the divine names are manifest in creatures. Gerard Manley Hopkins's "The world is charged with the grandeur of God" is a poetic analogue.
matters: The section invites a way of perceiving in which ordinary experiences (water, light, sound) become occasions of recognition. It also suggests that what is best in each thing is where the divine shows itself.
questions: What is gained by identifying God with each thing's "essence" (taste in water, light in sun)?
How does "desire not opposed to dharma" (7.11) qualify the Gītā's critique of desire?
Explain 7.12. How can the guṇas come from God while God is not in them?

sections.title: Māyā, and the four who worship
sections.lead: Deluded by the guṇas and by divine māyā, most do not know God; four kinds of good people worship him, and dearest is the one who knows.
reconstruction: Deluded by the guṇas, the world does not know God, who is beyond them {7.13}. His divine māyā, made of the guṇas, is hard to cross, but those who take refuge in him cross it {7.14}. The wicked and deluded do not take refuge {7.15}. Four kinds of good people worship him: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the knower {7.16}. All are noble, but the knower, ever yoked and singly devoted, is foremost. God is dear to him and he to God, and God regards him as his own self {7.17–18}. After many births the knower realizes that "Vāsudeva is all." Such a great soul is rare {7.19}.
insight: The section introduces grace into the Gītā's soteriology. Māyā is God's power and cannot be crossed by effort alone. It is crossed by taking refuge in God {7.14}. This is the seed of the doctrine of surrender that culminates in 18.66. The typology of worshipers is notably generous. Even those who come out of distress or desire for wealth are called virtuous. Religious motivation need not be pure to be genuine. Yet there is a hierarchy. The knower, who loves God without ulterior motive, is "my very self." The ideal fuses knowledge and love. The highest devotee is a knower, and the highest knowledge is loving.
sources: The doctrine of grace overcoming māyā anticipates *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 4.10 ("know māyā as nature and the great lord as the wielder of māyā") and is developed in the Bhāgavata and Śrīvaiṣṇava traditions.
context: Typologies of religious motivation appear in Bernard of Clairvaux (four degrees of love, from self-interest to love of God for God's sake) and in Gordon Allport's psychology of "extrinsic" and "intrinsic" religiosity. The Gītā's generosity toward imperfect motives is notable by comparison.
matters: The section honors the many reasons people turn to the sacred (fear, curiosity, need) while pointing toward a love that asks for nothing.
questions: Why does the Gītā call the distressed and the wealth-seeker "virtuous" (7.16)?
What does it mean that māyā is God's own power (7.14)?
How do Advaitins and theists read 7.18 ("the knower is my very self")?

sections.title: Other gods, the unmanifest, and knowing God at death
sections.lead: God makes firm the faith of those who worship other gods, but their fruit is finite; the deluded do not know him as unborn; those who take refuge in him know brahman and all its aspects.
reconstruction: Those whose knowledge is carried off by desires worship other gods {7.20}. God makes their faith firm {7.21}, and through it they obtain wishes that he himself grants {7.22}. But the fruit is finite: worshipers of gods go to the gods, while God's devotees come to him {7.23}. The unintelligent think the unmanifest has merely become manifest, not knowing his higher being {7.24}. He is veiled by his yoga-māyā {7.25}. He knows all beings, past, present and future, but no one knows him {7.26}. Bewildered by the pairs of opposites from birth, beings wander {7.27}. Those whose evil has ended, free of delusion, worship him firmly {7.28}. Those who take refuge in him to escape old age and death know brahman, the inner self and all action {7.29}. Knowing him in all his aspects, they know him even at death {7.30}.
insight: The section's treatment of other gods is philosophically intriguing. God is both the *object* of all worship (the wishes are "granted by me alone") and the *guarantor* of other worship ("I make their faith unshakable"). This is inclusivism: other religious paths are real and effective, but their truth is grounded in the one God, and their fruits are limited compared with direct devotion. The closing verses introduce a concern that dominates Chapter 8: knowledge of God at the moment of death. The idea that one's final orientation determines one's destiny connects ethics, devotion and eschatology.
sources: The idea that worship of lesser gods brings finite results is found in *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* 1.4.10 ("whoever worships another deity, thinking 'he is one, I am another,' does not know"). The concern with the moment of death recalls *Chāndogya* 3.14.1 ("as one's resolve is in this world, so one becomes on departing").
context: Karl Rahner's idea of "anonymous Christians," people saved through Christ without knowing it, is a frequently cited parallel to 7.21–22. Critics find both views generous and patronizing at once.
matters: How should a religious tradition regard the sincere worship of others? The Gītā's answer, honoring others' faith while placing it within its own framework, is still the dominant model of inclusive religion.
questions: Is the inclusivism of 7.21–22 respectful of other religions? What would a member of another tradition say?
What does it mean that "no one knows me" (7.26) while God knows all?
Why does the chapter end with knowledge "at the time of death"?
