chapters.colophon: Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the seventh chapter, called “The Yoga of Knowledge and Discernment.”

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Imperishable Brahman

verses.text: What is that brahman? What is the inner self? What is action, Supreme Person? What is it that pertains to beings, and what is said to pertain to the gods?
verses.speaker: Arjuna
fnotes: Arjuna picks up the six terms from 7.29–30 and adds a seventh question: how is God known at death?

verses.text: What pertains to sacrifice, and how is it here in this body, Madhusūdana? And how are you to be known at the time of death by those who are self-controlled?
Brahman is the supreme imperishable [*akṣara*]. Its own nature [*svabhāva*] is called the inner self. The creative outpouring that brings beings into existence is called action.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: *Akṣaraṁ brahma paramam*: "brahman is the supreme imperishable." *Svabhāvo 'dhyātmam*: "its own nature (as present in the individual) is the inner self." *Visargaḥ karma*: "action is the creative outpouring," perhaps alluding to the sacrificial offering that creates beings.

verses.text: What pertains to beings is perishable existence. What pertains to the gods is the Person [*puruṣa*]. What pertains to sacrifice is I myself, here in the body, best of the embodied.
fnotes: *Adhiyajño 'ham evātra dehe*: "what pertains to sacrifice is I myself, here in the body." God is the indwelling recipient of all offerings.

verses.text: Whoever leaves the body at the time of death remembering me alone comes to my state of being. Of this there is no doubt.
fnotes: *Anta-kāle ca mām eva smaran*: "at the time of death, remembering me alone."

verses.text: Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, to that state one goes, son of Kuntī, having always been shaped by it.
fnotes: *Sadā tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ*: "always shaped by that state." The word *bhāvita* suggests long cultivation, so the final thought is not arbitrary.

verses.text: Therefore remember me at all times, and fight. With mind and understanding fixed on me, you will come to me without doubt.
fnotes: *Mām anusmara yudhya ca*: "remember me, and fight." A compact summary of the whole Gītā: devotion and duty together.

verses.text: With thought yoked by the yoga of practice, not straying elsewhere, meditating on the supreme divine Person, Pārtha, one goes to him.
He is the seer, the ancient, the ruler, smaller than the minute, the upholder of all, of unthinkable form, sun-colored, beyond darkness.
fnotes: A cluster of attributes: *kavi* (seer, poet), *purāṇa* (ancient), *anuśāsitṛ* (ruler), *aṇor aṇīyān* (smaller than the minute), *āditya-varṇa* (sun-colored), *tamasaḥ parastāt* (beyond darkness). Several echo *Śvetāśvatara* 3.8 ("I know that great Person, sun-colored, beyond darkness").

verses.text: At the time of departure, one who meditates on him with unmoving mind, yoked with devotion and the power of yoga, and directs the breath fully between the eyebrows, reaches that supreme divine Person.
fnotes: *Bhruvor madhye prāṇam āveśya*: "directing the breath between the eyebrows": a yogic technique of dying.

verses.text: Knowers of the Veda call it the imperishable. Ascetics free of passion enter it, and those who want it practice celibacy. I will tell you of that state briefly.
fnotes: Echoes *Kaṭha* 2.15: "that word which all the Vedas declare… I tell you briefly: it is Om."

verses.text: Close all the gates of the body, confine the mind in the heart, place the breath in the head, and stay established in yogic concentration.
fnotes: *Sarva-dvārāṇi saṁyamya*: "closing all the gates," the nine openings of the body (5.13).

verses.text: Whoever departs this way, leaving the body while uttering Om, the one-syllabled brahman, and remembering me, goes to the supreme goal.
fnotes: *Om ity ekākṣaraṁ brahma*: "Om, the one-syllabled brahman." *Akṣara* means both "syllable" and "imperishable."

verses.text: I am easy to reach, Pārtha, for the yogin who is always yoked and remembers me constantly, never thinking of anything else.
fnotes: *Ananya-cetāḥ satataṁ*: "with thought never on anything else, constantly." God is "easy to reach" (*sulabha*) for such a one.

verses.text: Having come to me, the great selves who have reached supreme perfection do not undergo birth again, that impermanent home of sorrow.
fnotes: Rebirth is *duḥkhālayam aśāśvatam*, "the impermanent home of sorrow."

verses.text: All worlds up to the realm of Brahmā are subject to return, Arjuna. But one who comes to me, son of Kuntī, is not reborn.
fnotes: *Ā-brahma-bhuvanāl lokāḥ punar āvartinaḥ*: "worlds up to the realm of Brahmā return." Even the highest heavens are temporary.

verses.text: People who know that a day of Brahmā lasts a thousand ages [*yuga*], and that his night ends after a thousand ages, truly know day and night.
fnotes: *Sahasra-yuga-paryantam*: a day of Brahmā lasts a thousand yugas. Later Purāṇic computation makes this 4.32 billion human years.

verses.text: At the coming of his day, all manifest things arise from the unmanifest. At the coming of his night, they dissolve into that same unmanifest.
fnotes: *Avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame*: at dawn all manifest things arise from the unmanifest. The "unmanifest" here is cosmic matter (*prakṛti*) in its latent state.

verses.text: This same multitude of beings comes into being again and again. It dissolves helplessly at the coming of night, Pārtha, and arises again at the coming of day.
fnotes: *Bhūta-grāmaḥ sa evāyaṁ bhūtvā bhūtvā pralīyate*: "this same multitude of beings, coming to be again and again, dissolves." *Avaśaḥ*, "helplessly": beings are not free in this cycle.

verses.text: But beyond that unmanifest is another, eternal unmanifest being, which does not perish when all beings perish.
fnotes: *Paras tasmāt tu bhāvo 'nyo 'vyakto 'vyaktāt sanātanaḥ*: "beyond that unmanifest is another, eternal unmanifest." Two levels of the unmanifest are distinguished.

verses.text: This unmanifest is called the imperishable, and they call it the supreme goal. Those who reach it do not return. That is my supreme abode.
fnotes: *Tad dhāma paramaṁ mama*: "that is my supreme abode." The eternal unmanifest is identified with God's dwelling.

verses.text: That supreme Person, Pārtha, in whom beings abide and by whom all this is pervaded, can be reached by exclusive devotion [*bhakti*].
fnotes: *Bhaktyā labhyas tv ananyayā*: "attainable by exclusive devotion." The supreme Person "in whom beings abide" is reached by love.

verses.text: Now, bull of the Bhāratas, I will tell you the times at which departing yogins return or do not return.
Fire, light, day, the bright half of the month, the six months when the sun moves north: those who know brahman and depart then go to brahman.
fnotes: The bright path (*devayāna*, "way of the gods"): fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the sun's northern course. Bhīṣma, in the epic, waits on his bed of arrows for the sun's northward turn before dying.

verses.text: Smoke, night, the dark half of the month, the six months when the sun moves south: the yogin who departs then reaches the light of the moon and returns.
fnotes: The dark path (*pitṛyāna*, "way of the ancestors"): smoke, night, the dark fortnight, the southern course. It leads to the moon and back to rebirth.

verses.text: These two paths, the bright and the dark, are held to be eternal for the world. By one, a person goes and does not return; by the other, a person returns again.
fnotes: *Śukla-kṛṣṇe gatī hy ete*: "these two paths, bright and dark." Note *kṛṣṇa*, "dark," the same word as Kṛṣṇa's name, though no wordplay is clearly intended.

verses.text: No yogin who knows these two paths is deluded, Pārtha. Therefore be yoked in yoga at all times, Arjuna.
fnotes: *Naite sṛtī pārtha jānan yogī muhyati kaścana*: "no yogin who knows these paths is deluded." Knowledge relativizes the cosmology.

verses.text: Merit and its fruit are assigned to the Vedas, to sacrifices, austerities, and gifts. Knowing this teaching, the yogin goes beyond all of it and reaches the supreme, primal place.
fnotes: The yogin goes beyond *all* the merit of Vedas, sacrifices, austerities and gifts.

chapters.summary: Arjuna asks seven questions about brahman, the inner self, action, and how God is known at death. Kṛṣṇa defines the terms, teaches that one becomes what one remembers at the end, and describes the yogin's departure with Om. He explains cosmic time, the days and nights of Brahmā, the imperishable unmanifest beyond them, and the bright and dark paths of the dead.
overview: Chapter 8 is the Gītā's chapter on death and cosmic time. It begins with a technical catechism: Arjuna asks what *brahman*, *adhyātma*, *karma*, *adhibhūta*, *adhidaiva* and *adhiyajña* are, and how God is known at death {8.1–2}. Kṛṣṇa answers briefly {8.3–4}, then turns to his real concern: the moment of death. The central teaching is that "whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body, to that one goes" {8.6}. This might seem to make salvation depend on a last-minute thought. But Kṛṣṇa's conclusion is that one should *always* remember him, while continuing to fight {8.7}. The final thought is the fruit of a whole life's orientation. A description of the yogin's death follows: closing the gates of the body, raising the breath, uttering Om {8.10–13}. The chapter then widens to cosmic scale. Even Brahmā's world is subject to return {8.16}. Cosmic history is a succession of days and nights of Brahmā, each a thousand ages, in which beings emerge and dissolve {8.17–19}. Beyond this cycle is an eternal unmanifest, God's supreme abode, from which there is no return {8.20–21}. It is reached by devotion {8.22}. The chapter closes with the ancient doctrine of the bright and dark paths of the dead {8.23–26}, then relativizes it: the yogin who knows both is not deluded {8.27}.
research: Chapter 8 is a key source for the history of Indian ideas about death and cosmology. The doctrine of the "last thought" (*anta-kāla smaraṇa*) became central in later devotional traditions, notably the practice of chanting the divine name at death, and in Pure Land Buddhism's emphasis on recollecting Amitābha at death, which has interesting parallels. Scholars debate whether the Gītā's version is magical (the final thought alone decides) or ethical (the final thought expresses a life). Kṛṣṇa's "remember me at all times, and fight" {8.7} supports the second reading. The cosmology of 8.16–21, with its days of Brahmā and thousand-yuga cycles, is an early form of the Purāṇic system of *yugas*, *manvantaras* and *kalpas*. The relation between the "two unmanifests" (cosmic matter, and the eternal beyond it) is a point where Sāṅkhya and Vedānta are visibly combined. Historians of religion study the bright and dark paths {8.24–26} as a survival of Upaniṣadic eschatology (*Chāndogya* 5.10). The Gītā's relativization of it in 8.27 suggests a self-conscious distance from older cosmological doctrine.
questions: Does the teaching of 8.6 make salvation depend on a last-minute thought? How does 8.7 change that?
What is the relation between the cosmic unmanifest of 8.18 and the eternal unmanifest of 8.20?
How literally should a modern reader take the cosmology of 8.17–19 and the paths of 8.24–26?
What does it mean to "remember God at all times" while fighting a battle?

sections.title: Seven questions, and remembering God at death
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa defines brahman, the inner self, action and the rest, and teaches that one goes to whatever one remembers at death; therefore remember him always, and fight.
reconstruction: Arjuna asks for definitions and how God is known at death {8.1–2}. Brahman is the supreme imperishable. The inner self is its own nature in the individual. Action is the creative outpouring that brings beings forth {8.3}. What pertains to beings is the perishable, what pertains to the gods is the Person, and what pertains to sacrifice is God himself in the body {8.4}. Whoever dies remembering God goes to God {8.5}. Whatever one remembers at death, one becomes, having been shaped by it all along {8.6}. So remember God at all times, and fight. With mind and understanding fixed on him, Arjuna will reach him {8.7}.
insight: The definitions are terse and have puzzled commentators, but the section's point is clear. It moves from abstract categories to the existential question of death. The doctrine of 8.6 can sound mechanical, as if a final thought were a ticket. But the word *bhāvita* ("shaped, cultivated") and the conclusion of 8.7 show the real teaching. The mind at death is what the mind has become through life. Hence the instruction is not "remember God at death" but "remember God always." The juxtaposition "remember me, and fight" is one of the Gītā's most compressed formulations. Devotion does not replace duty. It is the inner orientation from which duty is done.
sources: *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 3.14.1: "As one's resolve is in this world, so one becomes on departing." *Praśna Upaniṣad* 3.10: "with whatever thought one has at death, one goes to the breath." *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* 4.4.5: "as one acts, as one behaves, so one becomes."
context: The *ars moriendi* ("art of dying") tradition in late medieval Christianity, the Tibetan *Bardo Thödol*, and Pure Land Buddhist practices at the deathbed all share the concern with the dying mind. Montaigne's essay "That to philosophize is to learn to die" offers a secular parallel: a life of reflection prepares the final moment.
matters: Whatever one believes about an afterlife, the teaching that we become what we habitually attend to, and that our final state reveals our life's orientation, is a powerful prompt to examine where our minds dwell.
questions: Does 8.6 describe a cause (the last thought determines destiny) or a sign (the last thought reveals a life)?
What does "remember me, and fight" (8.7) ask of a person in ordinary life?
How do the definitions of 8.3–4 connect the abstract and the personal?

premises.label: Brahman is the imperishable; God is the indweller of sacrifice
premises.text: The technical terms are defined.

premises.label: One goes to what one remembers at death
premises.text: The final state, shaped by life, determines destiny.

claim.label: Remember God always, and fight
claim.text: Devotion and duty together.

implications.label: The final thought is a life's fruit
implications.text: Hence constant remembrance, not deathbed piety.

sections.title: The yogin's departure and the world of no return
sections.lead: The yogin who meditates on the supreme Person and departs with Om reaches the supreme goal; all other worlds, even Brahmā's, are subject to return.
reconstruction: One who meditates on the supreme Person with the yoga of practice goes to him {8.8}. That Person is the ancient seer, the ruler, subtler than the subtle, sun-colored, beyond darkness {8.9}. At death, with steady mind, devotion and yogic power, directing the breath between the brows, one reaches him {8.10}. Kṛṣṇa will tell of the imperishable state that sages enter {8.11}. Closing the body's gates, holding the mind in the heart and the breath in the head {8.12}, uttering Om and remembering God, one goes to the supreme goal {8.13}. But for one who remembers God constantly, he is easy to reach {8.14}. Those who reach him are not reborn into this home of sorrow {8.15}. All other worlds, even Brahmā's, are subject to return; reaching God, there is no rebirth {8.16}.
insight: The section holds together two models of the path. One is the technical yoga of dying, a demanding practice of breath, posture and syllable. The other is the simple constant remembrance of 8.14, which makes God "easy to reach." The juxtaposition is typical of the Gītā. It honors demanding practices while offering a path open to all. The statement that even Brahmā's world is subject to return {8.16} is a radical relativization of heavenly rewards. It places the Gītā's goal outside the whole cosmic system of reward and rebirth.
sources: *Śvetāśvatara* 3.8 and *Kaṭha* 2.15–17 (Om as the imperishable) are direct sources. *Praśna Upaniṣad* 5 teaches meditation on Om as a means to the highest. The yogic technique of departure through the crown of the head appears in *Kaṭha* 6.16 (the artery leading upward).
context: Comparable traditions include the Tibetan practice of *phowa* (transference of consciousness at death), Neoplatonic ascent, and the Hesychast "Jesus Prayer" as continuous remembrance. Contemporary palliative care literature on "good death" shows renewed interest in the dying person's state of mind.
matters: The section asks whether the most important preparation for death is a technique or a habit of the heart, and answers that the second makes the first easy.
questions: What is the difference between the yogic death of 8.12–13 and the constant remembrance of 8.14?
Why does it matter that even Brahmā's world is subject to return (8.16)?
Is "God is easy to reach" (8.14) a comforting or a demanding claim?

premises.label: For the constant rememberer, God is easy to reach
premises.text: A simple path open to all.

sections.title: Cosmic time and the eternal unmanifest
sections.lead: Worlds emerge and dissolve in the days and nights of Brahmā; beyond that cosmic unmanifest is an eternal one, God's supreme abode, reached by devotion.
reconstruction: Those who know that Brahmā's day and night each last a thousand ages know true day and night {8.17}. At his dawn, all manifest things arise from the unmanifest, and at dusk they dissolve back into it {8.18}. The same beings arise and dissolve again and again, helplessly {8.19}. But beyond this unmanifest is another, eternal one, which does not perish when all beings perish {8.20}. It is called the imperishable, the supreme goal. Those who reach it do not return, and it is God's supreme abode {8.21}. That supreme Person, in whom all abides and by whom all is pervaded, is reached by exclusive devotion {8.22}.
insight: The section places human life against an immense backdrop of cosmic time. Its effect is to make all worldly achievement, even cosmic, provisional. Everything that emerges dissolves. Yet the vision is not nihilistic, because it points to a level that does not dissolve: the eternal unmanifest. The distinction between two unmanifests is philosophically important. The first is Sāṅkhya's latent matter, the dormant seed of the world. The second is the transcendent reality beyond the cosmic cycle. The Gītā places God's abode at the second level. Then, characteristically, it says that this transcendent goal is reached not by cosmic knowledge but by devotion {8.22}.
sources: The cosmology of Brahmā's days anticipates the Purāṇic system (*Viṣṇu Purāṇa* 1.3; *Manu* 1.64–74 already has the days and nights of Brahmā). The "two unmanifests" correspond to the *Kaṭha*'s hierarchy, in which the person (*puruṣa*) is higher than the unmanifest (*avyakta*, *Kaṭha* 3.11).
context: Cyclic cosmologies appear in Stoicism (*ekpyrosis*, the periodic conflagration), in Nietzsche's eternal return, and in contemporary cosmological speculation about cyclic universes (e.g., Roger Penrose's "conformal cyclic cosmology"). Carl Sagan noted that Hindu cosmology alone among the great traditions works with timescales comparable to modern cosmology.
matters: Seeing one's life against the scale of cosmic time can be terrifying or freeing. The Gītā uses it to free: to loosen attachment to what passes and orient toward what does not.
questions: What is the effect of placing human life against cosmic cycles of billions of years?
How do the two "unmanifests" (8.18, 8.20) differ?
Why is the eternal goal reached by devotion (8.22) rather than by knowledge of cosmic order?

premises.text: It does not perish with beings.

sections.title: The bright and dark paths
sections.lead: The departed travel either the bright path of no return or the dark path of return; the yogin who knows both is not deluded, and goes beyond all merit.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa will now tell of the times when yogins depart to return or not to return {8.23}. Those who know brahman and depart on the path of fire, light, day, the bright fortnight and the northern course go to brahman {8.24}. Those who depart on the path of smoke, night, the dark fortnight and the southern course reach the lunar light and return {8.25}. These two paths are eternal {8.26}. But the yogin who knows them is not deluded; so be yoked always {8.27}. Knowing this, the yogin goes beyond all the merit of Vedic study, sacrifice, austerity and gift, and reaches the supreme, primal abode {8.28}.
insight: The passage preserves an archaic Upaniṣadic eschatology but subordinates it. The point is not to time one's death auspiciously, though tradition sometimes took it so (as Bhīṣma did). The point is that the yogin who *knows* the cosmic mechanics is free of them. Knowledge and constant yoga, not cosmic timing, decide. The final verse confirms this. The yogin surpasses all the fruits of conventional religion. This is a recurring Gītā strategy. It preserves the older religious world and then relativizes it from a higher standpoint, rather than rejecting it.
sources: *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.10.1–6 and *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* 6.2.15–16 describe the two paths in nearly identical terms. Bhīṣma's waiting for the *uttarāyaṇa* is told in *Mahābhārata* 6.114 and 13.153.
context: Ancient Greek and Egyptian religion also mapped the soul's journey after death through celestial stations. Comparative mythologists (Mircea Eliade) study such "celestial ascents" as a widespread pattern.
matters: The passage models how a tradition can keep its ancient inheritance while placing it in perspective, a lesson for anyone reading old texts today.
questions: Should the bright and dark paths be read literally, symbolically, or as superseded?
What does it mean that knowledge of the paths frees the yogin from delusion (8.27)?
How does 8.28 relate the yogin to the conventional religious life of Veda, sacrifice and gift?

premises.label: The yogin who knows both is not deluded
premises.text: Knowledge frees from cosmic mechanics.

chapters.colophon: Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the eighth chapter, called “The Yoga of the Imperishable Brahman.”

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Royal Knowledge and the Royal Secret

verses.text: Since you do not find fault, I will declare to you this most secret knowledge together with discernment. Knowing it, you will be freed from evil.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord
fnotes: *Anasūyave*, "to you, who do not find fault." The teaching is given to one who listens without cavil.

verses.text: It is royal knowledge, a royal secret [*rāja-vidyā, rāja-guhya*]: the supreme purifier, directly seen, in accord with dharma, very easy to practice, and imperishable.
fnotes: *Rāja-vidyā rāja-guhyam*: "king of knowledges, king of secrets." *Pratyakṣāvagamam*, "directly perceived": unlike speculative doctrines, this can be experienced.

verses.text: People without faith in this dharma, scorcher of foes, do not reach me. They return to the path of death and saṁsāra.
fnotes: *Aśraddadhānāḥ*, "those without faith," return to the path of saṁsāra.

verses.text: This whole world is pervaded by me in my unmanifest form. All beings abide in me, but I do not abide in them.
fnotes: *Mayā tatam idaṁ sarvaṁ jagad avyakta-mūrtinā*: "by me, in my unmanifest form, this whole world is pervaded." *Mat-sthāni sarva-bhūtāni na cāhaṁ teṣv avasthitaḥ*: "all beings rest in me, but I do not rest in them."

verses.text: And yet beings do not abide in me. Behold my sovereign yoga! My self sustains beings and is their source, but it does not abide in them.
fnotes: *Na ca mat-sthāni bhūtāni*: "and yet beings do not rest in me." An intentional paradox, followed by *paśya me yogam aiśvaram*, "behold my sovereign yoga!"

verses.text: The great wind moves everywhere yet always abides in space. In the same way, understand that all beings abide in me.
fnotes: The image of wind in space (*ākāśa*): the wind moves everywhere within space, yet space is not affected by the wind.

verses.text: At the end of a cosmic age [*kalpa*], son of Kuntī, all beings pass into my nature. At the beginning of a cosmic age I send them forth again.
fnotes: *Kalpa-kṣaye*, "at the end of a cosmic age," beings return into God's nature (*prakṛti*); *kalpādau*, "at its beginning," he sends them forth.

verses.text: Resting on my own nature, I send forth again and again this whole multitude of beings, which is helpless under the power of nature.
fnotes: *Prakṛtiṁ svām avaṣṭabhya*: "resting on (or controlling) my own nature." *Avaśam*, "helpless": beings are under the sway of nature.

verses.text: These actions do not bind me, Dhanañjaya. I sit as if indifferent, unattached to those actions.
fnotes: *Udāsīna-vad āsīnam*: "sitting as if indifferent." God is active through nature yet unbound, the model of the non-attached agent.

verses.text: With me as overseer, nature gives birth to the moving and the unmoving. For this reason, son of Kuntī, the world revolves.
fnotes: *Mayādhyakṣeṇa prakṛtiḥ sūyate*: "with me as overseer, nature gives birth." A Sāṅkhya-theistic synthesis: nature acts, God presides.

verses.text: The deluded despise me when I take on a human body. They do not know my higher being as the great lord of beings.
fnotes: *Avajānanti māṁ mūḍhā mānuṣīṁ tanum āśritam*: "the deluded despise me when I take a human body." It is a key verse for the theology of incarnation.

verses.text: Their hopes, their actions, and their knowledge are vain, and they lack insight. They take on the deluding nature of fiends and demons.
But the great selves, Pārtha, rely on the divine nature. Knowing me as the imperishable source of beings, they worship me with minds that do not stray.
fnotes: *Mahātmānaḥ*, "great selves," take refuge in the *daivī prakṛti*, the divine nature, contrasted with the "demonic" nature of 9.12.

verses.text: Always glorifying me, striving with firm vows, bowing to me with devotion, always yoked, they worship me.
Others worship me by offering the sacrifice of knowledge. They worship me as one, as distinct, and as manifold, facing in all directions.
fnotes: *Ekatvena pṛthaktvena bahudhā*: worshiped "as one, as distinct, as manifold." Commentators see here the Advaita (one), Dvaita (distinct) and other modes of worship, all valid.

verses.text: I am the ritual; I am the sacrifice; I am the offering to the ancestors; I am the healing herb. I am the mantra; I am the clarified butter; I am the fire; I am the oblation.
fnotes: *Ahaṁ kratur ahaṁ yajñaḥ*: a litany of ritual terms. *Kratu* is the Vedic rite, *svadhā* the offering to ancestors, *auṣadha* the healing herb, *ājya* clarified butter.

verses.text: I am the father of this world, its mother, its establisher, its grandfather. I am what is to be known, the purifier, the syllable Om, the Ṛg, the Sāman, and the Yajus.
fnotes: *Pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ*: "I am the father of this world, the mother, the establisher, the grandfather." God includes both masculine and feminine roles.

verses.text: I am the goal, the supporter, the lord, the witness, the dwelling, the refuge, the friend. I am the origin, the dissolution, the ground, the treasure-house, the imperishable seed.
fnotes: *Gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt*: "goal, supporter, lord, witness, abode, refuge, friend." Seven terms recited in many devotional settings.

verses.text: I give heat; I hold back the rain and send it forth. I am immortality and death, being and non-being [*sat* and *asat*], Arjuna.
fnotes: *Amṛtaṁ caiva mṛtyuś ca sad asac cāham arjuna*: "immortality and death, being and non-being." God includes the opposites.

verses.text: Knowers of the three Vedas, drinkers of soma purified of evil, worship me with sacrifices and pray for the way to heaven. They reach the pure world of the lord of the gods and enjoy in heaven the divine enjoyments of the gods.
fnotes: *Trai-vidyāḥ*, "knowers of the three Vedas," who drink soma and seek heaven.

verses.text: Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, they enter the world of mortals again when their merit is used up. So those who follow the dharma of the three Vedas, desiring desires, gain only coming and going.
fnotes: *Kṣīṇe puṇye martya-lokaṁ viśanti*: "when merit is used up, they enter the world of mortals." Heaven is like a bank account that runs out.

verses.text: But some people think of no other and worship me alone. They are always yoked, and for them I secure both gain and safekeeping [*yoga-kṣema*].
fnotes: *Yoga-kṣemaṁ vahāmy aham*: "I bring them gain and safekeeping." A promise of divine provision. It is the motto of India's Life Insurance Corporation.

verses.text: Even those who are devoted to other gods and sacrifice to them with faith are in fact sacrificing to me, son of Kuntī, though not according to the rule.
fnotes: *Avidhi-pūrvakam*: worshipers of other gods worship God "not according to the rule," that is, without knowing it.

verses.text: For I am the enjoyer and the lord of all sacrifices. But they do not recognize me in truth, and so they fall.
Those vowed to the gods go to the gods; those vowed to the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who sacrifice to spirits go to the spirits. Those who sacrifice to me come to me.
Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, I accept that offering of devotion from one whose self is pure.
fnotes: *Patraṁ puṣpaṁ phalaṁ toyam*: "a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water." These are the simplest offerings, available to the poorest. The condition is *bhakti* and a pure self.

verses.text: Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer, whatever you give, whatever austerity you perform, son of Kuntī, do it as an offering to me.
fnotes: *Yat karoṣi yad aśnāsi*: "whatever you do, whatever you eat…" It is the devotional form of karma-yoga: all action as offering.

verses.text: In this way you will be freed from the bonds of action and their good and evil fruits. With your self yoked in the yoga of renunciation, you will be freed and come to me.
fnotes: *Saṁnyāsa-yoga-yuktātmā*: "your self yoked by the yoga of renunciation." Offering all to God is the true renunciation.

verses.text: I am the same toward all beings. No one is hateful to me, and no one is dear. But those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I am in them.
fnotes: *Samo 'haṁ sarva-bhūteṣu*: "I am the same toward all beings." It is balanced by *ye bhajanti tu māṁ bhaktyā mayi te teṣu cāpy aham*, "those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I in them."

verses.text: Even if someone of very bad conduct worships me with undivided devotion, that person should be considered good, for he has resolved rightly.
fnotes: *Api cet su-durācāraḥ*: "even if one of very bad conduct" worships with undivided devotion, *sādhur eva sa mantavyaḥ*, "he should be considered good."

verses.text: He quickly becomes a self of dharma and reaches lasting peace. Son of Kuntī, know for certain: my devotee does not perish.
fnotes: *Na me bhaktaḥ praṇaśyati*: "my devotee does not perish." *Kaunteya pratijānīhi*: "know for certain," or "declare it!" Some read it as Kṛṣṇa asking Arjuna to proclaim it.

verses.text: For those who take refuge in me, Pārtha, even those of lowly birth [*pāpa-yonayaḥ*], and women, vaiśyas, and śūdras too, reach the supreme goal.
tnotes: The Sanskrit can be read in two ways. One makes "of lowly birth" a separate group. The other makes it a label for the women, vaiśyas, and śūdras that follow. Many modern readers take the first, more inclusive reading.
fnotes: See the translator's note on *pāpa-yonayaḥ*.

verses.text: How much more, then, pure brāhmaṇas and devoted royal seers! You have come into this impermanent, joyless world, so worship me.
Let your mind be on me; be devoted to me; sacrifice to me; bow down to me. Having yoked your self in this way, with me as your highest aim, you will come to me.
fnotes: *Man-manā bhava mad-bhakto mad-yājī māṁ namaskuru*: repeated at 18.65.

chapters.summary: Kṛṣṇa reveals the "royal secret": all beings rest in him, yet he does not rest in them; he sends forth and withdraws the worlds while remaining unattached. He is the ritual, the father and mother, the goal and the friend. Devotion is the easiest and surest path: whatever is offered with love, even a leaf or water, he accepts; whoever takes refuge in him, of whatever birth, reaches the highest.
overview: Chapter 9 is the heart of the Gītā's devotional theology. Kṛṣṇa calls its teaching "royal knowledge, a royal secret" {9.2}, a knowledge both supreme and directly accessible. The chapter moves in three phases. The first is metaphysical {9.4–10}. God pervades the world in his unmanifest form. All beings rest in him, yet he does not rest in them, "and yet beings do not rest in me" {9.4–5}. These paradoxes express a relation that is neither identity nor separation. God sends forth the worlds at each cosmic dawn and withdraws them, presiding as overseer while nature does the work, and remains unbound {9.7–10}. The second is a hymn of identification {9.16–19}. God is the ritual, the offering, the mantra and the fire. He is father, mother and grandfather of the world, its goal, friend and refuge, being and non-being. Here the Gītā's language becomes liturgical. The third is devotion {9.22–34}. God secures the welfare of those who worship him alone {9.22}. Even worship of other gods reaches him {9.23}. He accepts "a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water" offered with love {9.26}. Everything one does can be offered to him {9.27}. Most radically, God is the same to all, and devotion overrides birth and conduct. The sinner who worships him becomes righteous, and "women, vaiśyas and śūdras" reach the supreme goal {9.30–32}. The chapter ends with the four-fold injunction repeated in 18.65: "Let your mind be on me; be devoted to me; sacrifice to me; bow down to me" {9.34}.
research: Chapter 9's radical statements about devotion transcending birth and conduct {9.30–32} are central to debates about the Gītā's social vision. Historians of bhakti (e.g., John Stratton Hawley, *A Storm of Songs*, 2015) note that later devotional movements drew on these verses to include women and low castes, though the movements' own social effects were mixed. The phrase *pāpa-yonayaḥ* {9.32} remains grammatically and ethically contested. Some take it to brand women, vaiśyas and śūdras as of "sinful birth." Others take it as a separate category, the "lowly born," listed alongside them. The paradoxes of 9.4–5 are a crux in Vedānta. Śaṅkara resolves them by the doctrine of appearance: beings "rest" in God only as illusory appearances, and do not "really" rest in him. Rāmānuja resolves them by the body-soul model. Beings depend on God as body on soul, but God is not dependent on them. Contemporary philosophers of religion have connected these verses to analytic discussions of panentheism (e.g., Philip Clayton, Yujin Nagasawa's work on "modal panentheism").
questions: How can all beings rest in God while God does not rest in them, and also not rest in him (9.4–5)? Which resolution do you find most convincing?
What does it mean to offer "a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water" (9.26)? Why does the value of the gift not matter?
Do 9.30–32 overturn the social hierarchy, or include the excluded while keeping the hierarchy?
Why might the Gītā call this teaching a "secret" when it is so easy to practice?

sections.title: The royal secret: all beings rest in God
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa reveals the supreme secret: he pervades all in his unmanifest form; beings rest in him, yet he does not rest in them.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa will teach Arjuna the most secret knowledge, which frees from evil {9.1}. It is royal knowledge and the royal secret: purifying, directly experienced, righteous, easy and imperishable {9.2}. Those without faith in it return to saṁsāra {9.3}. God pervades the world in his unmanifest form. All beings rest in him, but he does not rest in them {9.4}. And yet beings do not rest in him either. This is his sovereign yoga, for he sustains beings without being contained by them {9.5}. As the wind moves everywhere within space, so beings move within him {9.6}.
insight: The section deliberately frustrates simple metaphysics. If all beings rest in God and God does not rest in them, the relation is asymmetric: dependence without containment. The further claim that beings do not rest in God either pushes toward a mystery. The relation is unlike any spatial containment. The wind-and-space image helps. Space holds the wind without being disturbed or limited by it. God is the "space" in which beings exist, not one of the beings. Calling this a "secret" that is "directly perceived" and "easy" is itself paradoxical. The secret is not hidden information but a way of seeing that, once seen, is simple.
sources: *Īśā Upaniṣad* 1 ("all this is to be pervaded by the Lord") and *Śvetāśvatara* 6.11 ("the one God hidden in all beings, all-pervading") are close sources. The rhetoric of the "secret" (*guhya*) teaching recalls the Upaniṣads' own self-description as *rahasya* (secret).
context: Paradoxical formulations of God's relation to the world appear in Nicholas of Cusa ("God is in all things in such a way that all things are in God"), in the Christian doctrine of God's immanence and transcendence, and in Islamic theology's tension between *tanzīh* (transcendence) and *tashbīh* (likeness). Process theology and contemporary panentheism are modern heirs.
matters: How we picture the relation of the sacred to the world shapes our attitudes to nature, to others and to ourselves. The Gītā's paradox resists both a God far away and a God dissolved into the world.
questions: Why does the Gītā state the relation of God and world as a paradox?
How well does the wind-and-space image (9.6) express the relation?
What makes this teaching "directly perceived" rather than speculative?

sections.title: Sending forth the worlds; the deluded and the great-souled
sections.lead: God sends forth and withdraws the worlds by his nature while remaining unattached; the deluded despise him in human form, the great-souled worship him.
reconstruction: At the end of each age beings enter God's nature, and at the beginning he sends them forth again {9.7}. Resting on his nature, he emits this helpless host again and again {9.8}. These acts do not bind him, for he sits as if indifferent {9.9}. Under his oversight nature produces the moving and unmoving, and the world turns {9.10}. The deluded despise him in human form, not knowing his higher being {9.11}. Their hopes, actions and knowledge are vain {9.12}. The great-souled, resorting to the divine nature, worship him single-mindedly {9.13}. They praise him, strive with firm vows, bow in devotion {9.14}, or worship him through knowledge, as one, as distinct, or as manifold {9.15}.
insight: God in this section is the supreme karma-yogin. He creates and dissolves the cosmos but is not bound, "sitting as if indifferent." The theology thus grounds the ethics of Chapters 2–6: non-attached action is not merely a human technique but an imitation of the divine mode of acting. The verse about despising God "in human form" {9.11} addresses a real scandal. How can the supreme God appear as a charioteer? The Gītā answers that only delusion mistakes the human form for the whole. 9.15's three modes of worship (one, distinct, manifold) show the Gītā's capacity to contain the later disputes of Vedānta within itself.
sources: The cosmic emission and reabsorption follows the Sāṅkhya-Purāṇic cycle (cf. 8.17–19). The divine "overseer" (*adhyakṣa*) appears in *Ṛg Veda* 10.129.7, the Creation Hymn ("he who is its overseer in the highest heaven, he surely knows, or perhaps he does not know").
context: God's non-attached activity can be compared with Aristotle's unmoved mover (who moves without being moved), with Neoplatonic emanation, and with the Christian idea of creation as free, not needed. The scandal of divine humanity (9.11) has parallels in Christian debates about Christ's two natures.
matters: If God acts without attachment, then non-attached action is not an inhuman ideal but participation in the deepest pattern of reality.
questions: How does God's "sitting as if indifferent" (9.9) model the karma-yoga of earlier chapters?
Why is God's human form a stumbling block (9.11)?
What do the three modes of worship in 9.15 suggest about religious diversity?

sections.title: God as ritual, father and goal; the limits of heaven
sections.lead: God is every element of sacrifice and every relation of the world; those who seek heaven through ritual return, while those who worship him alone are secured by him.
reconstruction: God is the rite, the sacrifice, the ancestral offering, the herb, the mantra, the butter, the fire and the oblation {9.16}. He is father, mother, establisher, grandfather, the object of knowledge, the purifier, Om and the Vedas {9.17}. He is goal, supporter, lord, witness, abode, refuge, friend, origin, dissolution, ground, treasure-house and seed {9.18}. He gives heat and rain, and is immortality and death, being and non-being {9.19}. Ritualists who seek heaven go there and enjoy it {9.20}, but when their merit is spent they return {9.21}. Those who worship God alone, ever yoked, he secures in gain and safety {9.22}. Even those who worship other gods with faith worship him, though not according to rule {9.23}, for he is the enjoyer of all sacrifices {9.24}. Each goes to what he worships; God's worshipers come to him {9.25}.
insight: The hymn of 9.16–19 performs a theological transformation. Every element of the Vedic ritual, and every relation of the world, is identified with God. Ritual is not abolished but transfigured. Its true recipient and substance is God. The inclusion of "mother" alongside "father" and of death alongside immortality signals a God beyond human categories. The contrast between heaven-seekers and devotees refines the critique of 2.42–44. Ritual works, but its fruit is finite, a balance that runs out. Devotion is different, because God himself takes responsibility for the devotee's welfare {9.22}. This shifts religion from transaction to relationship.
sources: The identification of God with ritual elements follows the Brāhmaṇas' and Upaniṣads' "equations" (*bandhu*) of ritual and cosmos. *Chāndogya* 5.10.5–6 describes the return from the lunar world when merit is exhausted.
context: Similar litanies of divine names appear in the Psalms ("my rock, my fortress, my deliverer," Psalm 18:2), in the Islamic ninety-nine names of God, and in the Christian litanies. Martin Buber's distinction between relations of use (I–It) and of encounter (I–Thou) illuminates the move from ritual transaction to devotion.
matters: The section asks whether our religious or ethical life is transaction (doing good to gain rewards) or relationship (doing good as an expression of love). Only the second, the Gītā says, does not run out.
questions: What is the effect of identifying God with every element of ritual (9.16)?
Why does the Gītā include "mother" and "death" in its litany of God?
Is the contrast between ritual transaction and devotional relationship (9.20–22) fair to ritual?

sections.title: A leaf, a flower: devotion open to all
sections.lead: God accepts the humblest offering made with love; every act can be offered to him; he is the same to all, and devotion lifts the sinner and the excluded to the highest goal.
reconstruction: Whatever is offered with love, even a leaf, flower, fruit or water, God accepts from a pure heart {9.26}. So offer everything you do, eat, give and endure to him {9.27}. You will be freed from the bonds of action and come to him {9.28}. God is the same to all and favors no one, but those who worship him with love are in him and he in them {9.29}. Even the worst sinner who worships him single-mindedly should be considered good, for his resolve is right {9.30}. He soon becomes righteous and finds peace, and God's devotee never perishes {9.31}. All who take refuge in him, even those of low birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras, reach the highest {9.32}. How much more the pure brāhmaṇas and royal sages! Having come into this transient, joyless world, worship God {9.33}. Fix your mind on him, be devoted, sacrifice to him and bow to him, and you will come to him {9.34}.
insight: The section is the Gītā's most egalitarian, and also among its most contested. Its central claim is that devotion is decisive and that its condition is love, not wealth, learning, birth or even prior righteousness. A leaf is enough. A sinner who turns to God is good. Those excluded from Vedic learning reach the highest. Two tensions are worth weighing. First, God is "the same to all" yet "in" his devotees. Impartiality and special love seem to conflict. The tradition's answer is that God's love is offered equally, but only those who turn toward it receive it, as sunlight falls on all but warms only those who stand in it. Second, the inclusion of women and śūdras is framed in a hierarchical vocabulary ("how much more the brāhmaṇas…"). The verse is liberating in content and conservative in form. Honest reading must register both.
sources: The offering of simple items (*pūjā*) became the template of Hindu home and temple worship. The *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* develops 9.26 into famous stories (e.g., Kṛṣṇa's friend Sudāmā offering flattened rice).
context: Parallels include the widow's mite (Mark 12:41–44), in which the smallest gift given wholly is the greatest. Another is the Christian doctrine of grace for sinners, and the Pure Land Buddhist teaching that Amida saves even the wicked (Shinran: "if even a good person is saved, how much more a wicked one"). Shinran's inversion is striking beside 9.33's "how much more the brāhmaṇas."
matters: The section affirms that the deepest religious and ethical life is open to everyone, whatever their resources or past, and that what counts is the love with which one acts.
questions: Why does the value of the offering not matter (9.26)? What does matter?
How can God be "the same to all" yet especially present in devotees (9.29)?
Compare 9.30–33 with Shinran's "how much more a wicked person." Which inversion is more radical?
How should a modern reader handle the hierarchical framing of 9.32–33?

chapters.colophon: Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the ninth chapter, called “The Yoga of the Royal Knowledge and the Royal Secret.”

chapters.title: The Yoga of Divine Manifestations

verses.text: Once again, mighty-armed one, hear my supreme word. You take delight in it, and I will speak it to you because I wish for your good.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin, for in every way I am the source of the gods and the great seers.
One who knows me as unborn and without beginning, the great lord of the world, is undeluded among mortals and freed from all evils.
Understanding, knowledge, freedom from delusion, patience, truth, self-restraint, calm, pleasure and pain, existence and non-existence, fear and fearlessness,
non-harming [*ahiṁsā*], equanimity, contentment, austerity, generosity, fame and infamy: these various states of beings come from me alone.
The seven great seers of old and the four Manus came from my mind and share my nature. From them come these creatures in the world.
One who knows in truth this extended power [*vibhūti*] and yoga of mine is yoked by unwavering yoga. Of this there is no doubt.
I am the origin of all, and from me everything proceeds. Knowing this, the wise worship me, filled with love [*bhāva*].
With their thoughts on me and their lives given to me, they enlighten one another and always speak of me. They are content and full of delight.
To those who are always yoked and worship me with love, I give the yoga of understanding by which they come to me.
Out of compassion for them, abiding in their own being, I destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.
You are the supreme brahman, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier: the eternal divine Person, the first god, unborn and all-pervading.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: So all the seers say of you, and the divine seer Nārada, Asita Devala, and Vyāsa. And you yourself tell me so.
I hold all that you tell me to be true, Keśava. Neither the gods nor the demons, Blessed One, know your manifestation.
You alone know yourself by yourself, Supreme Person: source of beings, lord of beings, god of gods, lord of the world.
Tell me fully of your divine extended powers, by which you pervade these worlds and abide in them.
How may I know you, yogin, through constant meditation? In what forms of being should I meditate on you, Blessed One?
Tell me again in detail of your yoga and extended power, Janārdana. I never tire of hearing your nectar.
Very well. I will tell you of my divine extended powers, best of Kurus, but only the principal ones, for there is no end to my extent.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: I am the self, Guḍākeśa, abiding in the heart of all beings. I am the beginning, the middle, and the end of beings.
Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among lights, the radiant sun. I am Marīci among the Maruts, and among the stars I am the moon.
Among the Vedas I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods, Indra. Among the senses I am the mind, and in beings I am consciousness [*cetanā*].
Among the Rudras I am Śaṅkara; among yakṣas and rākṣasas, Kubera, lord of wealth. Among the Vasus I am fire, and among mountains, Meru.
Among household priests, Pārtha, know me as the chief, Bṛhaspati. Among generals I am Skanda; among bodies of water, the ocean.
Among the great seers I am Bhṛgu; among utterances, the single syllable [Om]. Among sacrifices I am the sacrifice of murmured prayer [*japa*]; among immovable things, the Himālaya.
Among all trees I am the aśvattha [sacred fig]; among divine seers, Nārada. Among gandharvas I am Citraratha; among the perfected, the sage Kapila.
Among horses know me as Uccaiḥśravas, born of the nectar; among lordly elephants, Airāvata; and among men, the king.
Among weapons I am the thunderbolt; among cows, the wish-granting cow. I am Kandarpa [Love], who begets; among serpents I am Vāsuki.
Among nāgas I am Ananta; among water-beings, Varuṇa. Among the ancestors I am Aryaman; among those who restrain, Yama.
Among the daityas I am Prahlāda; among those who reckon, I am time. Among beasts I am the lion; among birds, Garuḍa, son of Vinatā.
Among purifiers I am the wind; among those who bear arms, Rāma. Among sea-creatures I am the makara; among rivers, the Gaṅgā.
Of creations I am the beginning, the end, and the middle, Arjuna. Among sciences I am the science of the self; in those who debate, I am the reasoning.
Among letters I am the letter A; among compounds, the copulative compound [*dvandva*]. I am imperishable time; I am the establisher, facing in all directions.
I am all-seizing death and the origin of all that is to come. Among feminine powers I am fame, fortune, speech, memory, intelligence, steadfastness, and patience.
tnotes: These seven nouns are feminine in Sanskrit, and each is also a goddess.

verses.text: Among chants I am the Bṛhat-sāman; among meters, the gāyatrī. Among months I am Mārgaśīrṣa; among seasons, the flowering spring.
I am the gambling of cheats and the splendor of the splendid. I am victory, I am resolve, I am the goodness [*sattva*] of the good.
Among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, Dhanañjaya. Among sages I am Vyāsa; among poets, the poet Uśanas.
I am the rod of those who punish and the statecraft of those who seek victory. I am the silence of secret things and the knowledge of those who know.
Whatever is the seed of all beings, that I am, Arjuna. No being, moving or unmoving, could exist without me.
There is no end to my divine extended powers, scorcher of foes. What I have said of their extent is only a set of examples.
Whatever being has power, splendor, or vigor, understand that it arises from a fraction of my brilliance.
But what use is all this detailed knowledge to you, Arjuna? I stand supporting this whole world with a single fraction of myself.

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Vision of the Universal Form

verses.text: As a favor to me, you have spoken the supreme secret called the inner self [*adhyātma*]. Through these words of yours my delusion is gone.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: For I have heard from you in detail, lotus-eyed one, of the arising and passing away of beings, and of your imperishable greatness.
It is just as you have described yourself, supreme lord. Now, Supreme Person, I wish to see your sovereign form.
If you think it possible for me to see it, Lord, lord of yoga, then show me your imperishable self.
Behold, Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and thousands: various, divine, of many colors and shapes.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts. Behold many wonders never seen before, Bhārata.
Behold today the whole world, moving and unmoving, standing as one here in my body, Guḍākeśa, and whatever else you wish to see.
But you cannot see me with this eye of yours. I give you a divine eye. Behold my sovereign yoga!
Having spoken thus, O king, Hari, the great lord of yoga, showed Pārtha his supreme sovereign form.
verses.speaker: Sañjaya

verses.text: It had many mouths and eyes and many wondrous sights, many divine ornaments and many divine weapons raised.
It wore divine garlands and garments and was anointed with divine perfumes: the infinite god, all-wondrous, facing in all directions.
If the light of a thousand suns were to rise at once in the sky, it might be like the light of that great self.
There, in the body of the god of gods, Pāṇḍava saw the whole world, divided in many ways, standing as one.
Then Dhanañjaya, filled with amazement and with his hair standing on end, bowed his head to the god, joined his palms, and said:
O God, I see in your body the gods and all the hosts of beings: Brahmā the lord, seated on the lotus, and all the seers and divine serpents.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: I see you on every side, endless in form, with countless arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes. I see no end of you, no middle, and no beginning, lord of all, whose form is the universe.
I see you wearing a crown and bearing a mace and discus, a mass of brilliance shining everywhere. You are hard to look at, blazing on all sides like burning fire and sun, beyond measure.
You are the imperishable, the supreme thing to be known. You are the final resting place of all this. You are the undying guardian of eternal dharma. You are the ancient Person, I believe.
I see you without beginning, middle, or end, of infinite power and countless arms, with moon and sun as eyes and blazing fire as mouth, burning this whole world with your radiance.
The space between heaven and earth and all the directions are filled by you alone. Seeing this wondrous and terrible form of yours, great self, the three worlds tremble.
These hosts of gods enter into you. Some, terrified, praise you with joined palms. Crying "Hail!", the hosts of great seers and the perfected praise you with abundant hymns.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts, and the ancestors, and the hosts of gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras, and the perfected all gaze at you in amazement.
Your form is great, mighty-armed one, with many mouths and eyes, many arms, thighs, and feet, many bellies, terrible with many tusks. Seeing it, the worlds tremble, and so do I.
You touch the sky, blazing and many-colored, with gaping mouths and huge blazing eyes. Seeing you, Viṣṇu, my innermost self trembles, and I find no steadiness or peace.
Seeing your mouths, terrible with tusks, like the fire of time [*kāla*] at the world's end, I lose all sense of direction and find no refuge. Be gracious, lord of gods, home of the world!
And all these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with hosts of kings, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a charioteer [Karṇa], together with our own chief warriors,
are rushing into your terrible mouths with their fearsome tusks. Some are seen caught between your teeth, their heads crushed.
As the many rushing torrents of rivers race toward the ocean, so these heroes of the human world enter your blazing mouths.
As moths rush with great speed into a blazing fire to their destruction, so these worlds rush with great speed into your mouths to their destruction.
Devouring all the worlds on every side with your flaming mouths, you lick your lips. Your terrible rays fill the whole world with brilliance and scorch it, Viṣṇu.
Tell me who you are, with so terrible a form. Homage to you, best of gods; be gracious! I want to understand you, the primal one, for I do not understand what you are doing.
I am time [*kāla*], the mighty destroyer of worlds, set in motion here to annihilate the worlds. Even without you, all these warriors drawn up in the opposing ranks will cease to be.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Therefore stand up and win glory. Conquer your enemies and enjoy a prosperous kingdom. I have already slain them. Be merely the instrument [*nimitta-mātra*], left-handed archer.
Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Jayadratha, Karṇa, and the other heroic warriors are already slain by me. Kill them, and do not waver. Fight! You will conquer your rivals in battle.
Hearing these words of Keśava, the crowned one [Arjuna], trembling, joined his palms and bowed down. Overwhelmed with fear, he bowed again and spoke to Kṛṣṇa in a faltering voice:
verses.speaker: Sañjaya

verses.text: It is right, Hṛṣīkeśa, that the world rejoices and delights in praising you. The demons flee in terror in all directions, and all the hosts of the perfected bow down to you.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: And why should they not bow to you, great self? You are greater even than Brahmā, the first creator. Infinite lord of gods, home of the world, you are the imperishable: being and non-being, and what is beyond both.

You are the first god, the ancient Person, the supreme resting place of this world. You are the knower and what is to be known, and the supreme abode. The world is pervaded by you, whose form is infinite.
You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, and the moon; you are Prajāpati and the great-grandfather. Homage, homage to you a thousand times, and again and yet again homage to you!
Homage to you in front and behind, homage to you on every side, you who are all. Your valor is infinite and your might is immeasurable. You encompass everything, so you are everything.
I thought of you as a friend, and spoke rashly: "O Kṛṣṇa, O Yādava, O friend." I did not know this greatness of yours, and spoke from carelessness or from affection.
If I showed you disrespect in jest, at play, lying down, sitting, or eating, whether alone or before others, Acyuta, I ask forgiveness of you, the immeasurable one.

You are the father of the world, of all that moves and does not move. You are its object of worship and its most venerable teacher. No one equals you in the three worlds; how could anyone surpass you, whose power is beyond compare?
So I bow down and lay my body before you, and seek your grace, praiseworthy Lord. Bear with me, O God, as a father with a son, a friend with a friend, a lover with the beloved.
I am thrilled to have seen what was never seen before, yet my mind is shaken with fear. Show me that other form of yours, O God. Be gracious, lord of gods, home of the world.
I want to see you as before, wearing your crown, with mace and discus in hand. Take on that four-armed form, thousand-armed one, whose form is the universe.
By my grace, Arjuna, through my own yoga, I have shown you this supreme form. It is made of brilliance, universal, infinite, and primal, and no one but you has seen it before.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Not through the Vedas, sacrifices, or study, not through gifts or rites or fierce austerities, can anyone but you in the human world see me in this form, hero of the Kurus.
Do not be afraid or bewildered at seeing this terrible form of mine. Free of fear and with a glad mind, behold again this form of mine.
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva showed his own form again. Taking on his gentle form once more, the great self consoled the frightened Arjuna.
verses.speaker: Sañjaya

verses.text: Seeing this gentle human form of yours, Janārdana, I am now composed and have returned to my own nature.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: This form of mine that you have seen is very hard to see. Even the gods always long to see it.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Not through the Vedas, austerity, gifts, or sacrifice can I be seen as you have seen me.
But through undivided devotion, Arjuna, I can be known in this way, seen in truth, and entered, scorcher of foes.
One who does my work, who holds me as highest, who is devoted to me, free of attachment and without hostility toward any being, comes to me, Pāṇḍava.

chapters.title: The Yoga of Devotion

verses.text: Some devotees, always yoked, worship you in this way. Others worship the imperishable, the unmanifest. Which of these know yoga better?
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: Those who fix their minds on me and worship me, always yoked and endowed with supreme faith, I consider the most fully yoked.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: But there are also those who worship the imperishable, which cannot be defined: the unmanifest, all-pervading and unthinkable, unchanging [*kūṭa-stha*], unmoving and constant.
They restrain all the senses, are equal-minded toward everything, and delight in the welfare of all beings. They too reach me.
The struggle is greater for those whose thought is fixed on the unmanifest, for the goal of the unmanifest is hard for the embodied to reach.
But others surrender all actions in me and are intent on me. They meditate on me and worship me with undivided yoga.
Their thought has entered into me, Pārtha, and I soon become their deliverer from the ocean of death and saṁsāra.
Place your mind in me alone, and let your understanding enter into me. From then on you will dwell in me alone. Of this there is no doubt.
But if you cannot fix your thought firmly on me, then seek to reach me through the yoga of practice, Dhanañjaya.
If you are not capable even of practice, devote yourself to doing work for my sake. Even by doing actions for my sake you will reach perfection.
If you cannot do even this, then rely on my yoga, control yourself, and give up the fruit of all actions.
Knowledge is better than practice. Meditation is better than knowledge. Giving up the fruit of action is better than meditation, and from giving it up, peace follows at once.
One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, without "mine" and without I-making, the same in pain and pleasure, and patient,
always content, a yogin, self-controlled and firm in resolve, with mind and understanding offered to me: that devotee of mine is dear to me.
One from whom the world does not shrink and who does not shrink from the world, free from elation, impatience, fear, and agitation, is dear to me.
One who expects nothing, who is pure and capable, impartial and free of anxiety, who has given up all ambitious undertakings: that devotee of mine is dear to me.
One who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has given up both good and bad and is full of devotion, is dear to me.
One who is the same toward enemy and friend, in honor and dishonor, the same in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, free from attachment,
who treats blame and praise alike, who is silent and content with whatever comes, without a fixed home, steady-minded, and full of devotion: that person is dear to me.
But those devotees who, full of faith and holding me as highest, follow this nectar of dharma as I have taught it are exceedingly dear to me.

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Field and the Knower of the Field

verses.text: This body, son of Kuntī, is called the field [*kṣetra*]. Those who know it call the one who knows it the knower of the field [*kṣetrajña*].
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Know that I am the knower of the field in all fields, Bhārata. Knowledge of the field and of the knower of the field is what I hold to be true knowledge.
Hear from me briefly what the field is and what it is like, what its changes are and where it comes from, and who the knower is and what powers he has.
Seers have sung of this in many ways and in various distinct hymns, and in the reasoned, conclusive words of the Brahma-sūtras.
The great elements, I-making, understanding, and the unmanifest; the ten senses and the one [the mind]; the five domains of the senses;
desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the bodily whole, awareness, and steadfastness: this, in brief, is the field with its changes.
Absence of pride, absence of deceit, non-harming, patience, uprightness, service to the teacher, purity, steadiness, self-restraint;
dispassion toward sense objects, absence of I-making, seeing clearly the evil of birth, death, old age, sickness, and pain;
non-attachment, not clinging to son, wife, home, and the like, and constant evenness of mind whether the wanted or the unwanted comes;
unwavering devotion to me through undivided yoga, resort to solitary places, distaste for crowds;
constancy in knowledge of the inner self, and insight into the aim of the knowledge of truth: this is called knowledge. What is contrary to it is ignorance.
I will declare what is to be known, knowing which one reaches immortality: the beginningless supreme brahman, which is said to be neither being nor non-being.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and mouths everywhere, with ears everywhere, it stands enveloping everything in the world.
It seems to have the qualities of all the senses, yet it is free of all the senses. It is unattached, yet it supports all. It is free of the guṇas, yet it experiences the guṇas.
It is outside and inside beings, unmoving and moving. It is too subtle to be known. It is far away, and it is near.
It is undivided, yet it seems to be divided among beings. It is to be known as the one who sustains beings, devours them, and brings them forth.
It is the light of lights, said to be beyond darkness. It is knowledge, what is to be known, and what knowledge reaches, seated in the heart of all.
So the field, knowledge, and what is to be known have been briefly described. My devotee who understands this enters into my state of being.
Know that nature [*prakṛti*] and person [*puruṣa*] are both beginningless, and that the changes and the guṇas arise from nature.
Nature is said to be the cause of effect, instrument, and agency. The person is said to be the cause of the experience of pleasure and pain.
For the person, situated in nature, experiences the guṇas born of nature. Attachment to the guṇas causes its births in good and evil wombs.
The supreme person in this body is called the witness, the one who consents, the supporter, the experiencer, the great lord, and the supreme self.
One who knows the person, and nature together with the guṇas, in this way is not born again, however one may live.
Some see the self in the self by the self through meditation; others through the yoga of Sāṅkhya; and others through the yoga of action.
Yet others, not knowing this, hear it from others and worship. Devoted to what they have heard, they too cross beyond death.
Whatever being comes into existence, moving or unmoving, know, bull of the Bhāratas, that it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field.
One who sees the supreme lord abiding equally in all beings, not perishing when they perish, truly sees.
Seeing the same lord established everywhere, one does not harm the self by the self, and so goes to the supreme goal.
One who sees that all actions are done by nature alone, and that the self is therefore not the doer, truly sees.
When one sees the separate existence of beings as resting in the One, and their unfolding from that One alone, one reaches brahman.
Because it is beginningless and free of the guṇas, this imperishable supreme self neither acts nor is tainted, son of Kuntī, even though it dwells in the body.
Space pervades everything yet is not tainted, because it is so subtle. In the same way the self, dwelling everywhere in the body, is not tainted.
As the one sun lights up this whole world, so the lord of the field lights up the whole field, Bhārata.
Those who, with the eye of knowledge, know this difference between the field and the knower of the field, and know the release of beings from nature, go to the supreme.
tnotes: Some manuscripts open this chapter with an extra verse (Arjuna's question about nature, person, field, and knower), which would make it 35 verses. The standard numbering, used here, leaves that verse out.

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Three Guṇas

verses.text: I will declare again the supreme knowledge, the highest of all knowledge. Knowing it, all the sages have gone from here to supreme perfection.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Relying on this knowledge, they have come to share my nature. They are not born at the creation of the world, and they are not disturbed at its dissolution.
My womb is the great brahman [here, primal nature]. In it I place the seed, and from that, Bhārata, all beings come to be.
Whatever forms arise in any womb, son of Kuntī, the great brahman is their womb, and I am the father who gives the seed.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas, the guṇas born of nature, bind the imperishable embodied one in the body, mighty-armed one.
Of these, sattva is stainless, so it gives light and is free of disorder. It binds by attachment to happiness and attachment to knowledge, sinless one.
Know that rajas is passion in nature, arising from craving and attachment. It binds the embodied one, son of Kuntī, by attachment to action.
But know that tamas is born of ignorance and deludes all embodied beings. It binds by negligence, laziness, and sleep, Bhārata.
Sattva attaches one to happiness and rajas to action, Bhārata. But tamas covers knowledge and attaches one to negligence.
Sattva arises by overpowering rajas and tamas, Bhārata. Rajas arises by overpowering sattva and tamas. In the same way, tamas arises by overpowering sattva and rajas.
When the light of knowledge shines through all the gates of this body, then know that sattva has grown strong.
Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and longing arise when rajas has grown strong, bull of the Bhāratas.
Darkness, inactivity, negligence, and delusion arise when tamas has grown strong, joy of the Kurus.
When the embodied one dies while sattva prevails, it reaches the stainless worlds of those who know the highest.
Dying in rajas, one is born among those attached to action. Dying in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.
The fruit of good action is said to be pure and of the nature of sattva. The fruit of rajas is pain, and the fruit of tamas is ignorance.
Knowledge arises from sattva and greed from rajas. Negligence and delusion arise from tamas, and ignorance too.
Those established in sattva go upward. Those of rajas stay in the middle. Those of tamas, living by the lowest guṇa, go downward.
When the seer sees no doer other than the guṇas and knows what is beyond the guṇas, he comes to my state of being.
Going beyond these three guṇas, from which the body arises, the embodied one is freed from birth, death, old age, and sorrow, and reaches immortality.
By what marks, Lord, is one known who has gone beyond these three guṇas? How does that person live, and how does he go beyond the three guṇas?
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: One who does not hate light, activity, or delusion when they arise, Pāṇḍava, and does not long for them when they cease;
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: who sits as if indifferent and is not disturbed by the guṇas; who knows "it is only the guṇas moving" and stands firm without wavering;

who is the same in pain and pleasure, abiding in the self, to whom a clod, a stone, and gold are the same; who is equal toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, steadfast, equal toward blame and praise;
who is equal in honor and dishonor, equal toward friend and foe, and has given up all ambitious undertakings: that one is said to have gone beyond the guṇas.
And one who serves me with the unwavering yoga of devotion goes beyond these guṇas and is fit to become brahman.
For I am the foundation [*pratiṣṭhā*] of brahman, of the immortal and imperishable, of eternal dharma, and of absolute happiness.

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Supreme Person

verses.text: They speak of an imperishable aśvattha tree with its roots above and its branches below. Its leaves are the Vedic hymns. One who knows it knows the Veda.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Its branches spread below and above, nourished by the guṇas, with sense objects as their shoots. And below, its roots stretch out, binding people to action in the human world.
Its form cannot be perceived here, nor its end, nor its beginning, nor its foundation. Cut down this firmly rooted aśvattha with the strong axe of non-attachment.
Then seek that place from which those who go there never return, thinking: "I take refuge in that primal Person from whom the ancient stream of activity flowed forth."

Without pride or delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, always devoted to the inner self, with desires turned away and freed from the pairs called pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable place.
Neither sun nor moon nor fire lights it. Those who go there do not return. That is my supreme abode.
A fragment of me, becoming an eternal living being [*jīva*] in the world of the living, draws to itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which rest in nature.
When the lord takes on a body and when he leaves it, he takes these with him and goes, as the wind carries scents from their sources.
Presiding over hearing, sight, touch, taste, and smell, and over the mind, he enjoys the objects of the senses.
The deluded do not see him departing, staying, or enjoying, joined with the guṇas. Those with the eye of knowledge see him.
Yogins who strive see him established in themselves. But those whose selves are unformed and who lack insight do not see him, even when they strive.
The brilliance in the sun that lights up the whole world, the brilliance in the moon and in fire: know that this brilliance is mine.
Entering the earth, I sustain beings with my vigor. Becoming soma, the essence of sap, I nourish all plants.
Becoming the digestive fire, I dwell in the bodies of living beings. Joined with the in-breath and out-breath, I digest the four kinds of food.
I am seated in the heart of all. From me come memory and knowledge, and their loss. I am what is to be known through all the Vedas. I am the maker of the Vedānta, and I am the knower of the Veda.
There are two persons in this world: the perishable [*kṣara*] and the imperishable [*akṣara*]. The perishable is all beings. The imperishable is called the unchanging one [*kūṭa-stha*].
But there is another, the highest person, called the supreme self. As the imperishable lord, he enters the three worlds and sustains them.
Because I am beyond the perishable and higher even than the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person [*puruṣottama*].
One who is undeluded and knows me in this way as the Supreme Person knows all, and worships me with one's whole being, Bhārata.
So I have declared this most secret teaching, sinless one. Understanding it, one becomes wise and has done all that needs to be done, Bhārata.
